topics.name: Nomenclature and Structure of the Carbonyl Group in Aldehydes and Ketones
topics.summary: Aldehydes are named with the suffix '-al' (e.g. ethanal) and ketones with '-one' (e.g. propan-2-one), replacing the '-e' of the parent alkane; an aldehyde's carbonyl carbon is always C1, while a ketone's carbonyl locant is chosen to be as low as possible. Common names (formaldehyde, acetone, acetophenone, benzaldehyde) remain widely used alongside IUPAC names. The carbonyl carbon is sp² hybridised, trigonal planar, with bond angles near 120°, using three sigma bonds plus one unhybridised p orbital that forms the C=O pi bond with oxygen. Because oxygen is more electronegative, the C=O bond is strongly polarised: carbon carries a partial positive charge (δ+) and oxygen a partial negative charge (δ−). This polarisation is the single most important structural fact in the chapter — it is why the carbonyl carbon is electrophilic and attacked by nucleophiles, and why the oxygen's lone pairs let carbonyl compounds accept hydrogen bonds. When a molecule has more than one functional group, IUPAC's seniority order (carboxylic acid > ... > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol) decides which is cited as the suffix and which becomes a prefix.
key_formulas: Carbonyl carbon hybridisation: sp², ~120° bond angles
topics.worked_example: Name CH₃−CH₂−CO−CH₃: the longest chain has 4 carbons with the carbonyl at C2 (giving the lower of the two possible locants, 2 vs. 3); replacing '-e' with '-one' and citing the locant gives butan-2-one.
common_mistakes: Confusing which suffix ('-al' vs. '-one') belongs to aldehydes and which to ketones, or applying '-oic acid' or '-ol' to a plain carbonyl compound.
Assuming the carbonyl carbon is sp³ (tetrahedral) or sp (linear) rather than correctly identifying it as sp² (trigonal planar).
Reversing the C=O polarisation (treating carbon as δ− and oxygen as δ+), which would incorrectly predict the carbon is nucleophilic rather than electrophilic.

topics.name: Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
topics.summary: Aldehydes and ketones are built from several starting points. Controlled oxidation of alcohols is central: PCC (mild, anhydrous) stops a primary alcohol at the aldehyde; a secondary alcohol oxidises to a ketone. From acid chlorides, Rosenmund reduction (H₂ over Pd poisoned with BaSO₄) stops cleanly at the aldehyde, while Gilman reagents (R′₂CuLi) add just once to give a ketone. From nitriles, Stephen reduction (SnCl₂/HCl) or low-temperature DIBAL-H both stop at the aldehyde via a stable intermediate that only releases the aldehyde on hydrolysis; full hydride reduction over-reduces to the amine. Aromatic aldehydes are made directly on the ring by the Gatterman−Koch reaction (CO/HCl, anhydrous AlCl₃/CuCl); aromatic ketones by Friedel−Crafts acylation (RCOCl/AlCl₃) — both fail on strongly deactivated rings. Ozonolysis of an alkene (O₃, then Zn/H₂O) cleaves C=C into two carbonyl fragments, aldehyde from a =CH− carbon and ketone from a fully substituted =C< carbon. Markovnikov hydration of an alkyne (dil. H₂SO₄/HgSO₄) gives a ketone (or, uniquely for ethyne, acetaldehyde) via an unstable enol that tautomerises.
key_formulas: RC≡N --DIBAL-H, low T, then H₂O--> RCHO
topics.worked_example: Ozonolysis (O₃, then Zn/H₂O) of 2-methylbut-2-ene, (CH₃)₂C=CH−CH₃: the disubstituted carbon gives acetone, (CH₃)₂C=O, and the monosubstituted carbon gives acetaldehyde, CH₃CHO.
common_mistakes: Using a strong, uncontrolled hydride (LiAlH₄) or an unpoisoned hydrogenation catalyst where a controlled, stop-at-the-aldehyde method (PCC, Rosenmund, DIBAL-H at low temperature) was actually needed, over-reducing past the aldehyde stage.

Attempting Friedel−Crafts acylation or Gatterman−Koch formylation on a strongly deactivated (e.g. nitro-substituted) aromatic ring, not recognising that both require a sufficiently electron-rich ring to generate the necessary electrophile−ring interaction.
Forgetting that ozonolysis needs a REDUCTIVE workup (Zn/H₂O) to stop at the carbonyl stage; an oxidative workup would push any resulting aldehyde fragment further to a carboxylic acid.

topics.name: Physical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones
topics.summary: The polar C=O group gives aldehydes and ketones dipole−dipole attractions between their own molecules, so they boil higher than non-polar alkanes of similar mass. But carbonyl compounds have no O−H (or N−H) bond of their own, so they cannot hydrogen-bond to each other, and their boiling points fall below alcohols of comparable mass, which do form such hydrogen bonds. Carboxylic acids (covered in later topics) go a step further, forming strong, cyclic hydrogen-bonded dimers, giving them the highest boiling points of the three classes at comparable mass. Despite lacking O−H themselves, aldehydes and ketones CAN accept hydrogen bonds from water through their carbonyl oxygen's lone pairs, which is why the lower members (formaldehyde, acetaldehyde, acetone) are appreciably soluble in water; solubility falls off as the hydrocarbon chain lengthens and the non-polar portion of the molecule comes to dominate. Molecular size also matters independently through dispersion forces — a larger carbonyl compound of otherwise comparable polarity boils higher than a much smaller one, which is why formaldehyde is a gas at room temperature but acetone is a liquid.
key_formulas: Boiling point order (comparable mass): alkane < aldehyde/ketone < alcohol < carboxylic acid
Solubility in water: via H-bond ACCEPTANCE at the carbonyl oxygen, decreasing with chain length
topics.worked_example: Rank butanal, butan-1-ol, and pentane by boiling point: pentane (dispersion only) is lowest, butanal (dipole−dipole, no O−H) is next, and butan-1-ol (hydrogen bonding via O−H) is highest: pentane < butanal < butan-1-ol.
common_mistakes: Assuming aldehydes/ketones can hydrogen-bond to their OWN molecules the way alcohols do, since both classes contain oxygen; only the O−H bond in an alcohol (or the O−H/N−H in other classes) permits that specific interaction.

Ranking boiling points using molecular mass/size alone and ignoring the type of intermolecular force available, leading to a swapped order between, say, a larger carbonyl compound and a smaller alcohol.

Concluding that because a carbonyl compound cannot hydrogen-bond to itself, it also cannot dissolve well in water; the carbonyl oxygen's lone pairs can still ACCEPT a hydrogen bond from water even though the molecule has no O−H of its own to donate.

topics.name: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
topics.summary: Because the carbonyl carbon is electrophilic, nucleophiles attack it directly, pushing the C=O pi electrons onto oxygen to give a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, which is then typically protonated. Reactivity depends on both sterics and electronics at that carbon: aldehydes (one small substituent, at most an H) are more reactive than ketones (two alkyl/aryl substituents), since fewer/smaller groups mean less steric blocking of the incoming nucleophile and less electron-donating (+I, hyperconjugative) character reducing the carbon's electron deficiency. Within aldehydes, formaldehyde (no substituents at all) is the most reactive, and reactivity falls as alkyl substitution grows or as aryl groups are introduced, since an aromatic ring conjugated with the carbonyl donates electron density into it by resonance, further reducing electrophilicity — aromatic aldehydes/ketones are therefore less reactive than comparable aliphatic ones. Electron-withdrawing substituents near the carbonyl (like the three chlorines in trichloroacetaldehyde) work in the opposite direction, inductively increasing electrophilicity and reactivity. Typical nucleophiles include CN⁻ (giving a cyanohydrin), NaHSO₃ (giving a bisulfite addition compound), Grignard reagents (giving alcohols), alcohols (giving hemiacetals/acetals), and hydride sources (giving alcohols).
key_formulas: Reactivity order: HCHO > aliphatic RCHO > aliphatic R₂C=O > aromatic ArCHO/ArCOR
topics.worked_example: Rank HCHO, CH₃CHO, CH₃COCH₃, and C₆H₅COC₆H₅ by decreasing reactivity toward nucleophilic addition: HCHO > CH₃CHO > CH₃COCH₃ > C₆H₅COC₆H₅, since each step adds either more/bulkier alkyl substitution or aromatic resonance donation, all of which reduce electrophilicity.
common_mistakes: Assuming ketones are more reactive than aldehydes by analogy with carbocation stability (where more substitution means more stability); the opposite logic applies here, since more alkyl substitution means more steric hindrance and less carbonyl electrophilicity, not more.
Treating aromatic and aliphatic carbonyl compounds as equally reactive, missing that ring conjugation specifically donates electron density into the carbonyl and lowers its electrophilicity.

Assuming an electron-withdrawing group near the carbonyl (like chlorine) DEcreases reactivity, when it actually inductively withdraws electron density and increases electrophilicity/reactivity, the opposite of an electron-donating alkyl group's effect.

topics.name: Reactions with Ammonia Derivatives and Other Addition–Elimination Reactions
topics.summary: Nitrogen nucleophiles derived from ammonia react with the carbonyl group by first adding (as any nucleophile would) and then eliminating a molecule of water, forming a C=N-containing product. Hydroxylamine (NH₂OH) gives an oxime; hydrazine (NH₂NH₂) gives a hydrazone; phenylhydrazine (C₆H₅NHNH₂) gives a phenylhydrazone; semicarbazide (H₂N−NH−CO−NH₂) gives a semicarbazone. 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNP) is the most widely used of these reagents as a qualitative TEST for the carbonyl group, since it gives a strikingly bright orange/yellow crystalline precipitate (the extended, electron-withdrawing-group-conjugated pi system of the nitro-substituted product intensifies its colour). All of these reagents share a practical purpose: converting an often liquid or oily aldehyde/ketone into a solid, sharply-melting crystalline derivative, historically useful for identifying an unknown carbonyl compound via its melting point. Since this reaction proceeds via the same electrophilic carbonyl carbon as any other nucleophilic addition, it follows the same aldehyde-more-reactive-than-ketone trend, and reagents like this one can, at least in principle, be used with limiting amounts to selectively derivatise the more reactive carbonyl group in a molecule bearing more than one.
topics.worked_example: Acetone + phenylhydrazine → acetone phenylhydrazone, (CH₃)₂C=N−NHC₆H₅ + H₂O, via nucleophilic addition of the terminal −NH₂ followed by elimination of water.
common_mistakes: Mismatching the reagent to its product name — e.g. calling the product of hydroxylamine a 'hydrazone' (that name belongs to hydrazine's product) or the product of semicarbazide an 'oxime'.

Treating this reaction as a simple one-step substitution, missing that it is a two-step ADDITION followed by ELIMINATION of water, analogous in mechanism to the dehydration step of aldol condensation.

Assuming 2,4-DNP reacts only with ketones (it is a general carbonyl test, reacting with both aldehydes and ketones) or forgetting that its intensely coloured product comes from the extended conjugation the nitro groups add, not from some unrelated crystal property.

topics.name: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
topics.summary: Aldol condensation requires an alpha-hydrogen: dilute base removes it to form a resonance-stabilised enolate, whose nucleophilic alpha-carbon attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of a second carbonyl molecule. The immediate product is the aldol ADDITION product, a beta-hydroxy aldehyde/ketone; only a separate, subsequent dehydration step (usually on heating) converts this into the alpha,beta-unsaturated aldol CONDENSATION product. Crossed aldol reactions between two DIFFERENT alpha-hydrogen-bearing carbonyl compounds typically give a mixture of up to four products (two self, two crossed) unless one partner lacks an alpha-hydrogen, in which case it is forced into the electrophile role, giving a cleaner crossed product. Aldehydes/ketones with NO alpha-hydrogen at all (HCHO, C₆H₅CHO) cannot form an enolate and instead undergo the Cannizzaro reaction under concentrated base: one molecule is oxidised to a carboxylate while a second is reduced to an alcohol (disproportionation). In a crossed Cannizzaro reaction, the more easily oxidised aldehyde (often formaldehyde) preferentially plays the reducing role.
key_formulas: 2 CH₃CHO --dil. NaOH, then heat--> CH₃CH=CHCHO + H₂O (crotonaldehyde)
Requirement: aldol needs an alpha-H; Cannizzaro needs NO alpha-H
topics.worked_example: Self-aldol condensation of acetone, then heating: enolate attack gives diacetone alcohol (4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one), which dehydrates to mesityl oxide, 4-methylpent-3-en-2-one, (CH₃)₂C=CH−CO−CH₃.
common_mistakes: Confusing the aldol ADDITION product (a beta-hydroxy carbonyl, before dehydration) with the aldol CONDENSATION product (the alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl, after a separate dehydration step), or assuming dehydration happens automatically/instantaneously rather than as a distinct, often heat-driven step.

Assuming any aldehyde can undergo the Cannizzaro reaction, missing that it specifically and only applies to aldehydes lacking an alpha-hydrogen; an alpha-hydrogen-bearing aldehyde follows the aldol pathway instead under the same basic conditions.

In a crossed aldol between an alpha-hydrogen-lacking aldehyde (like benzaldehyde) and an enolisable partner (like acetone), assuming either compound could equally be the nucleophile, rather than recognising that only the alpha-hydrogen-bearing partner CAN form the enolate, so it must be the nucleophile.

topics.name: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
topics.summary: Aldehydes are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids, even by mild reagents like Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal AgNO₃) and Fehling's solution, since they retain a C−H bond directly on the carbonyl carbon that these reagents' mechanisms specifically target; ketones, lacking that bond, resist oxidation except under vigorous, C−C-bond-cleaving conditions. Reduction runs the other way: NaBH₄ and LiAlH₄ deliver hydride to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, giving 1° alcohols from aldehydes and 2° alcohols from ketones — and this hydride delivery follows the same aldehyde-more-reactive-than-ketone trend as any other nucleophile. To remove the oxygen entirely (C=O → CH₂), two named methods are used depending on which conditions the rest of the molecule can tolerate: Clemmensen reduction (Zn−Hg/conc. HCl, ACIDIC) and Wolff−Kishner reduction (NH₂NH₂/KOH or ethylene glycol, BASIC). The haloform reaction (I₂/NaOH) requires a CH₃CO− (methyl ketone) group, or a CH₃CH(OH)− group that the mildly oxidising reagent first converts in situ to a methyl ketone; it cleaves off CHI₃ (iodoform) and leaves the rest of the molecule as a carboxylate one carbon shorter.
topics.worked_example: Haloform reaction of butan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₃: the CH₃CO− end is cleaved off as CHI₃, leaving sodium propanoate, CH₃CH₂COONa, as the second product.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that aromatic aldehydes (e.g. benzaldehyde) give a positive Tollens' test but a NEGATIVE Fehling's test, unlike aliphatic aldehydes, which give both positive results.

Confusing Clemmensen reduction (acidic: Zn−Hg/HCl) with Wolff−Kishner reduction (basic: NH₂NH₂/KOH), especially when choosing between them for a substrate bearing an acid-sensitive or base-sensitive group elsewhere in the molecule.

Misapplying the iodoform test's structural requirement (CH₃CO− or CH₃CH(OH)−) to any aldehyde/ketone generally, rather than checking specifically for that methyl-adjacent group (e.g. wrongly predicting a positive result for a ketone like pentan-3-one, whose carbonyl carbon is flanked by two ethyl groups, not a methyl).

topics.name: Distinguishing Tests for Aldehydes and Ketones (Tollens', Fehling's, Iodoform) and Uses
topics.summary: Three classic wet tests distinguish carbonyl compounds. Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal AgNO₃) is a mild oxidant specific to the aldehyde C−H bond: it gives a positive silver-mirror result for ANY aldehyde, aliphatic or aromatic, and a negative result for ketones. Fehling's solution (an alkaline Cu²⁺ tartrate complex) oxidises aliphatic aldehydes (giving a brick-red Cu₂O precipitate) but specifically fails with aromatic aldehydes like benzaldehyde, and gives a negative result for ketones — this Tollens'/Fehling's mismatch is a frequently tested fact. The iodoform test (I₂/NaOH) is structurally specific rather than aldehyde/ketone-specific: it is positive for any compound with a CH₃CO− group directly, or a CH₃CH(OH)− group the reagent's own mild oxidising component first converts to a methyl ketone in situ (making ethanol a specifically-cited exception among simple alcohols). Beyond the laboratory, formalin (aqueous formaldehyde) is used as a biological preservative and, with phenol, to manufacture Bakelite (exploiting formaldehyde's small, unhindered, highly reactive carbonyl carbon for extensive cross-linking); acetone is a versatile, fast-evaporating solvent, being both water-miscible and able to dissolve many organic substances.
key_formulas: Tollens' (ammoniacal AgNO₃): positive for ALL aldehydes (aliphatic + aromatic)
Fehling's (alkaline Cu²⁺): positive for ALIPHATIC aldehydes only
Iodoform (I₂/NaOH): positive for CH₃CO− or CH₃CH(OH)−
topics.worked_example: Given {acetaldehyde, benzaldehyde, acetone}, the compound giving a positive Tollens' but negative Fehling's test is benzaldehyde (aromatic aldehyde: Tollens' oxidises any aldehyde, but Fehling's specifically fails on aromatic ones).
common_mistakes: Assuming Tollens' and Fehling's reagents always agree with each other, missing the specific exception that Fehling's solution fails with aromatic aldehydes while Tollens' reagent still succeeds.

Treating the iodoform test as an 'aldehyde vs. ketone' test rather than recognising it is keyed to a specific structural motif (CH₃CO− or CH₃CH(OH)−) that some ketones have and some aldehydes (like acetaldehyde) also have, while other ketones (like pentan-3-one) do not.

Assuming any alcohol gives a positive iodoform test, rather than recognising it specifically requires the CH₃CH(OH)− pattern (satisfied by ethanol and other secondary alcohols of that type), not primary or tertiary alcohols lacking that motif.

topics.name: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
topics.summary: Carboxylic acids are named with the suffix '-oic acid' (e.g. ethanoic acid), with common names (formic, acetic, benzoic) still in wide use. The −COOH group combines a carbonyl (C=O) and a hydroxyl (−OH) on the same carbon. Losing the acidic O−H proton gives the carboxylate anion, whose two resonance structures are fully EQUIVALENT (charge spread symmetrically over both oxygens), a strong, symmetric stabilisation that makes carboxylic acids considerably more acidic than phenols (whose phenoxide ion delocalises charge less favourably, into ring carbons rather than a second oxygen) and far more acidic than simple alcohols (whose alkoxide has no such delocalisation at all): acids > phenols > alcohols. Substituents change acidity predictably through the inductive effect: electron-withdrawing groups (like Cl, NO₂) further stabilise the carboxylate and increase acidity; electron-donating groups (like alkyl, OCH₃) destabilise it and decrease acidity; and the effect of any given substituent weakens sharply with distance from −COOH (alpha > beta > gamma).
key_formulas: Acidity order: carboxylic acid > phenol > alcohol
Distance falloff: alpha-substituent effect > beta > gamma
topics.worked_example: Rank 2-chlorobutanoic, 3-chlorobutanoic, 4-chlorobutanoic, and plain butanoic acid: 2-chloro > 3-chloro > 4-chloro > butanoic acid, since the electron-withdrawing chlorine's inductive effect weakens the further it sits from −COOH.
common_mistakes: Reversing the acidity-distance relationship, assuming a substituent farther from −COOH has a stronger, not weaker, inductive effect.
Assuming an electron-donating group increases carboxylic-acid acidity, or an electron-withdrawing group decreases it, reversing the actual relationship to carboxylate-ion stabilisation.

Treating carboxylic acids and phenols as comparably acidic, rather than recognising that the carboxylate ion's two-equivalent-oxygen resonance is a distinctly stronger stabilisation than a phenoxide's delocalisation into just the ring.

topics.name: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
topics.summary: Several routes converge on the carboxylic acid oxidation level. Vigorous oxidation of a primary alcohol or aldehyde (hot acidified KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₄, used in excess) goes all the way to the acid, unlike the milder, controlled PCC oxidation that stops at the aldehyde. Hot, alkaline KMnO₄ oxidises ANY alkylbenzene side chain bearing a benzylic hydrogen down to a single ring-attached −COOH, regardless of the original chain's length or branching — so ethylbenzene, propylbenzene, and isopropylbenzene all converge on benzoic acid. Nitrile hydrolysis (aqueous acid or base, via an amide intermediate) gives the carboxylic acid directly, retaining the nitrile's original carbon count. A Grignard reagent's reaction with CO₂ (dry ice), followed by acidic workup, adds exactly ONE new carbon onto the Grignard's own carbon skeleton, giving a carboxylic acid one carbon longer than the starting alkyl halide. Simple substitution/oxidation routes (e.g. converting an alkyl halide to an alcohol, then oxidising) do NOT add a carbon and so cannot reach a target acid with more carbons than the starting halide.
key_formulas: Alkylbenzene --hot alkaline KMnO₄--> C₆H₅COOH (any chain length)
RMgX + CO₂, then H₃O⁺ --> R−COOH (one new carbon)
topics.worked_example: Bromoethane → Grignard (Mg/dry ether) → + CO₂ → dilute acid workup gives propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH (one new carbon added, from CO₂, onto the original 2-carbon ethyl group).
common_mistakes: Assuming the original alkyl side-chain length is retained after hot alkaline KMnO₄ oxidation of an alkylbenzene, rather than recognising that ANY chain length is cut down to a single −COOH carbon.
Forgetting that reaction with CO₂ adds exactly one NEW carbon to a Grignard reagent's own skeleton, and instead expecting the product to have the same carbon count as the starting alkyl halide.

Choosing a simple substitution/oxidation route (halide → alcohol → acid) when the target acid actually needs MORE carbons than the starting halide provides, since that route cannot add any new carbon to the chain.

topics.name: Reactions of Carboxylic Acids: Derivative Formation and Substituent Effects on Acidity
topics.summary: Carboxylic acids convert into more reactive derivatives for further synthesis. SOCl₂ (or PCl₃/PCl₅) replaces −OH with −Cl to give the acid chloride, a much better electrophile (Cl strongly withdraws electrons and is a good leaving group) that reacts efficiently with amines or alcohols, unlike the free acid, which mostly just undergoes simple acid−base proton transfer with an amine instead of substitution. Fischer esterification (acid + alcohol, catalysed by a trace of conc. H₂SO₄) is reversible and is driven toward the ester by removing water or using excess reagent. The Hell−Volhard−Zelinsky (HVZ) reaction (X₂/red P) installs a halogen at the ALPHA-carbon, not the carboxyl carbon itself, and this alpha-halogen further increases acidity by the same inductive mechanism used throughout the acidity topic. LiAlH₄ (but not the milder NaBH₄) reduces a free acid all the way to a primary alcohol, since the acid's own −OH oxygen donates into the carbonyl by resonance, making the carboxyl carbon considerably less electrophilic than a simple aldehyde/ketone. Heating a carboxylate salt with soda lime (decarboxylation) replaces −COONa with −H, giving an alkane one carbon shorter than the original acid.
topics.worked_example: HVZ reaction of propanoic acid with Br₂/red P gives 2-bromopropanoic acid, CH₃CHBrCOOH, with the halogen specifically on the alpha-carbon, not the carboxyl carbon itself.
common_mistakes: Assuming the HVZ reaction halogenates any carbon of a carboxylic acid, rather than specifically and only the alpha-carbon.

Expecting NaBH₄ to reduce a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol the way it reduces an aldehyde/ketone, missing that the acid's resonance-donating −OH oxygen makes its carbonyl carbon considerably less electrophilic, requiring the much stronger LiAlH₄ instead.

Reacting a free carboxylic acid directly with an amine and expecting clean amide formation at mild temperature, rather than recognising that this mostly gives a simple ammonium carboxylate salt, and that converting to the acid chloride first is the standard, more reliable strategy.

questions.topic: Nomenclature and Structure of the Carbonyl Group in Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: The IUPAC suffix used to name an aldehyde (replacing the '-e' of the parent alkane) is:
options: -ol
-al
-one
-oic acid
questions.explanation: Aldehydes are named by replacing the terminal '-e' of the corresponding alkane with '-al', e.g. ethane → ethanal (CH₃CHO).
questions.hint: Think of the common suffix in 'methanal' and 'ethanal'.
distractor_logic: '-ol' is the alcohol suffix (−OH), an entirely different functional group.
'-one' is the ketone suffix (e.g. propan-2-one), not the aldehyde suffix.
'-oic acid' is the carboxylic acid suffix, a more oxidised functional group than an aldehyde.

questions.topic: Nomenclature and Structure of the Carbonyl Group in Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: The carbon atom of the carbonyl group (C=O) in aldehydes and ketones is:
options: sp² hybridised, trigonal planar with bond angles ≈120°
sp³ hybridised, tetrahedral
Not hybridised at all
sp hybridised, linear
questions.explanation: The carbonyl carbon uses three sp² hybrid orbitals for its three sigma bonds (trigonal planar, ≈120°) and one unhybridised p orbital overlaps with oxygen's p orbital to form the pi bond of C=O.
questions.hint: The carbonyl carbon has exactly three sigma-bonded groups arranged in a flat triangle.
distractor_logic: sp³ hybridisation is tetrahedral (109.5°), appropriate for a saturated carbon with four single bonds, not a carbon bearing a double bond.
The carbonyl carbon is definitely hybridised (sp²); its geometry and bonding are a direct consequence of that hybridisation.
sp hybridisation is linear (180°), found at triple-bond carbons, not a carbon with only one pi bond and two other substituents.

questions.topic: Nomenclature and Structure of the Carbonyl Group in Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Due to the greater electronegativity of oxygen, the carbonyl group is polarised such that:
options: The polarity reverses depending on whether the compound is an aldehyde or a ketone
The carbonyl carbon bears a partial positive charge (δ+) and oxygen bears a partial negative charge (δ−)
Both atoms are exactly neutral, since C=O is a purely covalent, non-polar bond
The carbonyl carbon bears a partial negative charge and oxygen bears a partial positive charge
questions.explanation: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so it pulls the shared pi and sigma electron density of C=O toward itself, leaving the carbonyl carbon electron-deficient (δ+) and the oxygen electron-rich (δ−) — this is exactly why the carbonyl carbon is electrophilic and attacked by nucleophiles.
questions.hint: Compare the electronegativities of carbon and oxygen directly.
distractor_logic: The direction of polarisation (Cδ+, Oδ−) is fixed by the electronegativity difference between C and O, and does not flip between aldehydes and ketones.
C=O is one of the most polar common functional-group bonds in organic chemistry, not non-polar; this polarity is the basis of essentially all carbonyl reactivity.
This reverses the actual polarity; oxygen, being more electronegative, pulls density toward itself, not away from itself.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Oxidation of a primary alcohol with pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) gives an aldehyde rather than a carboxylic acid because:
options: PCC converts the alcohol into a ketone instead of an aldehyde
PCC first reduces the alcohol before oxidising it
PCC only reacts with secondary alcohols, never primary alcohols
PCC is a mild oxidant that stops at the aldehyde stage without further oxidising it to the acid
questions.explanation: PCC (in anhydrous, non-aqueous conditions, typically CH₂Cl₂) is a controlled, mild oxidising agent that oxidises a 1° alcohol only as far as the aldehyde, avoiding the further oxidation to a carboxylic acid that stronger aqueous oxidants (like KMnO₄ or acidic K₂Cr₂O₄) would cause.
questions.hint: Think about why a specific, milder reagent is chosen over a strong oxidant like KMnO₄ for this transformation.
distractor_logic: A primary alcohol oxidised by PCC gives an aldehyde (R−CH₂OH → R−CHO), not a ketone; ketones instead come from oxidising secondary alcohols.
PCC is an oxidising agent, not a reducing agent; it does not reduce anything before oxidising.
PCC does react with primary alcohols; that is precisely how it is used to make aldehydes.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: In the Rosenmund reduction, an acyl chloride (RCOCl) is converted into an aldehyde (RCHO) using:
options: NaBH₄ in aqueous ethanol
Zn−Hg amalgam with concentrated HCl
LiAlH₄ in dry ether
H₂ gas over a palladium catalyst partially poisoned with BaSO₄
questions.explanation: The Rosenmund reduction passes H₂ over an acyl chloride using Pd catalyst poisoned by BaSO₄ (sometimes with added quinoline/sulfur); the poisoning selectively lowers the catalyst's activity just enough to stop reduction cleanly at the aldehyde stage, preventing further reduction to the alcohol.
questions.hint: This method specifically uses a deliberately 'deactivated' hydrogenation catalyst to stop the reaction at the right stage.
distractor_logic: NaBH₄ is a much weaker hydride source generally used on aldehydes/ketones themselves, not the standard reagent for this specific acyl-chloride-to-aldehyde transformation.
Zn−Hg/conc. HCl is the Clemmensen reduction, which reduces a carbonyl all the way to a −CH₂− group; it does not convert an acyl chloride into an aldehyde.
LiAlH₄ is a strong hydride reducing agent that would reduce the acyl chloride all the way to the primary alcohol, not stop cleanly at the aldehyde.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Friedel−Crafts acylation of benzene with an acyl chloride (RCOCl) in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃ gives:
options: A simple alkylbenzene (C₆H₅−R)
An aryl aldehyde (C₆H₅−CHO)
An aromatic alcohol (C₆H₅−OH)
questions.explanation: AlCl₃ activates the acyl chloride to an acylium ion (RCO⁺), which attacks the benzene ring; loss of H⁺ restores aromaticity, giving an aryl ketone.
questions.hint: The incoming electrophile here is a full RCO group, not just R or H.
distractor_logic: Friedel−Crafts alkylation (not acylation) with an alkyl halide gives a simple alkylbenzene; acylation with an acid chloride installs a carbonyl-containing group instead.
An aryl aldehyde would require introducing just a −CHO group, which needs a different named reaction (e.g. Gatterman−Koch), not acylation with a general RCOCl.
No oxygen-only substituent is installed here; the product retains the full carbonyl-bearing acyl group attached to the ring.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Ozonolysis of an alkene, R₂C=CR₂′, followed by reductive (Zn/H₂O) workup, cleaves the double bond to give:
options: A single alcohol
Two alkyl halides
Two carbonyl compounds (aldehydes and/or ketones), reflecting the substituents on each original alkene carbon
Two carboxylic acids only, regardless of workup
questions.explanation: Ozone adds across C=C to form an ozonide; reductive workup (Zn/H₂O) cleaves this into two carbonyl fragments — an aldehyde forms at a =CH− carbon, a ketone forms at a fully substituted =C< carbon.
questions.hint: Reductive workup is specifically chosen so the aldehyde products are not oxidised further.
distractor_logic: Ozonolysis cleaves and oxidises the double bond; it does not simply add water to give a single alcohol.
No halogen source is present in ozonolysis; the reagents involved are ozone and the reductive workup only.
Carboxylic acids as the sole products would require an oxidative (not reductive) workup, which further oxidises any aldehyde fragment formed.

questions.topic: Physical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: For compounds of comparable molecular mass, the boiling points of aldehydes/ketones are generally:
options: Higher than alcohols but lower than alkanes
Higher than alkanes (dipole−dipole attraction) but lower than alcohols (which show hydrogen bonding)
Identical to alcohols, since both contain a C−O bond
Lower than both alkanes and alcohols
questions.explanation: The polar C=O group gives aldehydes/ketones dipole−dipole attractions stronger than the weak dispersion forces in non-polar alkanes, but carbonyl compounds cannot hydrogen-bond to each other (no O−H), so their boiling points fall below alcohols of similar mass, which do hydrogen-bond.
questions.hint: Rank the intermolecular forces: dispersion-only < dipole−dipole < hydrogen bonding.
distractor_logic: This reverses the correct order; alcohols, with O−H hydrogen bonding, boil higher than carbonyl compounds of similar mass, not lower.
Having a C−O bond is not the same as having an O−H bond; only the alcohol's O−H allows hydrogen bonding between its own molecules, a stronger effect than a carbonyl's dipole−dipole attraction.
Alkanes have only weak dispersion forces and boil lower than polar carbonyl compounds of comparable mass, not higher.

questions.topic: Physical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Lower aldehydes and ketones (e.g. formaldehyde, acetaldehyde, acetone) are appreciably soluble in water mainly because:
options: Solubility in water has nothing to do with the carbonyl group at all
They react irreversibly with water to form carboxylic acids
They ionise completely in water to give H⁺ ions
They can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules through their carbonyl oxygen's lone pairs
questions.explanation: Although carbonyl compounds cannot hydrogen-bond to each other, the oxygen's lone pairs can accept hydrogen bonds from water's O−H, allowing appreciable solubility for lower-molecular-weight members; solubility decreases as the hydrocarbon chain (and hence the non-polar portion) grows.
questions.hint: Water is a hydrogen-bond donor; the carbonyl oxygen has lone pairs it can accept a hydrogen bond into.
distractor_logic: The carbonyl oxygen's lone pairs are exactly what enables hydrogen bonding with water; the functional group is central to this solubility, not irrelevant to it.
Dissolving in water is a physical process (hydration via hydrogen bonding), not a chemical reaction converting the carbonyl into a carboxylic acid.
Aldehydes and ketones are not acids and do not ionise to release H⁺ in water; carboxylic acids do that, but simple carbonyl compounds do not.

questions.topic: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
questions.question: In the general mechanism of nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl compound, the first step is:
options: A nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate
The C=O bond is completely broken before any new bond forms
A hydrogen atom is abstracted from the alpha-carbon
The oxygen atom is protonated first, in every case, before any nucleophile approaches
questions.explanation: The carbonyl carbon is electrophilic (δ+); a nucleophile's lone pair attacks it directly, pushing the pi electrons onto oxygen and forming a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, which is then typically protonated.
questions.hint: Identify which atom of the carbonyl group is electron-deficient and therefore attractive to a nucleophile.
distractor_logic: The C=O pi bond breaks (its electrons move onto oxygen) as the new bond to the nucleophile forms; this is a single concerted step, not two separate steps of first fully breaking the bond and then forming a new one.

Removing an alpha-hydrogen is the first step of enolate/aldol-type chemistry, a different (base-catalysed, alpha-carbon) reaction, not the general nucleophilic addition mechanism at the carbonyl carbon.

Protonation of oxygen (acid catalysis) can accelerate the reaction by making the carbon even more electrophilic, but it is not a universal first step for every nucleophilic addition, and the defining event is still nucleophilic attack at carbon.

questions.topic: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
questions.question: Toward nucleophilic addition, aldehydes are generally:
options: More reactive than ketones
Unreactive, since aldehydes have no electrophilic carbon at all
Exactly as reactive as ketones in every case
Less reactive than ketones
questions.explanation: Aldehydes bear only one alkyl/aryl group (plus a small H) on the carbonyl carbon, giving less steric hindrance and less electron-donating (+I) character than the two alkyl/aryl groups on a ketone's carbonyl carbon — both factors make the aldehyde carbon more accessible and more electrophilic.
questions.hint: Compare how many alkyl/aryl groups are attached directly to the carbonyl carbon in each case.
distractor_logic: The carbonyl carbon of an aldehyde is very much electrophilic; it is precisely this electrophilicity that drives nucleophilic addition reactions in the first place.
Aldehydes and ketones differ systematically in both steric bulk and electron density at the carbonyl carbon, so their reactivity is not generally equal.
This is the reverse of the true reactivity order; ketones, with two alkyl groups sterically blocking and electronically donating into the carbonyl carbon, are less reactive than aldehydes.

questions.topic: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
questions.question: Addition of HCN to a carbonyl compound (R₂C=O) gives a product called a:
options: Cyanohydrin
Nitrile
Amide
Oxime
questions.explanation: HCN adds across C=O to give R₂C(OH)CN, a cyanohydrin, containing both a hydroxyl and a nitrile group on the same carbon.
questions.hint: The product name directly combines 'cyano' with the hydroxyl-bearing carbon.
distractor_logic: A simple nitrile (R−C≡N) has no hydroxyl group attached; the cyanohydrin product retains both the −OH (from the original C=O oxygen) and the −CN group.
An amide (R−CONH₂) would require a nitrogen-containing acyl derivative, not the direct addition of HCN across a carbonyl.
An oxime is the product of reaction with hydroxylamine (NH₂OH), not HCN.

questions.topic: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
questions.question: Addition of sodium bisulfite (NaHSO₃) to an aldehyde or methyl ketone gives a product called a:
options: Bisulfite addition compound
Hemiacetal
Grignard complex
Schiff base
questions.explanation: NaHSO₃ adds across the carbonyl to give a crystalline bisulfite addition compound, R₂C(OH)SO₃Na, useful for purifying aldehydes and methyl ketones (the reaction is reversible with dilute acid/base, regenerating the carbonyl compound).
questions.hint: The name of this product directly reflects the bisulfite reagent that added to the carbonyl.
distractor_logic: A hemiacetal forms from addition of an alcohol (one equivalent) to a carbonyl, not from sodium bisulfite.
A Grignard complex would form from reaction with an organomagnesium halide, a different nucleophile entirely, not bisulfite.
A Schiff base (imine) forms from reaction with a primary amine, not from sodium bisulfite addition.

questions.topic: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
questions.question: Compared to an aliphatic aldehyde of similar size, an aromatic aldehyde such as benzaldehyde is generally:
options: Equally reactive, since the benzene ring has no electronic effect on the attached carbonyl group
Less reactive toward nucleophilic addition, because resonance donates electron density from the ring into the carbonyl carbon, reducing its electrophilicity
More reactive, because the ring withdraws electron density from the carbonyl carbon
Completely unreactive toward all nucleophiles
questions.explanation: The aromatic ring can donate electron density into the carbonyl group by resonance (conjugation between the ring's pi system and the C=O), partially offsetting the carbon's electron deficiency and making it less electrophilic than a comparable aliphatic aldehyde's carbonyl carbon.
questions.hint: Consider whether the ring's pi system can conjugate with, and donate into, the adjacent carbonyl group.
distractor_logic: The aromatic ring is directly conjugated with the carbonyl group and does have a measurable electronic effect on it; it is not electronically silent.
This reverses the actual electronic effect; the ring's conjugation donates electron density into the carbonyl (reducing electrophilicity), rather than withdrawing it and increasing electrophilicity.

Aromatic aldehydes are still reactive toward nucleophilic addition (e.g. they give cyanohydrins, oximes, and undergo the Cannizzaro reaction); they are less reactive than aliphatic aldehydes, not completely unreactive.

questions.topic: Reactions with Ammonia Derivatives and Other Addition–Elimination Reactions
questions.question: Reaction of a carbonyl compound with hydroxylamine (NH₂OH) gives a product called an:
options: Amide
Oxime
Hydrazone
Acetal
questions.explanation: NH₂OH adds to the carbonyl, then eliminates water, giving R₂C=N−OH, an oxime.
questions.hint: This product's name is directly associated with hydroxylamine as the reagent.
distractor_logic: An amide is a carboxylic acid derivative (R−CO−NH₂), not the product of a simple carbonyl + hydroxylamine reaction.
A hydrazone forms from reaction with hydrazine (NH₂NH₂), not hydroxylamine.
An acetal forms from reaction with two equivalents of alcohol under acid catalysis, not from hydroxylamine.

questions.topic: Reactions with Ammonia Derivatives and Other Addition–Elimination Reactions
questions.question: Reaction of a carbonyl compound with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNP) gives:
options: A colourless gas with no visible change
An orange/yellow crystalline precipitate (2,4-DNP derivative), used as a classic test for the carbonyl group
A white precipitate identical to the AgNO₃ test's silver mirror
A blue-coloured solution
questions.explanation: 2,4-DNP condenses with the carbonyl group (addition−elimination of water) to give a characteristic orange/yellow crystalline hydrazone derivative, widely used as a qualitative test to detect the presence of a C=O group.
questions.hint: This reagent is specifically valued because its product is a solid with a very distinctive, easily observed colour.
distractor_logic: The defining feature of this test is precisely the visible, distinctively coloured (orange/yellow) precipitate that forms; there is no 'no visible change' outcome for a positive test.
The 2,4-DNP test's orange/yellow precipitate is chemically and visually distinct from the silvery metallic mirror formed in the Tollens' test, which is a completely different reagent and reaction.
The 2,4-DNP test does not produce a blue solution; that colour is not characteristic of this reagent's reaction with carbonyl compounds.

questions.topic: Reactions with Ammonia Derivatives and Other Addition–Elimination Reactions
questions.question: The overall reaction of a carbonyl compound with a primary amine derivative (like hydrazine or phenylhydrazine) to form a C=N-containing product proceeds via:
options: Simple nucleophilic substitution at the carbonyl carbon with no elimination step
Reduction of the carbonyl group to an alcohol, followed by dehydration
Direct radical substitution at the alpha-carbon
Nucleophilic addition of the amine to the carbonyl, followed by elimination of a water molecule
questions.explanation: The nitrogen nucleophile first adds to the carbonyl carbon (as in any nucleophilic addition), giving a tetrahedral intermediate bearing both −OH and −NHR groups; this intermediate then eliminates a molecule of water to form the C=N double bond of the final imine-type product.
questions.hint: This class of reaction is named for combining two mechanistic steps in sequence: addition, then loss of a small molecule.
distractor_logic: This reaction is not a single-step substitution; it proceeds through a distinct addition step first, followed by a separate elimination step that removes water.
The carbonyl carbon is not reduced (no hydride is added) in this reaction; instead, the amine's nitrogen directly attacks the carbonyl carbon in an addition−elimination sequence.
This is an ionic, polar mechanism involving lone-pair donation and proton transfers, not a radical process at the alpha-carbon.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: A necessary structural requirement for a carbonyl compound to undergo aldol condensation is that it must possess:
options: An odd number of carbon atoms
No oxygen atoms other than the carbonyl oxygen
At least one alpha-hydrogen atom
At least one aromatic ring
questions.explanation: Base removes a proton from the carbon adjacent (alpha) to the carbonyl to generate a resonance-stabilised enolate, which then acts as the nucleophile attacking a second carbonyl molecule; without an alpha-hydrogen, no enolate can form, and aldol condensation cannot occur.
questions.hint: Think about which hydrogen the base must remove to generate the key nucleophilic intermediate.
distractor_logic: Carbon count parity (odd or even) has no bearing on whether aldol condensation can occur; only the presence of an alpha-hydrogen matters.
The carbonyl oxygen itself is a normal, expected part of the molecule; the requirement concerns hydrogen atoms on the adjacent (alpha) carbon, not the absence of other oxygens.
Aromaticity is not a requirement; simple aliphatic aldehydes and ketones like acetaldehyde and acetone readily undergo aldol condensation.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: Aldol condensation is typically catalysed by:
options: A dilute base, such as dilute NaOH
A radical initiator, such as a peroxide
A Lewis acid, such as anhydrous AlCl₃
A strong mineral acid, such as concentrated H₂SO₄
questions.explanation: Dilute NaOH (or another mild base) deprotonates the alpha-carbon to generate the nucleophilic enolate ion that drives the aldol addition step.
questions.hint: The key first step of this mechanism is removing a proton, which calls for a base, not an acid or radical initiator.
distractor_logic: Radical initiators like peroxides are used for radical chain reactions (e.g. anti-Markovnikov HBr addition), not for base-catalysed enolate chemistry.
AlCl₃ is a Lewis acid catalyst associated with Friedel−Crafts reactions on aromatic rings, not the standard base-catalysed aldol mechanism.
Concentrated H₂SO₄ is a strong acid, associated with different reactions (e.g. alcohol dehydration); the standard aldol mechanism relies on base-generated enolate formation.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: The initial product formed when the aldol ADDITION step is complete (before any dehydration) is a:
options: Carboxylic acid
Alpha,beta-unsaturated aldehyde or ketone
Simple ether
Beta-hydroxy aldehyde or ketone
questions.explanation: The enolate's nucleophilic alpha-carbon attacks a second carbonyl molecule, and after protonation the product is a beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound (the new −OH sits on the carbon beta to the original carbonyl); only a subsequent, separate dehydration step converts this into the alpha,beta-unsaturated (aldol condensation) product.
questions.hint: This is the product BEFORE any water is lost; check where the new −OH group ends up relative to the carbonyl.
distractor_logic: The aldol addition product is not a carboxylic acid; it retains the original carbonyl group plus a new hydroxyl, with no change in oxidation state at the carbonyl carbon.
An alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl is the CONDENSATION product, formed only after a further, separate dehydration step; it is not the immediate addition product.
No ether linkage forms in this mechanism; the product is a hydroxy-substituted carbonyl compound, not an ether.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: The Cannizzaro reaction — disproportionation of an aldehyde under concentrated base into one molecule of alcohol and one of carboxylate — is specifically given by:
options: Only ketones, never aldehydes
Any aldehyde, regardless of alpha-hydrogen content
Aldehydes that have NO alpha-hydrogen atom, such as HCHO or C₆H₅CHO
Only carboxylic acids, never aldehydes
questions.explanation: An aldehyde lacking an alpha-hydrogen (like formaldehyde or benzaldehyde) cannot form an enolate and therefore cannot undergo the usual base-catalysed aldol pathway; instead, under concentrated base, one molecule is oxidised to a carboxylate while another is reduced to an alcohol (disproportionation).
questions.hint: Ask whether this specific aldehyde could instead undergo the more common alpha-hydrogen-dependent (aldol) pathway; if not, why not?
distractor_logic: Ketones (whether or not they have alpha-hydrogens) do not undergo the Cannizzaro reaction under these conditions; it is specifically a reaction of alpha-hydrogen-lacking aldehydes.

Aldehydes WITH an alpha-hydrogen preferentially undergo aldol condensation instead, since enolate formation is available to them; Cannizzaro is specifically the pathway taken when that option is unavailable.
Carboxylic acids are not the starting material for this reaction; an aldehyde is the starting material, and a carboxylate (salt of a carboxylic acid) is one of the two products formed.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: Cannizzaro reaction of formaldehyde (HCHO) with concentrated NaOH gives methanol and:
options: Formic acid (uncharged, HCOOH)
Another molecule of methanol, with no salt formed
Sodium acetate (CH₃COONa)
Sodium formate (sodium methanoate, HCOONa)
questions.explanation: In this disproportionation, one HCHO molecule is reduced to methanol (CH₃OH) while a second is oxidised all the way to the carboxylate salt under the basic conditions, giving sodium formate, HCOONa.
questions.hint: The reaction is run in a strongly basic (NaOH) medium, so the acid product exists as its sodium salt, not the free acid.
distractor_logic: Under the strongly basic (concentrated NaOH) reaction conditions, the carboxylic acid product exists deprotonated as its sodium salt, not as the free acid.

The reaction is a disproportionation (one molecule oxidised, one reduced) specifically because the substrate lacks an alpha-hydrogen; it does not simply give two molecules of the same reduced product.
Sodium acetate has two carbons; formaldehyde has only one carbon, so its oxidised fragment cannot become a two-carbon carboxylate.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: NaBH₄ and LiAlH₄ are commonly used to reduce the carbonyl group of an aldehyde or ketone to:
options: The corresponding alkane, by removing the oxygen entirely
The corresponding alcohol (1° from an aldehyde, 2° from a ketone)
The corresponding alkene
The corresponding carboxylic acid
questions.explanation: These hydride reagents deliver H⁻ to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon; after aqueous workup, an aldehyde is reduced to a primary alcohol and a ketone to a secondary alcohol.
questions.hint: Hydride reagents add hydrogen across the C=O bond, they do not remove the oxygen atom entirely.
distractor_logic: Complete removal of oxygen to give a hydrocarbon requires different, more specialised methods (Clemmensen or Wolff−Kishner reduction), not simple hydride reduction.
Forming an alkene would require removing an oxygen and forming a new pi bond elsewhere; simple hydride reduction of a carbonyl gives a saturated alcohol, not an alkene.
NaBH₄ and LiAlH₄ are REDUCING agents; oxidising the carbonyl to a carboxylic acid would require an oxidant instead.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Clemmensen reduction, which reduces a carbonyl group all the way to −CH₂−, uses which conditions?
options: Cold, dilute, alkaline KMnO₄
Ammoniacal AgNO₃ (Tollens' reagent)
NH₂NH₂/KOH or ethylene glycol, heated (basic conditions)
Zn−Hg amalgam with concentrated HCl (acidic conditions)
questions.explanation: Clemmensen reduction uses zinc amalgam (Zn−Hg) with concentrated hydrochloric acid, strongly acidic conditions, to fully reduce a carbonyl group to a methylene (−CH₂−) group.
questions.hint: This method is specifically the ACIDIC alternative to another named carbonyl-to-methylene reduction.
distractor_logic: Cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄ (Baeyer's reagent) is used to test for unsaturation by oxidation, unrelated to reducing a carbonyl group to −CH₂−.
Ammoniacal AgNO₃ (Tollens' reagent) is a mild OXIDISING test reagent for aldehydes, not a reducing agent for carbonyl-to-methylene conversion.
NH₂NH₂/KOH (or ethylene glycol) describes the Wolff−Kishner reduction, the basic-conditions alternative that achieves the same overall transformation, not the Clemmensen method.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Wolff−Kishner reduction, the basic-conditions alternative for reducing a carbonyl to −CH₂−, uses:
options: LiAlH₄ in dry ether
Hydrazine (NH₂NH₂) and KOH (or ethylene glycol), with heat
Zn−Hg amalgam and concentrated HCl
Dilute H₂SO₄ and heat
questions.explanation: The carbonyl first condenses with hydrazine to form a hydrazone, which then loses N₂ under strongly basic, heated conditions (KOH, often in high-boiling ethylene glycol), reducing the carbon to −CH₂−.
questions.hint: This method is specifically the BASIC alternative to the Zn−Hg/HCl method for the same overall transformation.
distractor_logic: LiAlH₄ simply reduces the carbonyl to an alcohol (does not remove the oxygen entirely); it does not achieve the full carbonyl-to-methylene reduction that Wolff−Kishner accomplishes.
Zn−Hg amalgam with concentrated HCl describes the Clemmensen reduction, the acidic-conditions alternative for the same overall transformation, not Wolff−Kishner.
Dilute H₂SO₄ with heat is not the reagent combination for this reduction; the defining reagents here are hydrazine plus a strong base.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: For a compound to give a positive iodoform test, it must contain a:
options: Benzene ring with no other requirement
Terminal alkyne group, ≡C−H
CH₃CO− group (methyl ketone) or a CH₃CH(OH)− group (which is oxidised to a methyl ketone in situ)
Any C=O group whatsoever, regardless of what is attached to it
questions.explanation: The iodoform test requires either a methyl ketone (CH₃CO−) directly, or a secondary alcohol of the type CH₃CH(OH)− that is first oxidised in situ (by the I₂/NaOH reagent itself) to a methyl ketone; this specific structural motif is what undergoes triiodomethylation and cleavage to give CHI₃ (iodoform).
questions.hint: The test is named after its yellow, characteristically-smelling product, CHI₃; the substrate must have exactly the right group next to the carbonyl (or potential carbonyl).
distractor_logic: A benzene ring alone, with no methyl ketone or CH₃CH(OH)− group present, does not confer a positive iodoform test.
A terminal alkyne's acidic ≡C−H is unrelated to the iodoform test's structural requirement, which concerns a methyl ketone or a specific secondary-alcohol pattern.
Not every carbonyl compound gives a positive iodoform test; ketones lacking a methyl group directly on the carbonyl carbon (e.g. diethyl ketone) give a negative result.

questions.topic: Distinguishing Tests for Aldehydes and Ketones (Tollens', Fehling's, Iodoform) and Uses
questions.question: Tollens' reagent, used as a test for aldehydes (the 'silver mirror' test), consists of:
options: Acidified potassium dichromate
Ammoniacal silver nitrate, [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺
A copper(II) tartrate complex in alkaline solution
Bromine water
questions.explanation: Tollens' reagent is freshly prepared ammoniacal AgNO₃; an aldehyde reduces the diamminesilver(I) complex to metallic silver, which deposits as a bright, mirror-like coating on the inside of the test tube.
questions.hint: The characteristic positive result of this specific test is a shiny metallic coating.
distractor_logic: Acidified potassium dichromate is a general oxidising agent (e.g. for oxidising alcohols) but is not the reagent named 'Tollens' reagent' or associated with the silver mirror test.
A copper(II) tartrate complex in alkaline solution describes Fehling's solution, a different reagent giving a different (red precipitate) positive result.
Bromine water is used to test for unsaturation (decolourisation) or for phenols, not as the reagent for the aldehyde-specific silver mirror test.

questions.topic: Distinguishing Tests for Aldehydes and Ketones (Tollens', Fehling's, Iodoform) and Uses
questions.question: Which statement about Fehling's solution and benzaldehyde is correct?
options: Benzaldehyde gives a positive Fehling's test, exactly like an aliphatic aldehyde
Fehling's solution does not react with any aldehyde, aliphatic or aromatic
Benzaldehyde gives a NEGATIVE Fehling's test, even though it gives a positive Tollens' test
Benzaldehyde reduces Fehling's solution to give a blue precipitate
questions.explanation: Fehling's solution oxidises ALIPHATIC aldehydes (giving a brick-red Cu₂O precipitate) but does NOT oxidise aromatic aldehydes like benzaldehyde; benzaldehyde still gives a positive (silver mirror) Tollens' test, since Tollens' reagent is a different, more universally effective oxidant for aldehydes.
questions.hint: This is a classic distinguishing fact: the two 'aldehyde tests' do not always agree with each other for aromatic substrates.
distractor_logic: This is the common student error the question tests directly; benzaldehyde specifically fails the Fehling's test, unlike aliphatic aldehydes such as acetaldehyde.
Fehling's solution does react with (and is oxidised by) aliphatic aldehydes; it simply fails specifically with aromatic aldehydes like benzaldehyde.
The positive Fehling's test result is a brick-RED precipitate (Cu₂O), not a blue precipitate; and in any case benzaldehyde does not give this positive result at all.

questions.topic: Distinguishing Tests for Aldehydes and Ketones (Tollens', Fehling's, Iodoform) and Uses
questions.question: 'Formalin', an aqueous solution used as a biological tissue preservative, is:
options: A concentrated aqueous solution of acetone
A solution of acetic acid in water
A solution of Tollens' reagent
An approximately 40% aqueous solution of formaldehyde (methanal)
questions.explanation: Formalin is the common name for an aqueous solution containing roughly 37−40% formaldehyde (HCHO) by mass, used for preserving biological specimens and in the manufacture of resins such as bakelite.
questions.hint: This substance's name is directly derived from the common name of the simplest aldehyde.
distractor_logic: Acetone is a ketone, not an aldehyde, and 'formalin' specifically refers to formaldehyde solution, not acetone solution.
Acetic acid in water is more commonly known as vinegar (in dilute form) or glacial acetic acid (concentrated), not formalin.
Tollens' reagent is a laboratory testing reagent for aldehydes, not a preservative solution; it is a completely different substance from formalin.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: The IUPAC suffix used to name a carboxylic acid (replacing the '-e' of the parent alkane) is:
options: -al
-ol
-one
-oic acid
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids are named by replacing the terminal '-e' of the corresponding alkane with '-oic acid', e.g. ethane → ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH).
questions.hint: Think of the suffix shared by 'methanoic acid' and 'ethanoic acid'.
distractor_logic: '-al' is the aldehyde suffix, a less oxidised functional group than a carboxylic acid.
'-ol' is the alcohol suffix, a much less oxidised functional group than a carboxylic acid.
'-one' is the ketone suffix, an entirely different functional group from −COOH.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: The common name 'formic acid' refers to which IUPAC-named compound?
options: Propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH
Benzoic acid, C₆H₅COOH
Methanoic acid, HCOOH
Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH
questions.explanation: Formic acid is the traditional common name for the simplest carboxylic acid, HCOOH, IUPAC name methanoic acid (originally isolated from ants, hence the Latin-derived name 'formic').
questions.hint: This is the one-carbon carboxylic acid, the carboxylic acid analogue of methane/methanal.
distractor_logic: Propanoic acid has three carbons, two more than formic acid.
Benzoic acid is an aromatic carboxylic acid (C₆H₅COOH) with a benzene ring, structurally very different from the simple one-carbon formic acid.
Ethanoic acid (acetic acid) has two carbons, one more than formic acid's single carbon.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Comparing acids of similar size, carboxylic acids are generally:
options: Less acidic than both phenols and simple alcohols
More acidic than both phenols and simple alcohols
More acidic than phenols but less acidic than alcohols
Exactly as acidic as alcohols, since both contain an O−H bond
questions.explanation: The carboxylate anion formed on deprotonation is resonance-stabilised by delocalisation of the negative charge over TWO equivalent oxygen atoms; this stabilisation is stronger than a phenoxide ion's delocalisation into the ring, and far stronger than a simple alkoxide's lack of any such delocalisation — giving the order carboxylic acids > phenols > alcohols in acidity.
questions.hint: Think about how effectively the negative charge can be spread out (stabilised) in the conjugate base of each type of compound.
distractor_logic: This reverses the actual acidity order; carboxylic acids, with their especially well-stabilised carboxylate conjugate base, are considerably MORE acidic than phenols or alcohols, not less.
Carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenols, not less, since two-equivalent-oxygen resonance stabilisation in the carboxylate is stronger than a phenoxide's delocalisation into just the ring.

Although both classes have an O−H bond, the very different stability of their respective conjugate bases (carboxylate vs. simple alkoxide) makes carboxylic acids far more acidic than simple alcohols; the presence of O−H alone does not equalise acidity.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: The carboxyl group, −COOH, structurally consists of:
options: A carbonyl group only, with no oxygen−hydrogen bond present
A carbonyl group (C=O) and a hydroxyl group (−OH) both attached to the same carbon
Two separate, unconnected hydroxyl groups
An ether linkage between two carbon atoms
questions.explanation: The carboxyl group combines a C=O (carbonyl) and an −OH (hydroxyl) on the same carbon; this combination, together with resonance between the two oxygens once deprotonated, is what gives carboxylic acids their characteristic reactivity and enhanced acidity.
questions.hint: The name 'carboxyl' itself is a blend of 'carbonyl' and 'hydroxyl'.
distractor_logic: The carboxyl group does have an O−H bond (the hydroxyl part); this ionisable proton is exactly what is lost when the acid is deprotonated.
The group is not two separate hydroxyls; it is one carbonyl oxygen (C=O) and one hydroxyl oxygen (−OH) on the same carbon, a distinct combination.
There is no ether-type C−O−C linkage in a simple carboxyl group; both oxygens are attached to the same single carbon, not bridging two different carbons.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Vigorous oxidation of an alkylbenzene (such as toluene) with hot, concentrated alkaline KMnO₄, followed by acidification, gives:
options: Benzoic acid, regardless of how long the original alkyl side chain was
An aromatic aldehyde, stopping short of full oxidation
A simple phenol
The corresponding alkylbenzoic acid, retaining the full original side-chain length
questions.explanation: Hot alkaline KMnO₄ oxidises any benzylic-hydrogen-bearing alkyl side chain, regardless of its original length, all the way down to a single ring-attached −COOH group; the rest of the side chain is lost as CO₂/carbonate byproducts, so toluene, ethylbenzene, and propylbenzene all give the same product, benzoic acid, after acidification.
questions.hint: This oxidant is strong enough to shorten ANY alkyl side chain down to just the single ring-attached carbon.
distractor_logic: Hot, concentrated alkaline KMnO₄ is a vigorous oxidant that proceeds all the way to the carboxylic acid, not stopping at the intermediate aldehyde stage.
A phenol would require an −OH group directly on the ring, not oxidation of a side chain to a carboxylic acid group.
The alkyl side chain length is NOT retained; regardless of starting chain length, oxidation cuts the chain down to a single −COOH group directly on the ring.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: A Grignard reagent, RMgX, reacts with dry ice (solid CO₂), and the resulting product is then hydrolysed with dilute acid, to give:
options: An alcohol, R−OH, with the same number of carbons as the Grignard reagent
A carboxylic acid, R−COOH, with one more carbon than the original Grignard reagent's R group
No reaction occurs between a Grignard reagent and CO₂
An aldehyde, R−CHO
questions.explanation: The Grignard carbanion attacks the electrophilic carbon of CO₂, giving a magnesium carboxylate salt (R−COOMgX); acidic hydrolysis then liberates the free carboxylic acid, R−COOH — this route adds exactly one new carbon (from CO₂) to the original R group.
questions.hint: CO₂ itself contributes the new carbonyl carbon of the product.
distractor_logic: A simple alcohol with the SAME carbon count as R would come from reaction with an epoxide or a carbonyl already bearing R's own carbon skeleton, not from reaction with CO₂, which contributes an entirely new carbon.

Grignard reagents are highly reactive nucleophiles/strong bases that do react readily with the electrophilic carbon of CO₂; this is in fact a standard, reliable synthetic method for building carboxylic acids.
An aldehyde would be a less oxidised product than what actually forms here; reaction with CO₂ followed by hydrolysis gives the fully oxidised carboxylic acid directly.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Hydrolysis of a nitrile, R−C≡N, under either acidic or basic aqueous conditions gives:
options: An aldehyde, R−CHO
A carboxylic acid, R−COOH (or its salt, under basic conditions)
A primary amine, R−CH₂NH₂
The starting alkyl halide, R−X, is regenerated
questions.explanation: Nitrile hydrolysis proceeds through an amide intermediate and ultimately gives the carboxylic acid (isolated as its salt if the hydrolysis was carried out under basic conditions, and then acidified to the free acid).
questions.hint: Hydrolysis of a nitrile is a standard route used specifically to build up to the carboxylic acid oxidation level.
distractor_logic: An aldehyde would be a less oxidised, different product; nitrile hydrolysis proceeds through to the fully hydrolysed carboxylic acid (or amide intermediate), not an aldehyde.
Reduction (not hydrolysis) of a nitrile with, e.g., LiAlH₄ or catalytic H₂, gives a primary amine; hydrolysis with water instead gives the carboxylic acid.
Hydrolysis of the nitrile functional group does not regenerate an alkyl halide; no halogen is present in the nitrile to begin with.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Complete oxidation of a primary alcohol (e.g. with hot acidified KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₄, in excess) gives:
options: A ketone
An aldehyde only, with oxidation stopping there
An ether
A carboxylic acid
questions.explanation: Strong, excess oxidants like hot acidified KMnO₄ do not stop at the aldehyde stage; they continue oxidising a primary alcohol all the way to the corresponding carboxylic acid.
questions.hint: This question specifies a STRONG oxidant used in EXCESS, unlike the milder, controlled PCC oxidation.
distractor_logic: A ketone would require oxidation of a SECONDARY alcohol, not a primary one; a primary alcohol under strong oxidation gives a carboxylic acid, passing through the aldehyde stage.
Stopping cleanly at the aldehyde requires a milder, specifically chosen oxidant (like PCC); a strong oxidant in excess, as specified here, continues on to the carboxylic acid.
Oxidation of the O−H/C−H bonds at the alcohol carbon produces a carbonyl-containing product (ultimately the carboxylic acid), not an ether linkage.

questions.topic: Reactions of Carboxylic Acids: Derivative Formation and Substituent Effects on Acidity
questions.question: Treating a carboxylic acid with thionyl chloride (SOCl₂) converts it into:
options: The corresponding ester
The corresponding alcohol, R−CH₂OH
The corresponding acid chloride, R−COCl
The corresponding amide
questions.explanation: SOCl₂ replaces the acid's −OH with −Cl, giving the acid chloride, along with gaseous SO₂ and HCl byproducts, which conveniently escape the reaction mixture, simplifying purification.
questions.hint: This reagent is a standard way to convert −COOH into a much more reactive acyl derivative.
distractor_logic: Forming an ester would require reaction with an alcohol (Fischer esterification), not thionyl chloride, though the acid chloride made here is itself often used to make esters in a subsequent step.
SOCl₂ is not a reducing agent; converting the acid to an alcohol would require a strong hydride reducer like LiAlH₄, not SOCl₂.
Forming an amide directly would require reaction with ammonia or an amine, not thionyl chloride alone.

questions.topic: Reactions of Carboxylic Acids: Derivative Formation and Substituent Effects on Acidity
questions.question: Fischer esterification of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol is typically catalysed by:
options: No catalyst is needed at all
A radical initiator
A small amount of concentrated H₂SO₄ (or another strong acid)
A large excess of a strong base like NaOH
questions.explanation: Acid catalysis (commonly conc. H₂SO₄) protonates the carbonyl oxygen, making the carbonyl carbon more electrophilic and facilitating nucleophilic attack by the alcohol; the reaction is reversible and an excess of one reactant (or removal of water) is used to drive the equilibrium toward the ester.
questions.hint: This reaction proceeds through a protonated, more electrophilic carbonyl intermediate.
distractor_logic: The uncatalysed reaction between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol is very slow; a catalyst (typically acidic) is needed to achieve a useful reaction rate.
This is an acid-catalysed, polar mechanism (not a radical chain reaction), so a radical initiator has no role here.
Strong base would instead deprotonate/hydrolyse the ester product (saponification) rather than promote its formation from the acid and alcohol.

questions.topic: Reactions of Carboxylic Acids: Derivative Formation and Substituent Effects on Acidity
questions.question: The Hell−Volhard−Zelinsky (HVZ) reaction, which introduces a halogen at the alpha-carbon of a carboxylic acid, uses which reagents?
options: X₂ (Cl₂ or Br₂) in the presence of red phosphorus
H₂/Ni catalyst
Dilute aqueous KMnO₄
NaOH and heat
questions.explanation: Red phosphorus reacts with X₂ to generate PX₃, which converts the carboxylic acid into a small amount of the reactive acid halide in situ; this enolises readily and is halogenated at the alpha-carbon, ultimately giving the alpha-halo carboxylic acid after the halogen exchanges back onto the acid.
questions.hint: The reagents here specifically introduce a halogen next to (not onto) the carboxyl carbon itself.
distractor_logic: H₂/Ni is a hydrogenation (reducing) system, unrelated to introducing a halogen at the alpha-carbon.
Dilute aqueous KMnO₄ is an oxidising test reagent, not the halogenating reagent combination used in the HVZ reaction.
NaOH and heat describes conditions for other reactions (e.g. decarboxylation with soda lime, or ester hydrolysis), not the halogen-introducing HVZ reaction.

questions.topic: Nomenclature and Structure of the Carbonyl Group in Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃−CH₂−CH₂−CHO?
options: Butanal
Propanal
Butan-1-ol
Butan-2-one
questions.explanation: The 4-carbon chain ends in a −CHO group at C1; naming the parent chain 'butane' and replacing '-e' with '-al' (no locant needed, since an aldehyde carbon is always C1) gives butanal.
questions.hint: Count the carbons in the longest chain, including the carbonyl carbon.
distractor_logic: Propanal has only 3 carbons, one fewer than this 4-carbon chain.
Butan-1-ol would require an −OH group, not a −CHO (aldehyde) group, at C1.
Butan-2-one would require a ketone (C=O flanked by two carbon chains) at C2, but here the carbonyl carbon is a terminal −CHO, an aldehyde.

questions.topic: Nomenclature and Structure of the Carbonyl Group in Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃−CO−CH₂−CH₃?
options: Butan-2-one
Butanal
Butan-1-one
Butan-2-ol
questions.explanation: The carbonyl carbon is the second carbon of a 4-carbon chain, flanked by two carbon-containing groups (a ketone); numbering from the end that gives the carbonyl the lower locant gives butan-2-one.
questions.hint: Locate the carbonyl carbon's position within the 4-carbon chain, then number to give it the lowest locant.
distractor_logic: Butanal would require a terminal −CHO (aldehyde) group, but here the carbonyl carbon is internal, flanked by two alkyl groups, making it a ketone.
'Butan-1-one' is not a valid name; a ketone's carbonyl carbon must be flanked by carbon on both sides, which is structurally impossible at C1 of a simple unbranched chain.
Butan-2-ol would require an −OH group at C2 (an alcohol), not a C=O group; the given structure has a carbonyl, not a hydroxyl.

questions.topic: Nomenclature and Structure of the Carbonyl Group in Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: 'Acetophenone' (the common name for the simplest aryl methyl ketone, C₆H₅−CO−CH₃) has the IUPAC name:
options: Benzaldehyde
Phenylethanal
1-Phenylethan-1-one
1-Phenylethan-1-ol
questions.explanation: The parent chain is ethane (2 carbons: the carbonyl carbon and the methyl carbon), bearing a phenyl substituent at C1 and a ketone at C1, giving 1-phenylethan-1-one.
questions.hint: The parent chain here is only 2 carbons long (the C=O carbon plus its attached CH₃); the phenyl ring is a substituent, not part of the numbered chain.
distractor_logic: Benzaldehyde, C₆H₅CHO, is a completely different, simpler compound (the carbonyl carbon bears only H and phenyl, no methyl group).
'Phenylethanal' would describe an aldehyde (−CHO) attached to a phenyl-substituted chain, but acetophenone's carbonyl carbon is flanked by phenyl AND methyl, making it a ketone, not an aldehyde.
'1-Phenylethan-1-ol' would describe an alcohol (−OH) at C1, not the ketone (C=O) that is actually present in acetophenone.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: To convert a nitrile, R−C≡N, selectively into an aldehyde, R−CHO, WITHOUT over-reducing it further to the amine, a chemist should use:
options: DIBAL-H at low temperature (−78°C), followed by hydrolysis
NaBH₄ in aqueous ethanol at room temperature
Excess LiAlH₄, followed by hydrolysis
H₂ gas over a standard, unpoisoned Pd catalyst
questions.explanation: DIBAL-H (diisobutylaluminium hydride) at low temperature delivers only ONE hydride, forming a stable imine-aluminium intermediate that survives until aqueous workup, at which point it hydrolyses cleanly to the aldehyde, without further reduction to the amine.
questions.hint: This method is specifically chosen because it can be controlled to deliver just one equivalent of hydride under carefully cold conditions.
distractor_logic: NaBH₄ is generally too weak to reduce a nitrile at all under these mild conditions; it is typically used on the already-more-electrophilic carbonyl group of aldehydes/ketones, not nitriles.
Excess LiAlH₄ is a strong, uncontrolled hydride source that reduces a nitrile all the way to the primary amine, overshooting the aldehyde stage.

An unpoisoned Pd hydrogenation catalyst, without the controlled poisoning used in the Rosenmund reduction (which in any case applies to acid chlorides, not nitriles), would tend to over-reduce the nitrile rather than stop cleanly at the aldehyde.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: The Gatterman−Koch reaction, used to introduce a −CHO group directly onto an aromatic ring, uses which reagent combination?
options: O₃ followed by Zn/H₂O
H₂/Pd−BaSO₄
CO and HCl gas, with anhydrous AlCl₃/CuCl catalyst, under pressure
CH₃COCl with anhydrous AlCl₃
questions.explanation: This is essentially a formylation variant of Friedel−Crafts chemistry: CO and HCl generate a formyl cation (HCO⁺) in situ, activated by AlCl₃/CuCl, which attacks the aromatic ring to install −CHO directly.
questions.hint: This reaction is specifically used to put an aldehyde group directly ON a benzene ring, using two simple gases as the carbon/oxygen and chlorine sources.
distractor_logic: O₃ then Zn/H₂O is the ozonolysis sequence, used to cleave alkene double bonds, unrelated to formylating an aromatic ring.
H₂/Pd−BaSO₄ describes the Rosenmund reduction, which converts an acid chloride to an aldehyde; it does not install a formyl group directly onto an aromatic ring from scratch.
CH₃COCl/AlCl₃ is standard Friedel−Crafts ACYLATION, which installs a −COCH₃ (ketone) group, not a −CHO (aldehyde) group.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Acid-catalysed hydration of propyne (CH₃−C≡CH) with dilute H₂SO₄/HgSO₄ gives, via Markovnikov addition and tautomerisation, which product?
options: Propanal
Propene
Propan-2-one (acetone/propanone)
Propan-1-ol
questions.explanation: Markovnikov addition of water places −OH on the more substituted internal carbon, giving an unstable enol that tautomerises to the more stable keto form; for propyne this gives propan-2-one.
questions.hint: Apply Markovnikov's rule to decide which carbon receives the −OH, then convert the resulting enol to its keto tautomer.
