distractor_logic: Propanal would result only from ethyne's (not propyne's) hydration, or from anti-Markovnikov addition, which does not apply under these standard Hg²⁺-catalysed conditions.
Propene would be the product of partial reduction (addition of H₂), not hydration (addition of H₂O).

Propan-1-ol would require simple addition of water without any subsequent tautomerisation to a carbonyl; hydration of an alkyne always proceeds through an enol intermediate that tautomerises to a carbonyl compound.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Reaction of an acid chloride, R−COCl, with a lithium dialkylcuprate (Gilman reagent), R′₂CuLi, gives:
options: A ketone, R−CO−R′
A carboxylic acid
A tertiary alcohol
An alkane
questions.explanation: The soft, mild nucleophilicity of a Gilman reagent allows it to add just one R′ group cleanly to the acid chloride's carbonyl carbon, stopping at the ketone stage rather than over-adding as an ordinary Grignard reagent would.
questions.hint: This mild organocopper reagent is specifically chosen because it reacts with acid chlorides in a more controlled way than a Grignard reagent does.
distractor_logic: The starting acid chloride is already at the carboxylic acid oxidation level (one step more oxidised, with Cl replacing OH); this reaction does not oxidise it further to a free carboxylic acid.

A tertiary alcohol would form if the organometallic added twice (as an ordinary Grignard reagent often does with an acid chloride, first to the ketone stage and then again to the alcohol); Gilman reagents are specifically valued for stopping cleanly at the ketone.
Forming an alkane would require complete loss of the oxygen functionality, which does not occur in this carbon−carbon bond-forming addition reaction.

questions.topic: Physical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Arranging butanal, butan-1-ol, and pentane (all of comparable molecular mass) in order of INCREASING boiling point gives:
options: Butanal < pentane < butan-1-ol
Pentane < butanal < butan-1-ol
Butan-1-ol < butanal < pentane
All three have identical boiling points
questions.explanation: Pentane (only weak dispersion forces) boils lowest; butanal (polar C=O, dipole−dipole attraction, but no O−H hydrogen bonding between its own molecules) boils higher than pentane but lower than butan-1-ol, which can hydrogen-bond through its −OH group and therefore boils highest.
questions.hint: Rank the strength of intermolecular forces present in each: dispersion-only, dipole−dipole, or hydrogen bonding.
distractor_logic: This places pentane (dispersion forces only) above butan-1-ol (hydrogen bonding); pentane, with the weakest intermolecular forces, should be the lowest-boiling, not intermediate.

This places butan-1-ol (which hydrogen-bonds) as the lowest-boiling of the three, when it should be the highest, since hydrogen bonding is the strongest of the three intermolecular forces being compared.

The three compounds have distinctly different intermolecular forces available to them (dispersion only, dipole−dipole, and hydrogen bonding respectively), so their boiling points are measurably different, not identical.

questions.topic: Physical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Propan-2-one (acetone) is completely miscible with water, but hexan-2-one (a similarly-structured but larger ketone) is only slightly soluble. This trend is best explained by:
options: As the non-polar hydrocarbon portion of the molecule grows, it increasingly dominates over the ability of the small polar carbonyl group to hydrogen-bond with water
Hexan-2-one has no carbonyl group, unlike acetone
Larger ketones lose their carbonyl group's ability to accept hydrogen bonds entirely
Solubility in water is unrelated to molecular size for any class of organic compound
questions.explanation: Both ketones can hydrogen-bond to water through their carbonyl oxygen, but as the hydrocarbon chain lengthens, the growing non-polar portion becomes increasingly dominant relative to the fixed, small polar carbonyl group, progressively reducing overall water solubility — a general trend across homologous series of polar organic compounds.
questions.hint: The carbonyl group itself does not change between these two ketones; ask what else is different, and how it scales with molecular size.
distractor_logic: Hexan-2-one does have a carbonyl group (it is a ketone, C₄H₉COCH₃); the premise that it lacks one entirely is factually incorrect.

The carbonyl oxygen's lone pairs remain available to accept hydrogen bonds from water regardless of overall chain length; what changes is the relative PROPORTION of polar to non-polar character in the molecule as a whole.

Molecular size (specifically, the size of the non-polar hydrocarbon portion relative to the polar functional group) is a well-established, major factor in aqueous solubility trends across many classes of organic compounds, not just this one.
