stronger +I donation → C less electrophilic</text></svg> Based on the steric and electronic comparison shown above, rank the following four carbonyl compounds in DECREASING order of reactivity toward nucleophilic addition: (i) HCHO, (ii) CH₃CHO, (iii) CH₃COCH₃, (iv) C₆H₅COC₆H₅.
options: All four are equally reactive, since all contain the same C=O functional group
questions.explanation: HCHO has no alkyl/aryl groups at all (least steric hindrance, no +I donation) and is the most reactive. CH₃CHO has one small methyl group. CH₃COCH₃ has two alkyl groups (more steric bulk and +I donation). C₆H₅COC₆H₅ has two bulky aryl groups that both sterically block approach AND donate electron density into the ring/carbonyl by resonance, making it the least reactive of the four.
questions.hint: Count and compare the size/type (H, alkyl, or aryl) of the two groups flanking each carbonyl carbon.
distractor_logic: This is the exact reverse order; the diaryl ketone (most steric bulk, strongest electron donation via ring conjugation) is the LEAST reactive of the four, not the most.
The four compounds differ substantially in both steric bulk and electron-donating character at the carbonyl carbon; they are not all equally reactive despite sharing the same functional group.
This incorrectly places the dialkyl ketone above formaldehyde; formaldehyde, having no alkyl substituents at all, is always the most reactive of this series.

questions.topic: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
questions.question: Comparing di-tert-butyl ketone, (CH₃)₃C−CO−C(CH₃)₃, with acetone, CH₃−CO−CH₃, which is expected to react MORE SLOWLY with a bulky nucleophile such as a Grignard reagent, and why?
options: Di-tert-butyl ketone reacts faster, since bulkier groups always increase electrophilicity
Both react at exactly the same rate, since steric bulk of the flanking groups has no effect on nucleophilic addition
Acetone, because methyl groups are more electron-withdrawing than tert-butyl groups
Di-tert-butyl ketone, because its two bulky tert-butyl groups sterically shield the carbonyl carbon far more than acetone's two small methyl groups
questions.explanation: The bulky tert-butyl groups on either side of the carbonyl carbon in di-tert-butyl ketone create severe steric hindrance, blocking the approach of an incoming nucleophile far more than acetone's much smaller methyl groups do — steric hindrance is a major factor (alongside electronic effects) governing nucleophilic addition rates.
questions.hint: Compare the physical size of a tert-butyl group to a simple methyl group.
distractor_logic: Bulkier groups increase steric hindrance and typically increase electron donation into the carbonyl carbon, BOTH of which decrease (not increase) electrophilicity and reactivity toward nucleophilic addition.

Steric bulk of the flanking groups is a major, well-established factor in nucleophilic addition rates; larger groups block the approaching nucleophile and slow the reaction, as seen throughout the aldehyde/ketone reactivity trend.

Methyl groups are actually weakly electron-DONATING (+I, hyperconjugation), not withdrawing, relative to hydrogen; and in any case, tert-butyl groups are even more strongly electron-donating than methyl, which would only reinforce (not reverse) the slower reactivity of the di-tert-butyl ketone.

questions.topic: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
questions.question: Trichloroacetaldehyde, Cl₃C−CHO, is significantly MORE reactive toward nucleophilic addition than ordinary acetaldehyde, CH₃−CHO. What is the best explanation?
options: There is no real difference in reactivity; both compounds react identically toward nucleophiles
Chlorine atoms are simply larger than hydrogen, and larger substituents always increase carbonyl reactivity by steric strain
Chlorine atoms are strongly electron-donating, further stabilising the carbonyl carbon and enhancing its reactivity
The three electronegative chlorine atoms withdraw electron density inductively from the carbonyl carbon, making it even more electrophilic than in acetaldehyde
questions.explanation: The three highly electronegative chlorine atoms on the adjacent carbon pull electron density away from the carbonyl carbon via the inductive effect, making it even more electron-deficient (more electrophilic) than the carbonyl carbon of plain acetaldehyde, which bears only weakly electron-donating methyl-type hydrogens by comparison.
questions.hint: Consider the electronegativity of chlorine and how an electron-withdrawing group nearby would affect the carbonyl carbon's existing electron deficiency.
distractor_logic: The two compounds differ measurably in reactivity precisely because of this electron-withdrawing inductive effect; trichloroacetaldehyde is well known (e.g. in its hydrate, chloral hydrate) to be unusually reactive toward nucleophilic addition.

It is chlorine's ELECTRONIC effect (inductive withdrawal), not its physical size, that is responsible for the increased reactivity here; steric bulk alone does not explain why an electron-withdrawing group specifically increases electrophilicity.
Chlorine is a highly electronegative element and withdraws electron density inductively; it is not electron-donating, and this option describes the opposite of chlorine's actual inductive effect.

questions.topic: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
questions.question: Addition of a Grignard reagent, CH₃MgBr, to acetone (CH₃COCH₃), followed by acidic aqueous workup, gives which product?
options: Propan-2-ol (a secondary alcohol)
2-Methylpropanal
Isobutylene (2-methylpropene)
2-Methylpropan-2-ol (a tertiary alcohol)
questions.explanation: The Grignard's carbanion attacks acetone's carbonyl carbon, and after aqueous workup the alkoxide is protonated; since the carbonyl carbon already bore two methyl groups and now gains a third from the Grignard reagent, the resulting alcohol carbon is bonded to three carbon groups — a tertiary alcohol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tert-butanol).
questions.hint: Count how many carbon-containing groups end up attached to the former carbonyl carbon after the new C−C bond forms.
distractor_logic: A secondary alcohol would result from a Grignard reagent adding to an ALDEHYDE (which starts with only one alkyl group on the carbonyl carbon), not a ketone that already carries two.
This describes the starting ketone reduced to an alcohol without any new carbon added, which is not what a Grignard addition does; a new C−C bond forms, adding the Grignard's own carbon group.
No elimination reaction occurs here; this is a nucleophilic addition to the carbonyl, forming a new carbon−carbon bond and an alcohol, not an alkene.

questions.topic: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
questions.question: What is the structure of the cyanohydrin formed when HCN adds to butan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₃?
options: 2-Hydroxy-2-methylbutanenitrile, CH₃C(OH)(CN)CH₂CH₃
Butanenitrile, with no hydroxyl group present
Butan-2-ol
2-Aminobutanenitrile
questions.explanation: HCN adds across the C=O of butan-2-one: the carbon that was the carbonyl carbon now bears −OH (from the original oxygen, after protonation) and −CN (from the added cyanide), along with its original methyl and ethyl groups — giving 2-hydroxy-2-methylbutanenitrile.
questions.hint: Both a new −CN group and the original oxygen (now as −OH) end up on the same, former carbonyl carbon.
distractor_logic: The original carbonyl oxygen is retained as a hydroxyl group in the cyanohydrin product; it is not lost, and the product does contain both −OH and −CN on the same carbon.
Butan-2-ol would be the product of simple hydride reduction (e.g. with NaBH₄), not addition of HCN, which installs a −CN group, not just an additional hydrogen.
No nitrogen-containing amine forms directly from simple HCN addition; the nitrogen remains as part of the nitrile (−C≡N) group in the cyanohydrin product.

questions.topic: Reactions with Ammonia Derivatives and Other Addition–Elimination Reactions
questions.question: Reaction of a ketone with semicarbazide, H₂N−NH−CO−NH₂, gives a product called a:
options: Hydrazone
Semicarbazone
Cyanohydrin
Oxime
questions.explanation: Semicarbazide's terminal −NH₂ condenses with the carbonyl (addition, then loss of water) to give the C=N-containing semicarbazone, R₂C=N−NH−CO−NH₂, often used as a solid, sharply-melting derivative for identifying an unknown carbonyl compound.
questions.hint: This product's name directly reflects the reagent (semicarbazide) that formed it.
distractor_logic: A hydrazone forms specifically from plain hydrazine (NH₂NH₂) or its substituted derivatives like phenylhydrazine, not from semicarbazide.
A cyanohydrin forms from HCN addition, an entirely different reagent from semicarbazide.
An oxime forms specifically from hydroxylamine (NH₂OH), not from semicarbazide.

questions.topic: Reactions with Ammonia Derivatives and Other Addition–Elimination Reactions
questions.question: Reagents like 2,4-DNP, semicarbazide, and phenylhydrazine are all useful in the laboratory for the same underlying purpose, which is best described as:
options: Permanently destroying the carbonyl group so the compound can no longer react further
Converting a liquid or oily carbonyl compound into a solid, sharply-melting crystalline derivative that helps identify the original compound
Reducing the carbonyl compound all the way to the corresponding hydrocarbon
Making the compound significantly more volatile for easier gas-phase analysis
questions.explanation: Many aldehydes and ketones are liquids or oils with similar physical properties, making them hard to identify directly; converting them into solid, well-characterised, sharply-melting derivatives (2,4-DNP derivatives, semicarbazones, phenylhydrazones) with well-tabulated melting points is a classic technique to help identify the original unknown carbonyl compound.
questions.hint: These reagents all react with the SAME functional group (C=O) to form a class of solid, identifiable derivatives.
distractor_logic: The reaction with these reagents is reversible (the parent carbonyl compound can typically be regenerated by acidic hydrolysis of the derivative); it does not permanently destroy the carbonyl functionality.
These reagents form a new C=N-type derivative, they do not reduce the carbon skeleton down to a simple hydrocarbon.

The purpose is the OPPOSITE of increasing volatility; converting a volatile liquid into a solid, crystalline derivative with a sharp melting point is specifically useful because solids are easier to purify and characterise by melting point, not because they are more volatile.

questions.topic: Reactions with Ammonia Derivatives and Other Addition–Elimination Reactions
questions.question: What is the product when acetone (CH₃COCH₃) reacts with phenylhydrazine, C₆H₅NHNH₂?
options: Acetone semicarbazone
2-Phenylpropan-2-ol
Acetone oxime
Acetone phenylhydrazone, (CH₃)₂C=N−NHC₆H₅
questions.explanation: Phenylhydrazine's terminal −NH₂ condenses with acetone's carbonyl (addition−elimination of water) to give the phenylhydrazone, (CH₃)₂C=N−NHC₆H₅.
questions.hint: Match the reagent name directly to the type of derivative it forms.
distractor_logic: A semicarbazone would form from semicarbazide, not plain phenylhydrazine.
No alcohol forms here; this reaction is a condensation (addition then loss of water) with a nitrogen nucleophile, not a simple hydride reduction to an alcohol.
An oxime would form from hydroxylamine (NH₂OH), not phenylhydrazine.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: Self-aldol condensation of acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO) with dilute NaOH, followed by heating (dehydration), gives which final product?
options: 3-Hydroxybutanal (the aldol addition product, with no dehydration)
Ethanol
But-2-enal (crotonaldehyde), CH₃−CH=CH−CHO
Acetic acid
questions.explanation: Base removes an alpha-hydrogen from one acetaldehyde molecule to form its enolate, which attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second acetaldehyde molecule, giving 3-hydroxybutanal (the addition product); heating then dehydrates this beta-hydroxy aldehyde to the conjugated alpha,beta-unsaturated aldehyde, but-2-enal.
questions.hint: The question specifies heating AFTER the base treatment, which drives the dehydration step to completion.
distractor_logic: 3-Hydroxybutanal is only the intermediate ADDITION product, formed before the specified heating/dehydration step; the question asks for the final product after heating.

Ethanol would require a completely different reaction (e.g. Cannizzaro disproportionation, which does not apply here since acetaldehyde does have an alpha-hydrogen and follows the aldol pathway instead).
Acetic acid would require oxidation of the aldehyde, which is not what occurs under base-catalysed aldol condensation conditions.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: When acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO) and propanal (CH₃CH₂CHO) — both of which have alpha-hydrogens — are mixed together with dilute NaOH, the CROSSED aldol reaction between them typically gives:
options: No reaction at all, since aldol condensation requires two molecules of the SAME compound
A mixture of up to four different aldol products (two 'self' products and two 'crossed' products), since either compound's enolate can attack either compound's carbonyl
Only the two 'self' aldol products, with no crossed product forming at all
Only a single, clean crossed product, since crossed aldol reactions are always perfectly selective
questions.explanation: Since both starting carbonyl compounds have alpha-hydrogens, EITHER can be deprotonated to form an enolate, and that enolate can attack the carbonyl carbon of EITHER starting material (itself or the other compound) — giving up to four distinct possible aldol products: two 'self' products and two 'crossed' products, typically as a mixture rather than one clean product.
questions.hint: Consider how many different enolate/electrophile COMBINATIONS are possible when both starting materials can act as either partner.
distractor_logic: Aldol condensation does not require both molecules to be identical; a crossed aldol between two DIFFERENT alpha-hydrogen-bearing carbonyl compounds is a well-known (if often low-yielding/mixture-forming) reaction.

Since both compounds have alpha-hydrogens and can act as either the nucleophile (enolate) or electrophile (carbonyl), crossed products DO form alongside the two self-condensation products, not instead of them being entirely absent.

A crossed aldol between two different enolisable carbonyl compounds is generally NOT selective for a single product; without a specific strategy to control selectivity, a mixture of multiple products is the typical (and practically limiting) outcome.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: An aldol condensation product is identified as but-2-enal, CH₃−CH=CH−CHO. Working backward, which starting carbonyl compound, on self-aldol condensation, would give this product?
options: Acetone (CH₃COCH₃)
Acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO), via enolisation, addition, and subsequent dehydration
Propanal (CH₃CH₂CHO)
Butanal (CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO)
questions.explanation: But-2-enal has 4 carbons total; tracing back through the dehydration and addition steps of a self-aldol condensation shows it arises from two molecules of the 2-carbon aldehyde, acetaldehyde (the classic textbook example: 2 CH₃CHO → CH₃CH=CHCHO + H₂O).
questions.hint: A self-aldol condensation combines TWO molecules of the SAME starting compound; work out how many carbons the starting material must have contributed on each side.
distractor_logic: Acetone's self-aldol condensation product would be a ketone-derived enone (4-methylpent-3-en-2-one), not an aldehyde-derived enal like but-2-enal.

Propanal's self-aldol condensation product would have a different carbon count and branching pattern (it would form 2-methylpent-2-enal, not but-2-enal), since propanal itself already has 3 carbons before combining.
Butanal's self-aldol condensation product would likewise have more carbons and a different substitution pattern than but-2-enal.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: Cannizzaro reaction of benzaldehyde (C₆H₅CHO) with concentrated NaOH gives benzyl alcohol and:
options: Sodium acetate, CH₃COONa
Another molecule of benzyl alcohol, with no salt formed
Benzoic acid (uncharged, C₆H₅COOH)
Sodium benzoate, C₆H₅COONa
questions.explanation: Benzaldehyde has no alpha-hydrogen (the carbon adjacent to the carbonyl is the aromatic ring carbon, which is not available for enolisation in the usual sense), so it undergoes Cannizzaro disproportionation: one molecule is reduced to benzyl alcohol (C₆H₅CH₂OH) while a second is oxidised to the carboxylate salt, sodium benzoate, under the strongly basic conditions.
questions.hint: Benzaldehyde retains its full aromatic ring and carbon count in both products; track where each carbon ends up.
distractor_logic: Sodium acetate has only two carbons in a simple aliphatic chain; benzaldehyde's aromatic ring is retained in its oxidised product, giving the aromatic carboxylate sodium benzoate, not this unrelated aliphatic salt.

This is a disproportionation reaction (one molecule oxidised, one reduced) specifically because benzaldehyde lacks an alpha-hydrogen; it does not simply give two molecules of the same reduced product.
Under the strongly basic (concentrated NaOH) reaction conditions specified, the acid product exists deprotonated as its sodium salt, not as the free (uncharged) carboxylic acid.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: Given the set of carbonyl compounds {CH₃CHO, HCHO, C₆H₅CHO, CH₃CH₂CHO}, which one(s) can undergo the Cannizzaro reaction with concentrated base rather than aldol condensation?
options: HCHO and C₆H₅CHO only, since neither has an alpha-hydrogen available
CH₃CHO and CH₃CH₂CHO only, since these are the smallest aldehydes
None of the four, since Cannizzaro only applies to ketones, never aldehydes
All four compounds equally, since Cannizzaro applies to any aldehyde
questions.explanation: HCHO has no carbon attached to its carbonyl carbon at all (so no alpha-hydrogen exists), and C₆H₅CHO's carbonyl carbon is attached only to the aromatic ring (also no alpha-hydrogen in the aliphatic sense); both therefore cannot form an enolate and instead undergo Cannizzaro disproportionation. CH₃CHO and CH₃CH₂CHO both have accessible alpha-hydrogens on an adjacent sp³ carbon and preferentially undergo aldol condensation instead.
questions.hint: For each compound, check whether there is a carbon bearing a hydrogen directly adjacent to the carbonyl carbon.
distractor_logic: This identifies exactly the two compounds (CH₃CHO and CH₃CH₂CHO) that DO have alpha-hydrogens and therefore undergo aldol condensation instead of Cannizzaro, the reverse of the correct pairing.

The Cannizzaro reaction is specifically a reaction of certain ALDEHYDES (those without an alpha-hydrogen), not ketones; ketones generally do not undergo this disproportionation at all under these conditions.
Cannizzaro reaction is specific to aldehydes lacking an alpha-hydrogen; aldehydes that DO have an alpha-hydrogen (like the other two in this set) follow the aldol pathway instead, not Cannizzaro.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: The haloform reaction of butan-2-one (CH₃COCH₂CH₃) with I₂/NaOH gives iodoform (CHI₃) and which carboxylate salt?
options: Sodium acetate, CH₃COONa
Sodium butanoate, CH₃CH₂CH₂COONa
Sodium propanoate, CH₃CH₂COONa
No carboxylate forms; only iodoform is produced
questions.explanation: Butan-2-one's methyl ketone group (CH₃CO−) is triiodinated and cleaved by NaOH, releasing CHI₃ (iodoform) and leaving the REMAINING portion of the molecule (the ethyl group plus the original carbonyl carbon) as the carboxylate: CH₃CH₂COONa, sodium propanoate.
questions.hint: Trace which carbon becomes CHI₃ (the original methyl-ketone carbon) and which carbons remain attached to the carbonyl carbon that becomes the carboxylate.
distractor_logic: Sodium acetate (2 carbons) would be the byproduct if the starting ketone were a simpler methyl ketone like acetone; butan-2-one's larger ethyl group carries through into a 3-carbon carboxylate instead.
Sodium butanoate (4 carbons) overcounts; one carbon (as CHI₃) is cleaved away from the original 4-carbon ketone, leaving only 3 carbons in the carboxylate product.
The haloform reaction always produces a carboxylate salt as the second product alongside the haloform; it is not a reaction that gives only one product.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: A synthesis requires reducing a ketone that also bears a base-sensitive ester group elsewhere in the molecule, all the way to a −CH₂− group. Which named reduction should be chosen, and why?
options: Neither method can achieve a full carbonyl-to-methylene reduction; only catalytic H₂ can do this
Clemmensen reduction (Zn−Hg/conc. HCl), since its acidic conditions will not attack the base-sensitive ester group
Either method works identically well regardless of what other functional groups are present
Wolff−Kishner reduction (NH₂NH₂/KOH), since its basic conditions are always safer for any other functional group present
questions.explanation: Clemmensen reduction uses strongly ACIDIC conditions (Zn−Hg/conc. HCl), which would leave a base-sensitive group (like certain esters that might be hydrolysed or degraded under strong base) unaffected; Wolff−Kishner's strongly BASIC conditions (KOH) would instead risk attacking or hydrolysing such a group, making Clemmensen the safer choice here.
questions.hint: Match the ACIDIC or BASIC nature of each named reduction's conditions against what the OTHER functional group in the molecule can tolerate.
distractor_logic: Both Clemmensen and Wolff−Kishner ARE established, standard methods for the full carbonyl-to-methylene reduction; catalytic H₂ over a simple metal catalyst is not the standard method for this particular transformation.

The two methods use very different reaction conditions (strongly acidic vs. strongly basic); the choice between them specifically depends on which other functional groups are present and what they can tolerate, so they are not interchangeable in general.
Wolff−Kishner's strongly basic KOH conditions are specifically the ones that risk damaging a base-sensitive group; this option has the safety logic backwards for this substrate.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Which of the following compounds gives a POSITIVE iodoform test: pentan-3-one (CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃) or pentan-2-one (CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃)?
options: Pentan-3-one, since it is the more symmetrical of the two
Neither compound gives a positive test, since both are ketones with five carbons
Pentan-2-one, since it has a methyl group directly on the carbonyl carbon (a CH₃CO− group)
Both give a positive test equally
questions.explanation: Pentan-2-one has a terminal CH₃CO− group (methyl directly bonded to the carbonyl carbon), satisfying the iodoform test's structural requirement. Pentan-3-one's carbonyl carbon is flanked by two ethyl groups, with no methyl group directly attached to it, so it gives a negative test.
questions.hint: Check specifically whether either ketone has a CH₃ group bonded DIRECTLY to the carbonyl carbon.
distractor_logic: Molecular symmetry is not the deciding factor for the iodoform test; the specific requirement is a methyl group directly on the carbonyl carbon (or a CH₃CH(OH)− group), which pentan-3-one lacks despite its symmetry.
Carbon count (five carbons) is irrelevant to the iodoform test; what matters is the specific local structural motif (CH₃CO−) at the carbonyl carbon, which pentan-2-one possesses.

The two ketones differ specifically in whether a methyl group sits directly on the carbonyl carbon; pentan-2-one has one and gives a positive test, while pentan-3-one does not and gives a negative test — they do not behave identically.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Which reagent will selectively oxidise an aldehyde group to a carboxylic acid in a molecule that ALSO contains an isolated carbon−carbon double bond, WITHOUT oxidatively cleaving that double bond?
options: Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal AgNO₃), a mild oxidant specific to the aldehyde's C−H bond
Hot, concentrated, acidified KMnO₄, which vigorously oxidises everything in its path
O₃ followed by Zn/H₂O (ozonolysis conditions)
Excess H₂/Pt catalyst
questions.explanation: Tollens' reagent is a mild, selective oxidant that specifically targets the aldehyde's C−H bond (via the mechanism of the silver mirror test), leaving other functional groups such as an isolated alkene untouched; hot concentrated KMnO₄ and ozonolysis, by contrast, would both attack the double bond directly.
questions.hint: Choose the mildest, most functional-group-selective oxidant among the options, one that targets only the specific aldehyde C−H bond.
distractor_logic: Hot, concentrated, acidified KMnO₄ is a vigorous, non-selective oxidant that would also cleave or dihydroxylate the alkene double bond, not leave it untouched.
Ozonolysis conditions are specifically designed to CLEAVE a C=C double bond; using them here would destroy the alkene, the opposite of the selectivity required.
H₂/Pt is a REDUCING (hydrogenation) system, not an oxidant; it would not oxidise the aldehyde to an acid at all, and would instead tend to reduce the alkene.

questions.topic: Distinguishing Tests for Aldehydes and Ketones (Tollens', Fehling's, Iodoform) and Uses
questions.question: Given the set {acetaldehyde, benzaldehyde, acetone}, which compound gives a POSITIVE Tollens' test but a NEGATIVE Fehling's test?
options: Acetaldehyde
Benzaldehyde
None of the three gives a positive Tollens' test
Acetone
questions.explanation: Benzaldehyde, an aromatic aldehyde, reduces Tollens' reagent (giving a positive silver mirror test, since Tollens' reagent oxidises any aldehyde, aliphatic or aromatic) but does NOT reduce Fehling's solution, which specifically fails with aromatic aldehydes.
questions.hint: Recall the classic exception among aldehyde oxidation tests: one reagent works on all aldehydes, the other only on aliphatic ones.
distractor_logic: Acetaldehyde, an ALIPHATIC aldehyde, gives a positive result with BOTH Tollens' and Fehling's tests, not a mismatch between the two.
Aldehydes (both benzaldehyde and acetaldehyde here) do give a positive Tollens' test; the premise that none does is incorrect.
Acetone is a ketone, not an aldehyde, and gives a NEGATIVE result with both Tollens' and Fehling's tests; ketones do not reduce either reagent under these standard conditions.

questions.topic: Distinguishing Tests for Aldehydes and Ketones (Tollens', Fehling's, Iodoform) and Uses
questions.question: A simple chemical test that can distinguish acetophenone (C₆H₅COCH₃) from benzaldehyde (C₆H₅CHO) is:
options: Tollens' reagent: benzaldehyde gives a positive silver mirror test, while acetophenone (a ketone) gives a negative result
Neither compound can be distinguished by any simple chemical test
Litmus paper: only benzaldehyde turns litmus red
Bromine water: only acetophenone decolourises it
questions.explanation: Benzaldehyde, being an aldehyde, is readily oxidised by Tollens' reagent to give the characteristic silver mirror; acetophenone, being a ketone, is not oxidised by Tollens' reagent and gives no such positive result — a clean and simple way to distinguish the two.
questions.hint: The key structural difference between these two compounds is the presence (or absence) of a hydrogen directly on the carbonyl carbon.
distractor_logic: Tollens' reagent is a simple, well-established, classic test that clearly distinguishes an aldehyde (positive) from a ketone (negative) like this pair; the two ARE readily distinguishable.

Neither compound is significantly acidic or basic enough to give a clear, reliable litmus colour change under normal conditions; litmus is not the standard test used to distinguish aldehydes from ketones.
Bromine water is a test for unsaturation or phenols, not specifically for distinguishing an aldehyde from a ketone in this way; this is not the standard distinguishing test for this particular pair.

questions.topic: Distinguishing Tests for Aldehydes and Ketones (Tollens', Fehling's, Iodoform) and Uses
questions.question: Acetone (propan-2-one) is widely used industrially as a solvent, notably in nail polish remover and as a laboratory solvent, mainly because of which combination of properties?
options: It is completely miscible with water yet also dissolves many non-polar organic substances, and it is volatile enough to evaporate readily
It is completely non-volatile and remains liquid even at very high temperatures
It reacts readily and irreversibly with almost anything it is used to dissolve
It is insoluble in water, which is why it is chosen as a general-purpose solvent
questions.explanation: Acetone's polar carbonyl group makes it miscible with water, while its overall small, only moderately polar structure also lets it dissolve many organic (less polar) substances; its relatively low boiling point (56°C) means it evaporates quickly, both properties making it a practical, versatile, fast-drying solvent.
questions.hint: Think about what practical properties a good general-purpose, fast-drying solvent would need.
distractor_logic: Acetone is in fact quite VOLATILE (low boiling point, 56°C), which is exactly why it evaporates quickly and is useful as a fast-drying solvent, not because it is non-volatile.
A good solvent needs to dissolve substances WITHOUT reacting with (and destroying) them irreversibly; acetone's usefulness comes from being a relatively inert, non-reactive solvent for many purposes.

Acetone is in fact completely MISCIBLE with water (an important part of its usefulness), not insoluble in it; this solubility, combined with its ability to also dissolve non-polar substances, is exactly what makes it versatile.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Comparing chloroacetic acid (ClCH₂COOH) with plain acetic acid (CH₃COOH), chloroacetic acid is:
options: Less acidic, since chlorine donates electron density inductively, destabilising the carboxylate anion
Equally acidic, since chlorine is too far from the −COOH group to have any effect
Not an acid at all, since the chlorine atom removes the acidic proton entirely
More acidic, since the electronegative chlorine withdraws electron density inductively, stabilising the resulting carboxylate anion
questions.explanation: Chlorine's high electronegativity withdraws electron density inductively through the sigma-bond framework, helping to further stabilise (spread out) the negative charge on the carboxylate anion once the acidic proton is lost; a more stabilised conjugate base corresponds to a stronger (more acidic) parent acid.
questions.hint: Ask whether an electron-withdrawing group nearby would make the carboxylate anion's negative charge MORE or LESS stable.
distractor_logic: Chlorine is electron-WITHDRAWING (inductively), not donating, due to its high electronegativity; this option describes the opposite of chlorine's actual inductive effect.

Chlorine on the alpha-carbon (directly adjacent to −COOH) is close enough to have a significant inductive effect on the acidity of the carboxyl group; proximity does matter, and here the substituent is close, not remote.
The compound retains a fully intact, ionisable −COOH group; the chlorine substitution occurs at a different carbon (the alpha-carbon) and does not remove the acidic proton itself.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH?
options: Propanoic acid
Butanoic acid
Butanal
Butan-1-ol
questions.explanation: The 4-carbon chain terminates in −COOH at C1; naming the parent 'butane' and replacing '-e' with '-oic acid' gives butanoic acid.
questions.hint: Count the carbons in the chain, including the carboxyl carbon, then apply the carboxylic acid suffix.
distractor_logic: Propanoic acid has only 3 carbons, one fewer than this 4-carbon chain.
Butanal would require a −CHO (aldehyde) group, a less oxidised functional group than the −COOH present in this structure.
Butan-1-ol would require a simple −OH group, not the more oxidised −COOH group present here.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Among formic acid (HCOOH), acetic acid (CH₃COOH), and propanoic acid (CH₃CH₂COOH), which is generally the MOST acidic, and why?
options: Propanoic acid, since a longer alkyl chain always increases acidity
All three are exactly equally acidic, since all contain the same −COOH group
Acetic acid, since its methyl group is strongly electron-withdrawing
Formic acid, since it has no electron-donating alkyl group at all attached to the carboxyl carbon, unlike the other two
questions.explanation: Alkyl groups are weakly electron-DONATING (+I) relative to hydrogen, which slightly destabilises the carboxylate anion (pushing electron density onto an already negative centre); formic acid, lacking any alkyl group on its carboxyl carbon, has no such destabilising donation and is therefore somewhat more acidic than acetic or propanoic acid.
questions.hint: Consider whether an alkyl group (a weak electron donor) attached to the carboxyl carbon would help or hinder stabilisation of the resulting negative charge.
distractor_logic: A longer alkyl chain provides slightly MORE electron-donating (+I) character overall, which tends to slightly DECREASE (not increase) acidity relative to a shorter chain or no chain at all.
Even though all three share the same functional group, the presence and length of an attached alkyl group measurably affects acidity through the inductive effect; they are not exactly equal.
A simple methyl group is weakly electron-DONATING, not withdrawing, relative to hydrogen; this option describes the opposite of methyl's actual inductive character.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: The carboxylate ion, formed when a carboxylic acid loses its acidic proton, is stabilised by resonance in which the negative charge is delocalised:
options: Entirely onto just one of the two oxygen atoms, with no delocalisation onto the other
The carboxylate ion shows no resonance at all; the negative charge stays fixed on one specific oxygen
Onto the carbon atom itself, not either oxygen
Equally over the two oxygen atoms, since both carbon−oxygen bonds become equivalent (each with partial double-bond character)
questions.explanation: The two resonance structures of the carboxylate ion (R−C(=O)−O⁻ and R−C(−O⁻)=O) are equivalent by symmetry, so the true structure is a resonance hybrid with the negative charge, and the carbon−oxygen bond character, spread equally over both oxygens — this symmetric delocalisation is what makes the carboxylate especially stable.
questions.hint: Draw both resonance structures of the carboxylate ion and compare whether they are identical (equivalent) or different from each other.
distractor_logic: If the charge stayed on only one oxygen with no delocalisation, the two carbon−oxygen bond lengths would be measurably different, but experimentally they are found to be equal — direct evidence for the delocalisation being spread over both oxygens equally.

The carboxylate ion is a textbook example of resonance stabilisation; its two equivalent resonance structures are exactly what gives it its enhanced stability compared to a non-delocalised (localised) anion.

The negative charge in the carboxylate resonance structures resides on the oxygen atoms (which bear the lone pairs in each resonance form), not on the carbon, which remains part of the C=O/C−O framework in both structures.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Both n-propylbenzene (C₆H₅CH₂CH₂CH₃) and isopropylbenzene (C₆H₅CH(CH₃)₂) are treated separately with hot, concentrated alkaline KMnO₄, followed by acidification. What is observed?
options: Both are oxidised only at the ring itself, leaving the alkyl side chains completely untouched
Both give the same product, benzoic acid, since any benzylic side chain is oxidatively shortened all the way down to a single ring-attached −COOH group
n-Propylbenzene gives benzoic acid, but isopropylbenzene gives no reaction at all, since its branching prevents oxidation
Each gives a different product, retaining its own distinct side-chain length as a corresponding carboxylic acid
questions.explanation: Hot alkaline KMnO₄ oxidises any alkyl group bearing at least one benzylic hydrogen (which both of these side chains have) all the way down to a single −COOH group directly on the ring, regardless of the original chain's length or branching pattern; both n-propylbenzene and isopropylbenzene therefore give the same product, benzoic acid.
questions.hint: Recall that this oxidant shortens ANY oxidisable side chain down to just one carbon (the ring-attached carboxyl carbon), regardless of how that chain was originally branched.
distractor_logic: This oxidation specifically targets and shortens the ALKYL side chain (via its benzylic C−H bonds), not the aromatic ring itself, which remains intact throughout.

Isopropylbenzene does still have a benzylic hydrogen (on the CH carbon directly attached to the ring) and IS oxidised by hot alkaline KMnO₄, just as n-propylbenzene is; branching at the benzylic position does not prevent this oxidation.

The characteristic (and somewhat surprising) outcome of this reaction is that the ORIGINAL side-chain length is NOT retained; both compounds converge on the same single product, benzoic acid, regardless of their different starting side chains.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: A chemist wants to convert bromoethane (CH₃CH₂Br) into propanoic acid (CH₃CH₂COOH), a product with ONE MORE carbon than the starting material. Which two-step sequence achieves this?
options: Both (1) and (3) are valid routes that add exactly one new carbon to reach propanoic acid
(1) Mg/dry ether to form the Grignard reagent; (2) dry ice (CO₂), then dilute acid workup
(1) KCN, to substitute Br with CN; (2) hydrolysis with aqueous acid or base
(1) NaOH(aq), to substitute Br with OH; (2) PCC oxidation
questions.explanation: Forming the Grignard reagent (CH₃CH₂MgBr) and reacting it with CO₂ adds one new carbon (from CO₂) directly onto the existing ethyl group, and acidic workup liberates the free carboxylic acid, propanoic acid — matching both the correct carbon count and the product's identity as specified in the question.
questions.hint: Focus on which single option correctly adds exactly one new carbon while also giving the SPECIFIED product, propanoic acid.
distractor_logic: Only the Grignard/CO₂ route (and separately, the nitrile-hydrolysis route) genuinely adds a new carbon to reach propanoic acid; the substitution/oxidation route described elsewhere in this question set does not add a carbon and gives a different product (acetic acid) instead.

While KCN substitution followed by nitrile hydrolysis (CH₃CH₂Br → CH₃CH₂CN → CH₃CH₂COOH) IS a valid route that also adds one carbon and does correctly give propanoic acid, the specific combined claim in this option (that a DIFFERENT, non-carbon-adding route also works) is not correct as stated.

This route (substitution to ethanol, then oxidation) would give acetic acid (CH₃COOH, 2 carbons total), NOT propanoic acid (3 carbons), since no new carbon is added at any step; it retains the original 2-carbon skeleton.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Hydrolysis of propanenitrile, CH₃CH₂C≡N, under aqueous acidic conditions gives:
options: Propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH
Propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO
questions.explanation: Acidic hydrolysis of a nitrile proceeds through an amide intermediate and ultimately gives the corresponding carboxylic acid, retaining the same carbon skeleton and total carbon count as the starting nitrile.
questions.hint: Hydrolysis of the nitrile group (−C≡N) converts it directly to the carboxyl group (−COOH), on the same carbon.
distractor_logic: An alcohol would require reduction of the nitrile all the way past the amine stage or a completely different synthetic route; simple aqueous hydrolysis converts the nitrile carbon directly into a carboxyl carbon, not an alcohol carbon.
A primary amine would result from REDUCTION of the nitrile (e.g. with LiAlH₄ or catalytic H₂), not from hydrolysis with water.
An aldehyde is a less-oxidised, different product from nitrile hydrolysis; hydrolysis proceeds through to the fully hydrolysed carboxylic acid, not stopping at the aldehyde stage.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Complete oxidation of pentan-1-ol (a primary alcohol) with excess hot acidified K₂Cr₂O₄ gives:
options: Pentanal only, with oxidation stopping there
Pentan-2-one
Pentane, with the oxygen removed entirely
Pentanoic acid
questions.explanation: Excess strong oxidant (hot acidified K₂Cr₂O₄) does not stop at the intermediate aldehyde stage; it continues oxidising the primary alcohol all the way through to the carboxylic acid, pentanoic acid.
questions.hint: This question specifies a strong oxidant used in EXCESS, distinguishing it from the milder, controlled PCC oxidation that stops earlier.
distractor_logic: Stopping cleanly at the aldehyde requires a milder, specifically chosen oxidant (like PCC, in anhydrous conditions); excess hot acidified K₂Cr₂O₄ continues on to the carboxylic acid.
A ketone would require oxidation of a SECONDARY alcohol, not a primary one; pentan-1-ol, being primary, is oxidised through the aldehyde stage to the carboxylic acid, not to a ketone.
Oxidation adds oxygen-containing functionality (via loss of hydrogens, not addition/removal of the oxygen atom itself); it does not strip the oxygen from the molecule to give back a simple alkane.

questions.topic: Reactions of Carboxylic Acids: Derivative Formation and Substituent Effects on Acidity
questions.question: Fischer esterification of acetic acid (CH₃COOH) with ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH), catalysed by a trace of conc. H₂SO₄, gives:
options: Acetic anhydride
Acetamide
Ethyl chloride
Ethyl acetate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, plus water
questions.explanation: Acid-catalysed esterification joins the acid's carbonyl carbon to the alcohol's oxygen (with the acid's own −OH lost as part of the leaving water molecule), giving the ester ethyl acetate and water as the byproduct.
questions.hint: Esterification of an acid with an alcohol characteristically releases water as the only byproduct.
distractor_logic: Acetic anhydride would require reaction of the acid with itself (or with a dehydrating agent joining two acid molecules), not reaction with an alcohol.
Acetamide would require reaction with ammonia or an amine, not an alcohol; the nitrogen-free ester, not a nitrogen-containing amide, is the product of esterification with ethanol.
No chlorine source is present in this reaction (only the carboxylic acid, the alcohol, and a catalytic acid), so an alkyl chloride cannot form.

questions.topic: Reactions of Carboxylic Acids: Derivative Formation and Substituent Effects on Acidity
questions.question: The Hell−Volhard−Zelinsky (HVZ) reaction of propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH, with Br₂/red P gives which alpha-halo acid?
options: Propanoyl bromide, with no alpha-substitution at all
1-Bromopropanoic acid, with Br directly on the carboxyl carbon itself
3-Bromopropanoic acid, BrCH₂CH₂COOH
2-Bromopropanoic acid, CH₃CHBrCOOH
questions.explanation: The HVZ reaction specifically brominates the carbon ALPHA to the carboxyl group (C2 in propanoic acid's numbering), giving 2-bromopropanoic acid; the carboxyl carbon itself (C1) is not directly halogenated.
questions.hint: The halogen in this reaction always ends up on the carbon immediately NEXT TO the carboxyl group, not on the carboxyl carbon itself.
distractor_logic: Propanoyl bromide (an acid BROMIDE, with Br replacing the acid's −OH group) is a different type of product entirely; the HVZ reaction specifically installs Br at the alpha-CARBON, not at the carboxyl oxygen position.

The carboxyl carbon (C1) itself is not the site of halogenation in this reaction; '1-bromopropanoic acid' with Br directly on the carboxyl carbon is not a valid or intended product of the alpha-selective HVZ reaction.
3-Bromopropanoic acid would place the bromine on the BETA carbon (one carbon further from the carboxyl group) rather than the alpha carbon that the HVZ reaction specifically targets.

questions.topic: Reactions of Carboxylic Acids: Derivative Formation and Substituent Effects on Acidity
questions.question: Heating sodium acetate (CH₃COONa) with soda lime (NaOH/CaO) — a decarboxylation reaction — gives which product?
options: Carbon dioxide only, with no hydrocarbon formed
Acetic acid, regenerated unchanged
Methane, CH₄
questions.explanation: Decarboxylation removes the carboxylate carbon as carbonate (Na₂CO₃) and replaces the −COONa group with −H; since acetate has only one carbon remaining after the carboxyl carbon is removed, the product is methane, CH₄.
questions.hint: Count how many carbons remain in sodium acetate's alkyl portion once the carboxyl carbon itself is removed as carbonate.
distractor_logic: Decarboxylation of sodium acetate does produce a hydrocarbon (methane) as the main organic product, alongside sodium carbonate; it is not a reaction that yields only CO₂/carbonate with no hydrocarbon at all.
This is a decarboxylation (loss of the carboxyl group, replaced by H), not a reversible process that regenerates the starting acid; the carboxylate carbon is genuinely removed as carbonate.
Ethane (2 carbons) would require decarboxylation of a 3-carbon acid salt (sodium propanoate), not the 2-carbon sodium acetate, which yields a 1-carbon alkane after losing its carboxyl carbon.

questions.topic: Nomenclature and Structure of the Carbonyl Group in Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: A molecule contains both a −CHO group at one end of a chain and a free −OH group at the other end (5-hydroxypentanal). In IUPAC nomenclature, which group is cited as the principal characteristic group (suffix), and which becomes a mere prefix?
options: Both groups are cited as suffixes simultaneously, joined by a hyphen
−OH is senior and is cited as the suffix ('-ol'); −CHO is demoted to the prefix 'oxo-' or 'formyl-'
Neither group can be named as a suffix; only common names are permitted for such molecules
−CHO is senior and is cited as the suffix ('-al'); −OH is demoted to the prefix 'hydroxy-'
questions.explanation: IUPAC seniority order places the aldehyde group above the alcohol group (carboxylic acid > ... > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine, among others); when both groups are present in one molecule, the more senior group (here, −CHO) is cited as the suffix, and the lower-priority group (−OH) is demoted to a prefix, giving the name 5-hydroxypentanal.
questions.hint: Recall the standard IUPAC seniority order of functional groups and identify which of these two ranks higher.
distractor_logic: IUPAC rules require exactly ONE principal characteristic group per name (cited as the suffix); a name cannot cite two different suffixes simultaneously for two different groups.
This reverses the correct seniority; the aldehyde group ranks ABOVE the alcohol group in the standard IUPAC priority order, so −CHO (not −OH) is the one cited as the suffix.

IUPAC systematic names CAN and do handle molecules with multiple different functional groups, using the seniority-order rule to decide which becomes the suffix and which becomes a prefix; this is a routine, well-defined naming situation, not one restricted to common names only.

questions.topic: Nomenclature and Structure of the Carbonyl Group in Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Two isomeric compounds, both C₄H₈O, are known: one gives a positive Tollens' test, the other does not. Using only this molecular formula and this single test result, deduce the general structural class of each isomer.
options: The Tollens'-positive isomer is an aldehyde (e.g. butanal); the Tollens'-negative isomer is a ketone (e.g. butan-2-one) — both fit C₄H₈O (DoU = 1, one C=O, fully saturated otherwise) but only the aldehyde reduces Tollens' reagent
The Tollens'-positive isomer must be a carboxylic acid, since only acids react with Tollens' reagent
Both isomers must be ketones, since C₄H₈O only fits the ketone general formula
This molecular formula is inconsistent with any carbonyl compound at all
questions.explanation: C₄H₈O has DoU = (2×4+2−8)/2 = 1, consistent with a single C=O group in an otherwise saturated 4-carbon skeleton — fitting both an aldehyde (butanal, CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO) and a ketone (butan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₃). Tollens' reagent specifically oxidises the aldehyde's C−H bond (giving a positive silver-mirror result) but does not react with a ketone, which has no such hydrogen directly on the carbonyl carbon.
questions.hint: Work out the degree of unsaturation first, then consider which C₄H₈O isomer class(es) it is consistent with, and which one specifically reacts with Tollens' reagent.
distractor_logic: Tollens' reagent does not react with carboxylic acids (which would in any case require a different molecular formula, C₄H₈O₂, with two oxygens, not the single oxygen given here); the reagent specifically targets the aldehyde's C−H bond.
C₄H₈O (DoU=1) is consistent with BOTH an aldehyde and a ketone of this carbon count; it is not exclusively a ketone-only formula.
C₄H₈O is a perfectly valid, common molecular formula for saturated 4-carbon aldehydes and ketones; it is not inconsistent with carbonyl compounds.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: A chemist wants to convert benzonitrile, C₆H₅C≡N, into benzaldehyde, C₆H₅CHO, without over-reducing to the amine. Compare the Stephen reduction (SnCl₂/HCl, then hydrolysis) and DIBAL-H (low temperature, then hydrolysis) as two valid routes for this specific transformation.
options: Only Stephen reduction works; DIBAL-H always reduces nitriles straight to the corresponding alcohol
Only DIBAL-H works; Stephen reduction always over-reduces any nitrile straight to the primary amine
Neither method can stop selectively at the aldehyde stage for an aromatic nitrile specifically

Both are genuinely valid routes: Stephen reduction forms an imine-stannic chloride complex that hydrolyses to the aldehyde, while DIBAL-H at low temperature forms a stable imine-aluminium intermediate that similarly hydrolyses to the aldehyde on workup, both avoiding over-reduction to the amine
questions.explanation: Both the Stephen reduction (SnCl₂/HCl forming an imine salt that is then hydrolysed) and controlled, low-temperature DIBAL-H reduction (forming a stable metal-imine complex that survives until aqueous workup) are genuine, standard methods for selectively reducing a nitrile to an aldehyde without proceeding all the way to the amine; both rely on trapping a stable intermediate that only releases the aldehyde upon the final hydrolysis step.
questions.hint: Consider whether EACH named method has a specific mechanistic reason (a stable, isolable intermediate) for stopping short of the amine.
distractor_logic: DIBAL-H does not reduce a nitrile all the way to an alcohol at low temperature; its whole utility in this context is stopping cleanly at the aldehyde stage via a stable intermediate.

The Stephen reduction is specifically valued because it does NOT over-reduce to the amine; it selectively stops at the aldehyde via its stable imine-tin intermediate, just as DIBAL-H does via its own mechanism.

Both named methods work specifically because of their respective stable, hydrolysis-triggered intermediates; this selectivity is not restricted to only aliphatic nitriles and does apply to aromatic nitriles like benzonitrile.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Ozonolysis (O₃, then Zn/H₂O) of 2-methylbut-2-ene, (CH₃)₂C=CH−CH₃, gives which pair of carbonyl products?
options: Acetone, (CH₃)₂C=O, and acetaldehyde, CH₃CHO
Two molecules of acetaldehyde
Acetone and formaldehyde
A single ketone product, with no aldehyde formed
questions.explanation: The double bond's two carbons are unevenly substituted: one carbon carries two methyl groups (giving, on cleavage, the ketone acetone), and the other carries one methyl group and one hydrogen (giving, on cleavage, the aldehyde acetaldehyde).
questions.hint: Examine each double-bond carbon separately: how many carbon substituents (versus hydrogens) does each one carry?
distractor_logic: Two identical acetaldehyde molecules would only form from a SYMMETRIC alkene where each double-bond carbon carries exactly one methyl and one hydrogen (like but-2-ene), not this unsymmetrically-substituted alkene.
Formaldehyde would require a =CH₂ (two-hydrogen) terminal carbon, but this alkene's less-substituted carbon carries one methyl group and one hydrogen, giving acetaldehyde, not formaldehyde.

Since the two double-bond carbons carry DIFFERENT substitution patterns (one disubstituted, one monosubstituted), cleavage necessarily gives two DIFFERENT carbonyl products (one ketone, one aldehyde), not a single product.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Both Friedel−Crafts acylation and the Gatterman−Koch reaction fail on nitrobenzene as the substrate. Explain why, using a single shared underlying reason.
options: Both reactions actually proceed normally on nitrobenzene; there is no real limitation here
Nitrobenzene has no aromatic ring at all, so no electrophilic aromatic substitution of any kind can occur on it
Friedel−Crafts acylation fails due to steric hindrance from −NO₂, while Gatterman−Koch fails for a completely unrelated reason (lack of available CO gas)

Both reactions require electrophilic attack on the ring by a cationic species, and the strongly deactivating −NO₂ group makes the ring far too electron-poor for either electrophile to attack effectively
questions.explanation: Both reactions are variants of electrophilic aromatic substitution, requiring the ring to be sufficiently electron-rich to attack an electrophilic species (an acylium ion for Friedel−Crafts, a formyl cation for Gatterman−Koch); −NO₂ is one of the strongest deactivating groups (withdrawing electron density by both induction and resonance), making nitrobenzene's ring too electron-poor for either electrophile to react with under normal conditions — a general, well-known limitation shared by essentially all standard electrophilic aromatic substitutions on strongly deactivated rings.
questions.hint: Both of these reactions belong to the same broad mechanistic family; ask what that family fundamentally requires of the aromatic ring's electron density.
distractor_logic: This is a well-documented, standard limitation; neither Friedel−Crafts acylation nor the Gatterman−Koch reaction proceeds efficiently on a strongly deactivated ring like nitrobenzene's.

Nitrobenzene has a perfectly intact benzene ring (with a −NO₂ substituent); the ring exists and CAN in principle undergo electrophilic substitution, just much more slowly and only with sufficiently reactive electrophiles — these two specific reactions simply cannot generate a strong enough electrophile-ring interaction here.

The limitation for BOTH reactions traces back to the same underlying cause (an electron-poor ring unable to supply electron density to attack the electrophile), not two unrelated, independent causes for each reaction separately.

questions.topic: Physical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Formaldehyde (HCHO, molar mass 30 g/mol) is a gas at room temperature, while acetone (CH₃COCH₃, molar mass 58 g/mol, a larger molecule with the same polar C=O group) is a liquid. Reconcile this with the general trend that larger, more polar molecules tend to have higher boiling points.
options: Boiling point is determined solely by the presence or absence of a C=O group, with molecular size playing no role at all
Formaldehyde is actually less polar than acetone, which is why it has a lower boiling point
This is a genuine contradiction; one of the two observed physical states must be incorrect

Both trends are consistent: increasing MOLAR MASS (and hence the surface area available for dispersion forces) generally raises boiling point for a homologous series of similarly-polar molecules, and formaldehyde, being much smaller, simply falls below room temperature's boiling threshold while acetone, being larger, does not
questions.explanation: Both compounds experience similar TYPES of intermolecular force (dipole−dipole, from their comparable C=O polarity), but the STRENGTH of dispersion forces (which add to the overall attraction) scales with molecular size/surface area; formaldehyde, being much smaller, has correspondingly weaker total intermolecular attraction and a much lower boiling point (−19°C, a gas at room temperature), while acetone's larger size raises its boiling point (56°C) above room temperature, making it a liquid — both observations are fully consistent with the same underlying trend.
questions.hint: The general trend concerns TOTAL intermolecular attraction, which includes a size-dependent (dispersion) component in addition to the polar (dipole−dipole) component that both molecules share.
distractor_logic: Molecular size (via dispersion forces) is a well-established, significant contributor to boiling point, in addition to the presence of a polar functional group; it is not irrelevant.

Both molecules contain the same type of polar C=O group and are comparably polar per functional group present; the difference in boiling point is explained by their difference in overall molecular size, not by one being fundamentally less polar than the other.

Both physical states are correctly and independently observed; there is no contradiction once the size-dependent dispersion contribution to boiling point is properly accounted for alongside the shared dipole−dipole contribution.

questions.topic: Physical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Acetone and propan-1-ol have very similar molar masses (58 vs. 60 g/mol) but noticeably different boiling points (56°C vs. 97°C). Explain this difference despite their near-identical size.
options: Propan-1-ol's −OH group allows hydrogen bonding BETWEEN its own molecules, a considerably stronger intermolecular force than the dipole−dipole attraction available to acetone's C=O group, which cannot hydrogen-bond to itself
Both compounds should have identical boiling points, and any observed difference must be experimental error
Acetone is actually the larger, heavier molecule of the two, explaining nothing unusual
Propan-1-ol has weaker intermolecular forces than acetone, which is why it boils at a higher temperature
questions.explanation: Despite their nearly identical molar mass (similar dispersion-force contribution), propan-1-ol's O−H group can donate AND accept hydrogen bonds with other alcohol molecules, a substantially stronger intermolecular attraction than the dipole−dipole forces available between acetone's C=O-bearing molecules (which have no O−H or N−H to hydrogen-bond with each other); this difference in intermolecular force TYPE, not molecular size, explains the significant boiling point gap.
questions.hint: Since the two molecules are almost the same size, the boiling point difference must come from a difference in the TYPE (not just the strength-by-size) of intermolecular force available.
distractor_logic: This significant, reproducible boiling point difference is a real, well-documented consequence of hydrogen bonding being available to one compound and not the other; it is not an experimental error.
The molar masses given (58 vs. 60 g/mol) show the two compounds are almost identical in size, not that acetone is meaningfully larger; size is not the explanation for the boiling point gap here.
This reverses the correct comparison; propan-1-ol has the STRONGER intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonding), which is exactly why it has the HIGHER boiling point of the two, not the weaker one.

questions.topic: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
questions.question: Rank the following four carbonyl compounds in DECREASING order of reactivity toward nucleophilic addition, accounting for BOTH steric bulk and electronic (+I) donation: (i) pivaldehyde, (CH₃)₃C−CHO; (ii) acetaldehyde, CH₃CHO; (iii) acetone, CH₃COCH₃; (iv) di-tert-butyl ketone, (CH₃)₃C−CO−C(CH₃)₃.
options: Di-tert-butyl ketone > pivaldehyde > acetone > acetaldehyde
Acetaldehyde > pivaldehyde > acetone > di-tert-butyl ketone
Pivaldehyde > acetaldehyde > di-tert-butyl ketone > acetone
All four are equally reactive, since steric and electronic effects always cancel out exactly
questions.explanation: Acetaldehyde (one small methyl group) is the most reactive of the four. Pivaldehyde still has only ONE substituent on the carbonyl carbon (fitting the general aldehyde-more-reactive-than-ketone pattern), but that substituent (bulky tert-butyl) is far bulkier and more strongly +I-donating than acetaldehyde's simple methyl, making pivaldehyde notably less reactive than acetaldehyde but still generally more reactive than the two-substituent ketones. Acetone (two small methyls) outranks di-tert-butyl ketone (two very bulky tert-butyl groups, both sterically blocking and strongly electron-donating), which is the least reactive of the four.
questions.hint: First separate aldehydes (one substituent) from ketones (two substituents), then within each pair compare the bulk/electron-donating strength of the actual substituent(s).
distractor_logic: This is essentially the reverse order; the bulkiest, most electron-donating combination (di-tert-butyl ketone) is the LEAST reactive, not the most, and acetaldehyde (least bulky, single small substituent) is the most reactive, not the least.

This incorrectly ranks the bulky-substituted aldehyde (pivaldehyde) above the small-substituted aldehyde (acetaldehyde); acetaldehyde's smaller, less electron-donating methyl group makes it more reactive than pivaldehyde's bulky tert-butyl group.

Steric and electronic effects here both point in the SAME direction (bulkier groups both hinder approach AND donate more electron density), reinforcing rather than cancelling each other, which is exactly why reactivity varies so much across this series rather than staying constant.

questions.topic: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
questions.question: Di-tert-butyl ketone reacts very sluggishly (or not at all) with a Grignard reagent under standard conditions, even though Grignard reagents are normally excellent nucleophiles toward ketones. What is the most likely explanation, and what competing pathway often occurs instead?
options: The tert-butyl groups chemically deactivate the Grignard reagent itself before it can approach the ketone
Grignard reagents can never react with ANY ketone under any circumstances, so this outcome is entirely typical and unremarkable
The carbonyl carbon in this ketone is simply non-existent, so no reaction of any kind is chemically possible

Severe steric hindrance from the two bulky tert-butyl groups blocks the Grignard's approach to the carbonyl carbon; instead, the strongly basic Grignard reagent often simply deprotonates an available alpha-hydrogen (enolisation) rather than adding to the carbonyl
questions.explanation: The two very bulky tert-butyl groups create severe steric hindrance around the carbonyl carbon, physically blocking the Grignard's approach for direct nucleophilic addition; since the Grignard reagent is also a strong base, it often instead removes an available alpha-hydrogen from the substrate (acting as a base rather than a nucleophile), giving enolisation as a competing side reaction instead of the expected addition product.
questions.hint: Consider that a Grignard reagent is not just a nucleophile but also a strong base, and ask what alternative reaction pathway a strong base might take when the expected nucleophilic pathway is sterically blocked.
distractor_logic: The tert-butyl groups are part of the ketone substrate, not a reagent that could chemically deactivate the separate Grignard reagent; the actual issue is a steric mismatch preventing effective approach, not a direct chemical deactivation of the Grignard itself.

Grignard reagents DO react readily with most ordinary ketones (this is one of their classic, most useful reactions); di-tert-butyl ketone is a specific, unusually hindered EXCEPTION due to its extreme steric bulk, not representative of ketones generally.
Di-tert-butyl ketone does have a perfectly ordinary carbonyl carbon (C=O); the issue is that this carbon is severely sterically shielded by the two bulky flanking groups, not that it fails to exist.

questions.topic: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
questions.question: Compare acetophenone (C₆H₅COCH₃) with butan-2-one (CH₃COCH₂CH₃), both of which have the same total number of non-hydrogen atoms directly bonded around the carbonyl carbon's immediate environment in a loose sense, but very different reactivity toward nucleophilic addition. Which is less reactive, and why?
options: Both are equally reactive, since 'total number of atoms attached' is the only factor governing carbonyl reactivity
Acetophenone is more reactive, since aromaticity always increases electrophilicity of any attached functional group
Acetophenone, because the phenyl ring is directly conjugated with the carbonyl group and donates electron density into it by resonance, in addition to being bulkier than an ethyl group
Butan-2-one, because ethyl groups are always more strongly electron-withdrawing than phenyl groups
questions.explanation: Even setting aside simple atom-counting comparisons, the aromatic ring in acetophenone is directly conjugated with the carbonyl group; this conjugation allows the ring to donate electron density into the carbonyl carbon by resonance (in addition to steric bulk), reducing its electrophilicity well beyond what a simple ethyl group (in butan-2-one, which has no such conjugation available) would cause — making acetophenone measurably less reactive.
questions.hint: Beyond simple steric size, ask whether either substituent can donate electron density into the carbonyl group through an EXTRA pathway (resonance/conjugation) that the other substituent lacks.
distractor_logic: Simple atom-counting around the carbonyl carbon is not the only (or even the primary) factor; the AVAILABILITY of resonance conjugation (present for the aromatic ring, absent for a simple alkyl chain) is a distinct and often more significant factor.

Aromaticity conjugated directly with a carbonyl group typically DECREASES (not increases) that carbonyl's electrophilicity, by donating electron density into it via resonance; this is the opposite of what this option claims.

Ethyl groups donate electron density by the (comparatively weak) inductive/hyperconjugative effect only; they do not have the ADDITIONAL, generally stronger resonance-donation pathway that a directly conjugated aromatic ring provides to acetophenone's carbonyl group.

questions.topic: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
questions.question: An unknown carbonyl compound reacts very rapidly and completely with NaHSO₃ to give a bisulfite addition compound, but a structurally similar compound (differing only by one extra methyl group on the carbonyl carbon) reacts far more sluggishly and incompletely under the same conditions. What structural change most likely explains this large reactivity difference?
options: The sluggish compound must have lost its carbonyl group entirely due to the extra methyl substitution

The unknown compound is likely an aldehyde or a methyl ketone (both of which react well with NaHSO₃), while the sluggish compound is likely a more hindered, non-methyl ketone, since bisulfite addition is known to be sensitive to steric bulk around the carbonyl carbon
Adding one extra methyl group should always make a compound react FASTER with NaHSO₃, contradicting the given observation
NaHSO₃ addition is completely insensitive to the structure of the carbonyl compound, so no such reactivity difference should be observed at all
questions.explanation: The bisulfite addition reaction, like other nucleophilic additions, is known to be quite sensitive to steric hindrance at the carbonyl carbon; it proceeds well for aldehydes and for simple methyl ketones, but becomes progressively slower and less complete as the carbonyl carbon becomes more crowded (e.g. by additional/bulkier alkyl substitution) — consistent with the observed sluggish reactivity for the more substituted compound.
questions.hint: NaHSO₃ addition follows the same general steric-sensitivity trend as other nucleophilic additions to a carbonyl group.
distractor_logic: A structural change of just one additional alkyl substituent does not remove the carbonyl group itself; the compound remains a carbonyl compound, simply a more hindered one, which is exactly why its reactivity (not its fundamental functional group identity) changes.
Adding a bulkier group generally HINDERS (slows down), rather than speeds up, nucleophilic addition at the carbonyl carbon, the opposite of what this option claims.

NaHSO₃ addition, like other nucleophilic additions, IS sensitive to the steric and electronic environment of the carbonyl carbon; it is well known to work poorly on more hindered ketones, which is exactly the effect observed here.

questions.topic: Reactions with Ammonia Derivatives and Other Addition–Elimination Reactions
questions.question: An unknown compound contains BOTH a ketone group and, elsewhere in the molecule, an aldehyde group. Treating it with exactly ONE equivalent of 2,4-DNP under carefully controlled (limiting) conditions, is it possible to selectively derivatise just the more reactive of the two carbonyls?
options: This selectivity question is meaningless, since 2,4-DNP cannot react with any carbonyl group that is part of a larger, more complex molecule
No, because 2,4-DNP always reacts with ketones exclusively, never with aldehydes
No, because both carbonyls in the same molecule must always react at identical rates regardless of their type

In principle yes: since aldehydes are generally more reactive toward nucleophilic addition (and hence toward this addition−elimination condensation) than ketones, the aldehyde group would be expected to react preferentially under carefully limited (sub-stoichiometric) 2,4-DNP conditions
questions.explanation: The same reactivity trend that governs simple nucleophilic addition (aldehydes generally more reactive than ketones) also applies to this addition−elimination condensation; with a limited (sub-stoichiometric) amount of 2,4-DNP, the more reactive aldehyde carbonyl would be expected to react preferentially before the less reactive ketone carbonyl, allowing at least partial selectivity in principle (though in practice, achieving clean selectivity can be experimentally challenging).
questions.hint: The general aldehyde-more-reactive-than-ketone trend applies to this condensation reaction just as it does to simpler nucleophilic additions like cyanohydrin formation.
distractor_logic: 2,4-DNP is a general reagent for detecting the carbonyl functional group and reacts with it regardless of what other groups or complexity exist elsewhere in the molecule; it is not restricted to simple, isolated carbonyl compounds only.
2,4-DNP reacts with BOTH aldehydes and ketones (it is a general carbonyl-detecting reagent, not ketone-specific); it does not exclusively react with only one class of carbonyl compound.

Different carbonyl groups within the same molecule can and do have different intrinsic reactivities (governed by their local structural environment, e.g. aldehyde vs. ketone), so they are not expected to react at identical rates by default.

questions.topic: Reactions with Ammonia Derivatives and Other Addition–Elimination Reactions
questions.question: 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine gives a strikingly bright orange/yellow precipitate with carbonyl compounds, in contrast to plain phenylhydrazine, which gives a far less vividly coloured product. What structural feature of the 2,4-DNP reagent best explains this enhanced, distinctive colour?
options: Plain phenylhydrazine derivatives are always MORE intensely coloured than 2,4-DNP derivatives, the reverse of the premise given
The nitro groups have no electronic effect on colour at all; the difference is purely due to a different crystal shape

The two electron-withdrawing nitro groups extend the molecule's conjugated pi system and shift its light absorption, giving the resulting hydrazone derivative a much more intense, characteristic colour than a simple phenylhydrazone
2,4-DNP does not actually form a coloured product; the colour observed is always from an unrelated impurity
questions.explanation: The two strongly electron-withdrawing nitro groups on the 2,4-DNP-derived hydrazone extend and perturb the molecule's conjugated pi-electron system (a more extensively conjugated, push−pull chromophore), shifting its absorption into the visible region and producing a much more intensely coloured (orange/yellow) product than the less-conjugated, less electronically-activated plain phenylhydrazone.
questions.hint: Colour in organic molecules is generally linked to the extent and electronic character of a conjugated pi system (a chromophore); compare what the nitro groups do to that system.
distractor_logic: This reverses the well-established comparison; 2,4-DNP derivatives are known for their notably MORE intense, characteristic colour compared to simple phenylhydrazone derivatives, due to the additional electron-withdrawing nitro groups extending conjugation.

Electron-withdrawing substituents like nitro groups are well known to significantly affect a conjugated molecule's colour (by extending/perturbing its chromophore), not to have no electronic effect at all; crystal shape is not the basis of this classic colour difference.

The bright orange/yellow precipitate IS the genuine, characteristic, reproducible product of the 2,4-DNP test itself, not an artifact from an unrelated impurity; this colour is precisely why 2,4-DNP is preferred as a visually distinctive carbonyl test.
