(mesityl oxide)?
options: But-2-enal, CH₃CH=CHCHO
Hexane-2,5-dione
4-Methylpent-3-en-2-one, (CH₃)₂C=CH−CO−CH₃
3-Hydroxy-3-methylbutan-2-one, the addition product with no dehydration
questions.explanation: Base removes an alpha-hydrogen from one acetone molecule to form its enolate (the nucleophilic alpha-carbon shown reacting in the diagram), which attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second acetone molecule, giving diacetone alcohol (4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one) as the addition product; heating dehydrates this beta-hydroxy ketone to the conjugated enone, 4-methylpent-3-en-2-one (mesityl oxide).
questions.hint: The question specifies heating AFTER base treatment, which drives the dehydration step to give the fully conjugated enone.
distractor_logic: But-2-enal is the self-aldol condensation product of ACETALDEHYDE (a 2-carbon aldehyde), not acetone (a 3-carbon ketone); acetone's self-condensation gives a different, larger, ketone-derived enone.
Hexane-2,5-dione would require an entirely different bond-forming pattern (not a simple aldol self-condensation of two acetone molecules joined at one new C−C bond with loss of water).
This is only the intermediate ADDITION product (before dehydration); the question specifically asks for the product AFTER the heating/dehydration step, which is the alpha,beta-unsaturated enone.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: A CROSSED Cannizzaro reaction is carried out between formaldehyde (HCHO) and benzaldehyde (C₆H₅CHO), both lacking alpha-hydrogens, using concentrated NaOH. Since formaldehyde is known to be the more easily oxidised (better hydride-donating) of the two, what is the major outcome?
options: No reaction occurs at all when two DIFFERENT alpha-hydrogen-lacking aldehydes are mixed together
Formaldehyde is reduced to methanol while benzaldehyde is oxidised to benzoic acid, the reverse of the correct pairing
Formaldehyde is preferentially oxidised to sodium formate, while benzaldehyde is preferentially reduced to benzyl alcohol, rather than each aldehyde disproportionating with itself
Each aldehyde disproportionates independently and separately with itself, exactly as if the other were not present
questions.explanation: In a crossed Cannizzaro reaction, formaldehyde (the smallest, least hindered, and most easily oxidised of common aldehydes) preferentially acts as the hydride donor (reducing agent), being itself oxidised to formate, while the other aldehyde (here, benzaldehyde) is preferentially reduced to the corresponding alcohol (benzyl alcohol) — this crossed selectivity is a well-known, synthetically useful variant of the Cannizzaro reaction (the Tishchenko/crossed-Cannizzaro strategy), giving a cleaner product mixture than two competing self-disproportionations.
questions.hint: Consider which of the two aldehydes is intrinsically the better hydride donor, and infer that it will preferentially play that role when both are mixed together.
distractor_logic: Both aldehydes here lack an alpha-hydrogen and are each individually capable of Cannizzaro disproportionation; mixing them together does not switch off the reaction entirely, it instead enables a genuine crossed reaction pathway.

This reverses the correct roles; formaldehyde, being the more easily oxidised of the two, is the one that ends up oxidised (to formate) while benzaldehyde ends up reduced (to benzyl alcohol), not the other way around.

When two different alpha-hydrogen-lacking aldehydes with different intrinsic reducing ability are mixed, the crossed pathway (one acting mainly as reductant, the other mainly as the reduced product) tends to dominate over each aldehyde disproportionating independently with itself, precisely because of their differing ease of oxidation.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: An unknown aldol condensation product is identified as 4-phenylbut-3-en-2-one, C₆H₅−CH=CH−CO−CH₃ (from a crossed aldol condensation between acetone and benzaldehyde). Explain why benzaldehyde acts as the ELECTROPHILE (not the nucleophile) in this specific crossed aldol reaction.
options: Benzaldehyde has no alpha-hydrogen (its only 'alpha' position is the aromatic ring, which cannot form the required aliphatic enolate), so it cannot act as the nucleophile and can only serve as the electrophilic carbonyl partner being attacked by acetone's enolate
Acetone has no alpha-hydrogen either, so neither compound could act as the nucleophile, making this reaction mechanistically impossible
Aromatic aldehydes can never participate in any aldol-type reaction, whether as nucleophile or electrophile
Benzaldehyde is simply more electronegative than acetone overall, which is unrelated to why it specifically plays the electrophile role here
questions.explanation: Benzaldehyde's carbonyl carbon is flanked by the aromatic ring (no available aliphatic alpha-hydrogen for enolisation) and by hydrogen; lacking an alpha-hydrogen, it cannot be deprotonated to form the nucleophilic enolate needed to attack another carbonyl. Acetone, by contrast, DOES have alpha-hydrogens (on its two methyl groups) and can form an enolate, which then attacks benzaldehyde's electrophilic (and readily accessible, since aldehydes are generally more electrophilic than ketones) carbonyl carbon — giving the crossed product shown, with benzaldehyde specifically playing the electrophile role.
questions.hint: Check which of the two starting materials actually has an available alpha-hydrogen capable of being removed to form an enolate.
distractor_logic: Acetone DOES have alpha-hydrogens (on its methyl groups flanking the carbonyl), unlike benzaldehyde; it is specifically acetone's enolate that acts as the nucleophile in this reaction, not neither compound.

Aromatic aldehydes like benzaldehyde readily participate in crossed aldol reactions as the ELECTROPHILE (since they cannot form an enolate themselves but remain a good electrophilic carbonyl target); this is in fact a standard, well-precedented type of crossed aldol reaction, not an impossibility.

The determining factor for the nucleophile/electrophile roles here is specifically the presence or absence of an alpha-hydrogen (enabling or preventing enolate formation), not a vague, unrelated notion of overall electronegativity.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: Given the product 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one (diacetone alcohol, the aldol ADDITION product before any dehydration), deduce the starting carbonyl compound(s) that combined to give it.
options: Two molecules of acetone (CH₃COCH₃) underwent self-aldol addition, with no dehydration step applied
One molecule of acetone and one molecule of acetaldehyde underwent a crossed aldol addition
Two molecules of propanal underwent self-aldol addition
This product cannot arise from any aldol-type reaction
questions.explanation: Splitting diacetone alcohol, (CH₃)₂C(OH)−CH₂−CO−CH₃, at the new C−C bond (between the former enolate alpha-carbon and the former electrophilic carbonyl carbon) reveals two identical 3-carbon acetone fragments: one contributing its enolate (CH₂=C(O−)CH₃, from deprotonating one methyl) and the other its intact carbonyl, consistent with a straightforward SELF-aldol addition of two acetone molecules, stopped at the addition (hydroxy-ketone) stage before any dehydration.
questions.hint: Locate the new C−C bond in the product and split the molecule there, checking whether the two resulting fragments are identical (self-condensation) or different (crossed condensation).
distractor_logic: A crossed condensation between acetone and acetaldehyde would give a product incorporating structural features from a 2-carbon aldehyde fragment as well, which does not match this product's fully ketone-derived, symmetric-precursor structure.
Two molecules of propanal would give a different product altogether (an aldehyde-derived beta-hydroxy aldehyde, 2-methyl-3-hydroxypentanal), not this specific ketone-derived structure.

This product is a completely standard, well-known textbook example of the aldol ADDITION product (before dehydration) from two molecules of acetone; it arises directly from a standard aldol-type reaction.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: A synthesis requires reducing an aryl ketone to a −CH₂− group in a molecule that ALSO contains an acid-sensitive acetal protecting group elsewhere. Which named reduction should be avoided, and which should be used instead?
options: Avoid Clemmensen reduction (strongly acidic conditions would hydrolyse the acetal); use Wolff−Kishner reduction (basic conditions) instead
Either method is equally safe for an acid-sensitive acetal group
Neither method can be used if any other functional group is present anywhere in the molecule
Avoid Wolff−Kishner reduction (its basic conditions would hydrolyse the acetal); use Clemmensen reduction instead
questions.explanation: Acetals are specifically hydrolysed back to their parent carbonyl compound under ACIDIC aqueous conditions; Clemmensen reduction's strongly acidic medium (Zn−Hg/conc. HCl) would therefore likely destroy an acetal protecting group elsewhere in the molecule. Wolff−Kishner reduction's strongly BASIC conditions (KOH) leave acetals untouched (acetals are generally stable to base), making it the appropriate choice here.
questions.hint: Recall which type of condition (acidic or basic) is specifically known to hydrolyse an acetal group.
distractor_logic: The two methods use very different reaction conditions (strongly acidic vs. strongly basic) with correspondingly different functional-group compatibilities; they are not interchangeable when an acid-sensitive group is present.

Both Clemmensen and Wolff−Kishner reduction are routinely used on molecules containing other functional groups; the choice between them specifically depends on which OTHER groups are present and their acid/base sensitivity, not a blanket prohibition on using either method at all.

This has the vulnerability backwards; acetals are hydrolysed by ACID, not base, so it is specifically the ACIDIC Clemmensen conditions (not the basic Wolff−Kishner conditions) that would threaten the acetal protecting group.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: An unknown liquid gives a positive iodoform test. On its own, this test alone cannot distinguish between which TWO general classes of compound that could both give this same positive result?
options: An alkane and an alkene, since both are equally likely to give a positive iodoform test
A primary alcohol (R−CH₂OH) and a tertiary alcohol (R₃C−OH), since both types always give a positive result
A carboxylic acid and an ether, since both share the same test result universally
A methyl ketone (CH₃CO−R) and a secondary alcohol of the type CH₃CH(OH)−R (which is oxidised in situ to a methyl ketone by the test's own reagent)
questions.explanation: The iodoform reagent (I₂/NaOH) is itself a mild oxidant; a CH₃CH(OH)−R secondary alcohol is first oxidised in situ to the corresponding methyl ketone, CH₃CO−R, which THEN undergoes the standard haloform cleavage — so a positive test alone cannot distinguish whether the original compound was already a methyl ketone or was a secondary alcohol that got oxidised to one during the test itself.
questions.hint: Recall that the iodoform reagent has a mild oxidising component in addition to its halogenating/cleaving action.
distractor_logic: Neither simple alkanes nor simple alkenes (without the specific CH₃CO− or CH₃CH(OH)− structural motif) give a positive iodoform test; this pairing does not reflect the actual ambiguity in the test.

Primary and tertiary alcohols generally do NOT give a positive iodoform test (a primary alcohol like ethanol is a specific, named exception since it oxidises to acetaldehyde, CH₃CHO, which IS positive; but ordinary tertiary alcohols with no CH₃CH(OH)− motif do not), so this blanket claim about 'always' giving a positive result for both classes is incorrect.

Simple ethers and most carboxylic acids do not give a positive iodoform test at all (they lack the required methyl-ketone-generating structural motif); this pairing does not reflect the real test ambiguity.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: An unknown compound X is oxidised by hot acidified KMnO₄ to give a carboxylic acid, but X does NOT give a positive Tollens' test. What does this combination of observations most strongly suggest about X?
options: X is most likely a primary alcohol (which is oxidised to a carboxylic acid by the strong oxidant, but is not itself an aldehyde and so does not react with the mild, aldehyde-specific Tollens' reagent)
X must be an aldehyde, since only aldehydes are ever oxidised by KMnO₄
This combination of results is chemically impossible and cannot occur for any real compound
X must be a ketone, since only ketones fail the Tollens' test while still being oxidised by strong reagents
questions.explanation: Hot acidified KMnO₄ is a STRONG, general oxidant capable of oxidising a primary alcohol all the way to a carboxylic acid (passing through, but not stopping at, the aldehyde stage); Tollens' reagent, by contrast, is a MILD oxidant specific to aldehydes (which already have a C−H bond on the carbonyl carbon available for oxidation) and does not react with a simple alcohol at all — so a compound that is oxidised by the strong reagent but gives a negative result with the mild, aldehyde-specific one is consistent with being an alcohol (or, less commonly, certain other easily-oxidised structures), not necessarily an aldehyde itself.
questions.hint: Consider that these are two OXIDANTS of very different strength and functional-group selectivity, not interchangeable tests for the same thing.
distractor_logic: KMnO₄ oxidises MANY different functional groups (alcohols, aldehydes, alkylbenzene side chains, alkenes under vigorous conditions, etc.), not only aldehydes; being oxidised by KMnO₄ does not, by itself, prove the compound was an aldehyde.
This combination of results is entirely consistent and commonly observed for a simple primary alcohol; it is not chemically impossible at all.

A ketone is generally resistant to oxidation by KMnO₄ under ordinary conditions (it requires much more forcing, C−C-bond-cleaving conditions); a ketone being readily oxidised to give a carboxylic acid product under these conditions does not fit the typical behaviour described.

questions.topic: Distinguishing Tests for Aldehydes and Ketones (Tollens', Fehling's, Iodoform) and Uses
questions.question: An unknown compound gives: a POSITIVE Tollens' test, a NEGATIVE Fehling's test, and a NEGATIVE iodoform test. Which class of compound is most consistent with all three observations simultaneously?
options: An aliphatic aldehyde with a CH₃CO−-type fragment, such as acetaldehyde
A simple alkane with no functional groups at all
An aliphatic methyl ketone, such as acetone
An aromatic aldehyde without a methyl-ketone-type structural feature, such as benzaldehyde
questions.explanation: Positive Tollens' (works on ANY aldehyde, aliphatic or aromatic) plus negative Fehling's (specifically fails for AROMATIC aldehydes) together strongly point to an aromatic aldehyde; a negative iodoform test further confirms the absence of a methyl-ketone-generating fragment, which fits benzaldehyde (C₆H₅CHO) precisely, since it is an aromatic aldehyde with no CH₃CO− or CH₃CH(OH)− motif.
questions.hint: Work through each test one at a time: which functional class(es) does each individual result rule IN, and which does it rule OUT?
distractor_logic: Acetaldehyde, being an ALIPHATIC aldehyde, would give a POSITIVE Fehling's test (aliphatic aldehydes reduce Fehling's solution), inconsistent with the given negative Fehling's result; it would also give a POSITIVE iodoform test (it has a CH₃CO−-type carbon via its own structure, CH₃CHO), inconsistent with the given negative iodoform result.

A simple alkane would give NEGATIVE results on all three tests (no functional group to react with any of these reagents), but the question specifies a POSITIVE Tollens' result, which an alkane cannot give.
Acetone is a KETONE, not an aldehyde, and would give a NEGATIVE Tollens' test (ketones do not react with Tollens' reagent), inconsistent with the given positive Tollens' result.

questions.topic: Distinguishing Tests for Aldehydes and Ketones (Tollens', Fehling's, Iodoform) and Uses
questions.question: Bakelite, an early synthetic plastic, is manufactured from formaldehyde and phenol. Connecting this industrial use back to formaldehyde's own chemistry, why is formaldehyde (rather than, say, acetone) particularly well suited to forming such a cross-linked polymer network?
options: Acetone would actually be equally or more suitable for this specific polymerisation, so the choice of formaldehyde is essentially arbitrary
Formaldehyde cannot react with phenol at all under any conditions, making the premise of Bakelite's synthesis incorrect
Formaldehyde's exceptionally HIGH steric bulk is what allows it to bridge multiple phenol units together

Formaldehyde's small, highly electrophilic, unhindered carbonyl carbon (bearing no alkyl/aryl substituents at all) reacts very readily and repeatedly with multiple phenol molecules, enabling extensive cross-linking into a rigid, three-dimensional polymer network
questions.explanation: Formaldehyde's carbonyl carbon has no alkyl or aryl substituents at all (unlike a ketone such as acetone), making it maximally electrophilic and sterically unhindered; this allows it to react efficiently and repeatedly at multiple points with phenol's activated ring positions (ortho/para to −OH), forming the many cross-links needed to build up Bakelite's rigid, thermosetting three-dimensional network — a bulkier or less reactive carbonyl compound like acetone would be far less effective at this repeated, multi-point linking.
questions.hint: Connect formaldehyde's basic reactivity trend (most reactive of all common carbonyl compounds toward nucleophilic/electrophilic aromatic-type reactions) to the practical requirement of forming MANY cross-links in a polymer network.
distractor_logic: Acetone's two methyl groups make its carbonyl carbon considerably bulkier and less electrophilic than formaldehyde's completely unhindered carbonyl carbon, making it distinctly LESS suitable (not equally or more suitable) for this repeated cross-linking chemistry.

Formaldehyde is in fact the classic, industrially essential reagent that DOES react with phenol (via electrophilic aromatic substitution-type chemistry at phenol's activated ring positions) to form Bakelite; this reaction is a real, long-established industrial process, not a false premise.

Formaldehyde is in fact the SMALLEST and LEAST sterically bulky common carbonyl compound (having no alkyl/aryl substituents at all), the opposite of 'exceptionally high steric bulk'; its small size is precisely what allows it to react so efficiently and repeatedly.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Rank the following four compounds in DECREASING order of acid strength: 2-chlorobutanoic acid, 3-chlorobutanoic acid, 4-chlorobutanoic acid, and plain butanoic acid.
options: All four are equally acidic, since they share the same −COOH group and the same total number of carbons
2-Chlorobutanoic acid > 3-chlorobutanoic acid > 4-chlorobutanoic acid > butanoic acid
Butanoic acid > 4-chlorobutanoic acid > 3-chlorobutanoic acid > 2-chlorobutanoic acid
4-Chlorobutanoic acid > 2-chlorobutanoic acid > 3-chlorobutanoic acid > butanoic acid
questions.explanation: Chlorine's electron-withdrawing inductive effect stabilises the carboxylate anion and increases acidity, but this effect falls off sharply with distance through the sigma-bond framework; the chlorine closest to the carboxyl group (2-chloro, on the alpha-carbon) has the strongest effect, followed by 3-chloro (beta-carbon), then 4-chloro (gamma-carbon, weakest effect among the three substituted acids but still stronger than no substituent at all), with plain butanoic acid (no electron-withdrawing substituent) the least acidic of the four.
questions.hint: The inductive effect of an electron-withdrawing substituent weakens rapidly as it moves further from the −COOH group through the chain.
distractor_logic: The four compounds are NOT equally acidic; the presence, and specifically the POSITION, of the electron-withdrawing chlorine substituent measurably changes the acidity through the distance-dependent inductive effect, even though all four share the same carbon count and the same functional group.

This is exactly the reverse order; the compound with NO electron-withdrawing substituent (plain butanoic acid) is the LEAST acidic, not the most, and the substituent CLOSEST to −COOH (2-chloro) gives the STRONGEST inductive effect and highest acidity, not the weakest.

This misorders the chlorine positions; the inductive effect weakens monotonically with distance from −COOH (2- > 3- > 4-chloro), so 4-chlorobutanoic acid cannot be the most acidic of the three substituted acids, and this option also places 3-chloro above 2-chloro, reversing their correct order.

second O</text></svg> Based on the resonance comparison shown above, explain precisely why carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenols, even though both form a resonance-stabilised conjugate base upon deprotonation.
options: In the carboxylate ion, the negative charge is delocalised equally over TWO chemically equivalent oxygen atoms (a stronger, more symmetric stabilisation), whereas in the phenoxide ion, the negative charge is delocalised only into the ring's ortho/para carbons, a comparatively weaker form of stabilisation since it disperses charge onto carbon rather than onto a second, equally electronegative oxygen
Carboxylate ions are destabilised by resonance relative to a hypothetical non-delocalised anion, which is why carboxylic acids are more acidic
Both ions are stabilised by resonance to exactly the same extent, so the acidity difference must come from an entirely unrelated factor
Phenoxide ions show no resonance stabilisation at all, unlike carboxylate ions, which show resonance exclusively
questions.explanation: The carboxylate ion's two resonance structures are fully equivalent (charge spread over two identical, highly electronegative oxygen atoms), giving especially effective, symmetric stabilisation. The phenoxide ion's resonance structures place some of the negative charge on ring CARBON atoms (less electronegative, less able to comfortably bear a formal negative charge) rather than on a second oxygen; this asymmetric, carbon-based delocalisation is a comparatively weaker form of stabilisation, making the phenoxide ion less stable (and phenol therefore less acidic) than the carboxylate ion (and carboxylic acid).
questions.hint: Compare WHERE the negative charge ends up being delocalised in each ion — onto a second identical oxygen, or onto ring carbons — and consider which location is more comfortable for a negative charge.
distractor_logic: Resonance delocalisation STABILISES (lowers the energy of) the carboxylate ion relative to a hypothetical localised anion; it does not destabilise it. This stabilisation is exactly why the carboxylate (and hence carboxylic acid) is comparatively more acidic.

The two ions are NOT stabilised to the same extent; the symmetric, two-equivalent-oxygen delocalisation in the carboxylate is a measurably stronger stabilisation than the asymmetric, into-the-ring delocalisation in the phenoxide, which is precisely the structural reason for the acidity difference between the two classes of compound.

Phenoxide ions DO show genuine resonance stabilisation (delocalisation of charge into the ring at ortho/para positions); the comparison here is about the RELATIVE strength of two different (but both real) resonance stabilisations, not the presence versus complete absence of resonance in one of them.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Comparing p-nitrobenzoic acid, p-methoxybenzoic acid, and plain benzoic acid, rank them in DECREASING order of acid strength, using both inductive and resonance reasoning for the ring substituents.
options: p-Nitrobenzoic acid > p-methoxybenzoic acid > benzoic acid
All three are equally acidic, since ring substituents remote from −COOH have no effect on its acidity
p-Methoxybenzoic acid > benzoic acid > p-nitrobenzoic acid
p-Nitrobenzoic acid > benzoic acid > p-methoxybenzoic acid
questions.explanation: The −NO₂ group is strongly electron-withdrawing (by both induction and resonance, even from the para position, through the conjugated ring), further stabilising the carboxylate anion and increasing acidity relative to plain benzoic acid. The −OCH₃ group is net electron-donating into the ring at the para position (its resonance donation outweighing its inductive withdrawal), which destabilises the carboxylate anion and decreases acidity relative to plain benzoic acid — giving the order p-nitrobenzoic acid > benzoic acid > p-methoxybenzoic acid.
questions.hint: Even from the para position (conjugated through the ring), a strongly resonance-active substituent can meaningfully affect the stability of the carboxylate anion at the other end of the ring.
distractor_logic: This correctly identifies nitro as the most acidity-enhancing substituent but incorrectly ranks methoxybenzoic acid above plain benzoic acid; methoxy's net electron-donating character at the para position should make it LESS acidic than unsubstituted benzoic acid, not more.

Even though the substituents sit on the far side of the aromatic ring from −COOH, their electronic effects (especially resonance, conjugated through the ring) DO reach and measurably affect the stability of the carboxylate anion; ring substituents are not simply too remote to matter.
This is the reverse order; the electron-WITHDRAWING nitro group increases (not decreases) acidity relative to benzoic acid, while the net electron-DONATING methoxy group decreases (not increases) it.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: A chemist wants to synthesise phenylacetic acid, C₆H₅CH₂COOH, starting from benzyl chloride, C₆H₅CH₂Cl. Which two-step sequence achieves this?
options: (1) NaOH(aq), substitution to the alcohol; (2) PCC oxidation, stopping at the aldehyde
(1) KCN, substitution to form the nitrile C₆H₅CH₂CN; (2) hydrolysis (aqueous acid or base) to the carboxylic acid
(1) Mg/dry ether; (2) H₂O workup only, without any carbon dioxide step
(1) Hot alkaline KMnO₄, oxidising the benzylic position directly; (2) no further step needed
questions.explanation: Substituting the benzylic chloride with cyanide (Sₙ2, since a benzylic halide is highly reactive toward nucleophilic substitution) gives phenylacetonitrile, C₆H₅CH₂CN; hydrolysis of the nitrile then gives phenylacetic acid, C₆H₅CH₂COOH, correctly adding the needed carbon (from the cyanide) while preserving the original benzylic CH₂ group.
questions.hint: Track carefully how many carbons the target molecule needs beyond what benzyl chloride already provides, and which reagent supplies that extra carbon.
distractor_logic: This route (substitution to benzyl alcohol, then PCC oxidation) would give phenylacetaldehyde or, more directly for a CH₂Cl start, benzaldehyde-type chemistry is not even applicable here; in any case it stops at an aldehyde, one oxidation level short of the target carboxylic acid, and does not add the needed extra carbon either.

Simply forming the Grignard and quenching with water (protonolysis) would just regenerate toluene (C₆H₅CH₃), with no new carbon or oxygen-containing group added; reacting the Grignard with CO₂ (not shown here) would be needed to build a carboxylic acid.

Hot alkaline KMnO₄ would oxidise the ENTIRE benzylic side chain down to a single ring-attached −COOH (giving benzoic acid, C₆H₅COOH, with the extra −CH₂− carbon lost), not preserve the CH₂ group needed for phenylacetic acid.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: A student proposes making propanoic acid (CH₃CH₂COOH) from ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) using only a single-step oxidation (e.g. hot acidified KMnO₄). Identify the flaw in this proposed route.
options: This single-step oxidation of ethanol would give acetic acid (CH₃COOH, 2 carbons), not propanoic acid (3 carbons), since simple oxidation does not add any new carbon to the skeleton
The product of this oxidation would actually be methanoic acid, with one carbon lost entirely
This route works exactly as proposed, and no flaw exists
Ethanol cannot be oxidised by KMnO₄ under any conditions
questions.explanation: Oxidation changes the OXIDATION STATE of the carbon bearing the −OH group (ultimately to a carboxyl carbon) but does not add or remove any carbon atoms from the skeleton; ethanol (2 carbons) can only be oxidised up to acetic acid (2 carbons), never to a 3-carbon acid like propanoic acid, since the target requires an additional carbon that this route has no way of introducing.
questions.hint: Compare the carbon count of the starting material to the carbon count of the desired product; does simple oxidation change the number of carbons present?
distractor_logic: Oxidation removes hydrogens (raising oxidation state) without removing carbon atoms from the skeleton; the product retains ethanol's original 2 carbons (giving acetic acid), it does not lose a carbon to give the even-shorter methanoic acid.
The specific FLAW here is precisely a carbon-count mismatch (ethanol has too few carbons to directly reach propanoic acid by oxidation alone); the route as described does not achieve the stated goal.

Ethanol is in fact readily oxidised by hot acidified KMnO₄ (a classic textbook oxidation, passing through acetaldehyde to acetic acid); the flaw is not that no reaction occurs, but that the WRONG (too-short) product results relative to the stated target.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Working BACKWARD: a Grignard reagent was reacted with dry ice, then hydrolysed with dilute acid, to give 2-methylpropanoic acid, (CH₃)₂CHCOOH. What was the starting alkyl halide used to form the Grignard reagent?
options: 1-Bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Br
2-Bromopropane (isopropyl bromide), (CH₃)₂CHBr
1-Bromopropane, CH₃CH₂CH₂Br
2-Bromo-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl bromide), (CH₃)₃CBr
questions.explanation: Reaction of a Grignard reagent with CO₂ adds exactly ONE new carbon (the eventual carboxyl carbon) onto the existing R group; working backward from 2-methylpropanoic acid, (CH₃)₂CH−COOH, the carboxyl carbon is the new addition, so the original Grignard's R group must have been (CH₃)₂CH−, meaning the starting alkyl halide was 2-bromopropane (isopropyl bromide).
questions.hint: Remove the carboxyl carbon (the one contributed by CO₂) from the product and see what alkyl group remains — that is the original R group of the Grignard reagent.
distractor_logic: 1-Bromo-2-methylpropane would form a Grignard with R = (CH₃)₂CHCH₂−, which upon reaction with CO₂ would give 3-methylbutanoic acid (one carbon longer than the target), not 2-methylpropanoic acid.

1-Bromopropane would form a Grignard with a straight-chain (unbranched) R group, which upon reaction with CO₂ would give butanoic acid (a straight-chain acid), not the branched 2-methylpropanoic acid specified as the target.
tert-Butyl bromide would form a Grignard with R = (CH₃)₃C−, which upon reaction with CO₂ would give 2,2-dimethylpropanoic acid (pivalic acid), a different, more highly branched acid than the target.

questions.topic: Reactions of Carboxylic Acids: Derivative Formation and Substituent Effects on Acidity
questions.question: A synthesis plan converts propanoic acid into N-methylpropanamide via the following two steps: (1) SOCl₂, to form the acid chloride; (2) reaction of the acid chloride with methylamine, CH₃NH₂. Explain why converting to the acid chloride FIRST is the preferred strategy, rather than reacting propanoic acid directly with methylamine.
options: Direct reaction of a carboxylic acid with an amine mostly just gives an acid−base salt (ammonium carboxylate) at room temperature, requiring high-temperature dehydration to force amide formation; the acid chloride, by contrast, is a much more reactive electrophile that reacts efficiently and directly with the amine at mild temperatures to give the amide
SOCl₂ reacts directly with methylamine in the first step, bypassing the carboxylic acid entirely
Acid chlorides are completely unreactive toward amines, so this proposed two-step route would not work at all
Carboxylic acids are actually MORE electrophilic than acid chlorides, making the acid chloride intermediate step entirely unnecessary and wasteful
questions.explanation: A free carboxylic acid's −OH is a poor leaving group, and mixing it directly with a basic amine mostly just results in simple proton transfer (forming a stable ammonium carboxylate salt) rather than nucleophilic acyl substitution; achieving amide formation directly from the acid typically requires removing water at high temperature. Converting first to the acid chloride (a much better leaving group, Cl⁻, and a much more electrophilic carbonyl carbon due to chlorine's strong electron withdrawal) allows the amine to react efficiently and directly under much milder conditions, giving the amide cleanly.
questions.hint: Compare how good a leaving group −OH is (as in the free acid) versus −Cl (as in the acid chloride) for this type of substitution at the carbonyl carbon.
distractor_logic: SOCl₂ is added in the FIRST step specifically to react with the carboxylic acid (converting −OH to −Cl); it is the SECOND step, using the resulting acid chloride, that reacts with methylamine, not SOCl₂ itself reacting directly with the amine.

Acid chlorides are in fact HIGHLY reactive toward amines (this reactivity is precisely why the two-step route through the acid chloride is preferred); they are not unreactive toward this type of nucleophile.

Acid chlorides are considerably MORE electrophilic than the parent carboxylic acid (Cl's strong electron withdrawal, plus Cl being a much better leaving group than OH, both increase reactivity); this option reverses the actual comparison.

questions.topic: Reactions of Carboxylic Acids: Derivative Formation and Substituent Effects on Acidity
questions.question: The alpha-halo acid product of the HVZ reaction (e.g. 2-bromopropanoic acid, from propanoic acid) is measurably MORE ACIDIC than the parent, unsubstituted propanoic acid. Explain this using the same inductive reasoning applied elsewhere to substituted carboxylic acids.
options: The electronegative bromine on the alpha-carbon withdraws electron density inductively, further stabilising the resulting carboxylate anion and thereby increasing acid strength relative to the unsubstituted acid
Halogenation at the alpha-carbon has no effect whatsoever on the acidity of the distant carboxyl group
Bromine is electron-donating, which should make the halogenated acid LESS acidic than propanoic acid, contradicting the stated observation
The HVZ reaction converts the compound into a completely different, non-acidic functional group, so comparing acidities is meaningless here
questions.explanation: Just as with other alpha-substituted carboxylic acids (e.g. chloroacetic acid vs. acetic acid), the electronegative halogen introduced by the HVZ reaction withdraws electron density inductively through the sigma-bond framework, helping to stabilise the negative charge of the resulting carboxylate anion once the acidic proton is lost; this increased conjugate-base stability directly translates into increased acid strength for the alpha-halo acid relative to the unsubstituted parent acid.
questions.hint: Apply the same inductive-effect reasoning used earlier for comparing chlorine-substituted acids at different positions.
distractor_logic: The alpha-carbon (where the HVZ halogen is installed) is close enough to the carboxyl group for its inductive effect to be significant; this is exactly analogous to how a 2-chloro substituent measurably affects acidity elsewhere in this chapter's reasoning.
Bromine, like chlorine, is electronegative and electron-WITHDRAWING (inductively), not electron-donating; this option describes the opposite of the halogen's actual inductive character.

The HVZ reaction product retains a fully intact, ionisable −COOH group (the halogen is installed at the alpha-carbon, a different position); it remains a genuine carboxylic acid whose acidity can be meaningfully compared to the unsubstituted parent acid.

questions.topic: Nomenclature and Structure of the Carbonyl Group in Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Rosenmund reduction of pentanoyl chloride, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂COCl, gives an aldehyde product. What is its correct IUPAC name?
options: Pentan-2-one
Pentanoic acid
Pentan-1-ol
Pentanal
questions.explanation: Rosenmund reduction (H₂/Pd−BaSO₄) converts an acid chloride, R−COCl, into the corresponding aldehyde, R−CHO, with the same carbon count and skeleton; here, the 5-carbon acyl chloride gives the 5-carbon aldehyde, pentanal.
questions.hint: First identify what type of product the Rosenmund reduction generally gives, then apply standard IUPAC aldehyde naming.
distractor_logic: Pentan-2-one would require the carbonyl carbon to be internal (flanked by two carbon chains), but Rosenmund reduction of a straight-chain acyl chloride gives a terminal −CHO group, an aldehyde, not a ketone.
Pentanoic acid is the OXIDISED form, not a reduction product; Rosenmund reduction reduces the acid chloride, it does not oxidise anything.
Pentan-1-ol would be the product of a STRONGER reduction (e.g. LiAlH₄) that goes past the aldehyde stage to the alcohol; Rosenmund reduction is specifically designed to stop at the aldehyde.
mixed_topics: Nomenclature and Structure of the Carbonyl Group in Aldehydes and Ketones
Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones

questions.topic: Nomenclature and Structure of the Carbonyl Group in Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: A molecule contains both a −COOH group at one end and a −CHO group at the other end of the same chain (e.g. OHC−CH₂CH₂CH₂−COOH). Applying the standard IUPAC seniority order, which group is cited as the suffix, and what does the other become?
options: Only common names can describe a molecule containing both groups simultaneously
−COOH is senior and cited as the suffix ('-oic acid'); −CHO is demoted to the prefix 'oxo-', giving 5-oxopentanoic acid
−CHO is senior and cited as the suffix ('-al'); −COOH is demoted to a prefix
Both groups are cited as co-equal suffixes joined together in the name
questions.explanation: The standard IUPAC seniority order places carboxylic acids above aldehydes; when both are present in the same molecule, −COOH is cited as the principal suffix ('-oic acid') and the lower-priority −CHO is demoted to the prefix 'oxo-', giving 5-oxopentanoic acid for this specific structure.
questions.hint: Recall that carboxylic acids sit ABOVE aldehydes in the standard IUPAC functional-group seniority order.
distractor_logic: IUPAC systematic nomenclature handles molecules with multiple different functional groups routinely, using the established seniority-order rule; this is not restricted to common names.
This reverses the correct seniority; carboxylic acids rank ABOVE aldehydes in the IUPAC priority order, so −COOH (not −CHO) is the group cited as the suffix here.
IUPAC names cite exactly ONE principal characteristic group as the suffix; they do not combine two different functional-group suffixes into a single joint suffix.
mixed_topics: Nomenclature and Structure of the Carbonyl Group in Aldehydes and Ketones
Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: A chemist prepares acetophenone (C₆H₅COCH₃) by Friedel−Crafts acylation, then wants to further react it with a Grignard reagent. Compared to reacting the SAME Grignard reagent with a simple aliphatic ketone of similar size, is acetophenone expected to react faster or slower, and why?
options: Acetophenone cannot react with a Grignard reagent at all, since it was made by Friedel−Crafts acylation
Slower, because the phenyl ring conjugated with the carbonyl donates electron density into it by resonance, reducing its electrophilicity relative to a purely aliphatic ketone
Identically, since Grignard addition rates never depend on whether the substrate is aromatic or aliphatic
Faster, because aromatic rings always increase the electrophilicity of any attached carbonyl group
questions.explanation: The phenyl ring's pi system is conjugated with acetophenone's carbonyl group, allowing resonance donation of electron density into the carbonyl carbon; this makes the carbonyl carbon less electrophilic (and hence less reactive toward the Grignard's nucleophilic attack) than a comparable purely aliphatic ketone lacking this conjugation.
questions.hint: Recall the general principle that aromatic carbonyl compounds are less reactive toward nucleophilic addition than their aliphatic counterparts, and connect it to this specific reagent pair.
distractor_logic: How a ketone was originally synthesised (e.g. by Friedel−Crafts acylation) has no bearing on its subsequent reactivity toward a Grignard reagent; acetophenone reacts with Grignard reagents readily, just somewhat more slowly than a comparable aliphatic ketone.

Whether a carbonyl compound is aromatic or aliphatic IS a significant, well-established factor in nucleophilic addition rates, precisely because of the possibility of ring conjugation with the carbonyl group.

This reverses the actual electronic effect; ring conjugation DONATES electron density into the carbonyl (reducing, not increasing, its electrophilicity), making the aromatic ketone less reactive, not more.
mixed_topics: Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: A two-step synthesis converts pentanoyl chloride into pentan-1-ol: (1) Rosenmund reduction to pentanal; (2) treatment with NaBH₄. Explain why this two-step, milder route is preferred over directly reducing the acid chloride with a single equivalent of a strong hydride reagent like LiAlH₄.
options: NaBH₄ is actually a stronger reducing agent than LiAlH₄, which is why it is used in the second step
LiAlH₄ cannot reduce acid chlorides under any circumstances, making the two-step route the only possible option

This staged approach gives precise, deliberate control over the reduction level at each step (stopping cleanly at the aldehyde first, then reducing to the alcohol second), whereas a strong hydride like LiAlH₄ would likely reduce the acid chloride all the way to the alcohol in one uncontrolled step, which happens to give the same final product here but offers no intermediate control if an aldehyde were the desired final product instead
Rosenmund reduction and NaBH₄ reduction are chemically identical reactions performed twice for no real reason
questions.explanation: While LiAlH₄ could in principle reduce the acid chloride directly to the same final alcohol product, the staged Rosenmund-then-NaBH₄ route demonstrates (and provides) explicit control at the intermediate aldehyde stage — useful if the synthesis instead needed to isolate the aldehyde itself, or needed the milder, more chemoselective NaBH₄ step to avoid reducing other sensitive functional groups that a strong reagent like LiAlH₄ might also attack.
questions.hint: Think about WHY a chemist might deliberately choose a slower, two-step, more controlled route even when a faster one-step alternative exists.
distractor_logic: NaBH₄ is in fact a considerably MILDER, weaker hydride reducing agent than LiAlH₄, not stronger; this is precisely why NaBH₄ is often chosen when more selective, controlled reduction (or compatibility with other sensitive groups) is needed.

LiAlH₄ DOES reduce acid chlorides (readily, and typically all the way to the alcohol in one step); the two-step route is not the only chemically possible option, it is simply the more controlled/selective one.

The two steps are mechanistically and functionally distinct (Rosenmund reduction stops cleanly at the aldehyde using a poisoned catalyst; NaBH₄ then separately reduces that aldehyde to the alcohol); they are not the same reaction performed twice.
mixed_topics: Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Starting from pentan-1-ol, a chemist wants to isolate PURE pentanal without any pentanoic acid contamination. Which single reagent choice achieves this most reliably?
options: PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate) in anhydrous dichloromethane, which is specifically controlled to stop at the aldehyde stage
Excess hot, acidified KMnO₄, which drives the oxidation as far as possible
Excess hot, alkaline KMnO₄, followed by acidification
K₂Cr₂O₄ in aqueous H₂SO₄, refluxed for an extended period
questions.explanation: PCC, used under anhydrous conditions, is specifically valued as a mild, controlled oxidant that reliably stops at the aldehyde stage for a primary alcohol, avoiding the over-oxidation to the carboxylic acid that stronger, aqueous oxidants (excess/hot/refluxed KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₄) would cause.
questions.hint: Among these choices, identify the one specifically known for its controlled, mild, non-aqueous oxidising character.
distractor_logic: Excess hot acidified KMnO₄ is a strong, vigorous oxidant that drives oxidation all the way through the aldehyde stage to the carboxylic acid, the opposite of stopping cleanly at pentanal.
Hot alkaline KMnO₄, followed by acidification, is likewise a strong, complete oxidant, and would give pentanoic acid, not the desired pure aldehyde.
Refluxing with K₂Cr₂O₄/H₂SO₄ for an extended period is also a vigorous, complete oxidation condition, driving the reaction past the aldehyde stage to the carboxylic acid.
mixed_topics: Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Propyne is hydrated (dil. H₂SO₄/HgSO₄, Markovnikov) to give acetone. This acetone is then subjected to self-aldol condensation (dilute NaOH, then heat). What is the final product of this ENTIRE two-step sequence, starting from propyne?
options: But-2-enal (crotonaldehyde)
4-Methylpent-3-en-2-one (mesityl oxide)
Propan-2-ol
Propanoic acid
questions.explanation: Step 1 (Markovnikov hydration of propyne) gives acetone, CH₃COCH₃. Step 2 (self-aldol condensation of acetone, base then heat) proceeds via enolate addition followed by dehydration to give the conjugated enone, 4-methylpent-3-en-2-one (mesityl oxide) — the same product obtained starting directly from acetone, since the intermediate in this sequence IS acetone.
questions.hint: Work out the product of step 1 first, then apply the standard self-aldol condensation outcome to that specific intermediate.
distractor_logic: But-2-enal is the self-aldol condensation product of ACETALDEHYDE (a 2-carbon aldehyde, from a DIFFERENT starting alkyne, ethyne), not the acetone (a 3-carbon ketone) generated from propyne here.
Propan-2-ol would be the product of simply reducing acetone (e.g. with NaBH₄), not subjecting it to base-catalysed aldol condensation.

Propanoic acid would require oxidative chemistry on a different starting material; neither step in this sequence (Markovnikov hydration, then base-catalysed aldol condensation) is an oxidation of this type.
mixed_topics: Methods of Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions

questions.topic: Physical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Comparing propanal (CH₃CH₂CHO), propan-1-ol (CH₃CH₂CH₂OH), and propanoic acid (CH₃CH₂COOH), all of comparable molecular mass, rank them in INCREASING order of boiling point.
options: All three have essentially identical boiling points
Propan-1-ol < propanal < propanoic acid
Propanal < propan-1-ol < propanoic acid
Propanoic acid < propan-1-ol < propanal
questions.explanation: Propanal (dipole−dipole only, no O−H) boils lowest. Propan-1-ol (O−H, single hydrogen bonds between molecules) boils higher. Propanoic acid boils highest of all, since carboxylic acids characteristically form strong, cyclic DIMERS held together by TWO simultaneous hydrogen bonds between pairs of molecules, an even stronger overall intermolecular association than a simple alcohol's single hydrogen bonds.
questions.hint: Carboxylic acids are known to form a specific, especially strong type of hydrogen-bonded pairing (dimers) in the liquid/vapour state.
distractor_logic: The three compounds have distinctly different types and strengths of intermolecular force (dipole−dipole only, simple hydrogen bonding, and strong dimeric hydrogen bonding respectively), giving measurably different boiling points, not identical ones.
This places propan-1-ol below propanal, but propan-1-ol's hydrogen bonding (via O−H) gives it a higher boiling point than propanal, which has only dipole−dipole attraction and no O−H at all.
This is the reverse order; propanoic acid, with its strong dimeric hydrogen bonding, boils HIGHEST of the three, not lowest.
mixed_topics: Physical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones
Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids

questions.topic: Physical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: A student claims: 'Since acetaldehyde has a lower boiling point than acetone, acetaldehyde must also be LESS reactive than acetone toward nucleophilic addition, because both properties relate to the carbonyl group.' Evaluate this claim.
options: Boiling point differences always predict addition reactivity differences in the same direction for any pair of carbonyl compounds
The claim is correct, since both boiling point and reactivity are controlled by exactly the same underlying molecular property
Acetaldehyde and acetone are equally reactive toward nucleophilic addition, so the entire comparison is moot

The claim is incorrect; boiling point (governed by intermolecular forces between whole molecules) and nucleophilic addition reactivity (governed by steric/electronic effects AT the carbonyl carbon) are different physical/chemical properties that do not necessarily correlate, and in fact acetaldehyde (an aldehyde) is MORE reactive toward nucleophilic addition than acetone (a ketone), despite boiling lower
questions.explanation: Boiling point depends on the STRENGTH of INTERmolecular forces between whole molecules (here, acetone's larger size gives stronger dispersion forces, raising its boiling point relative to smaller acetaldehyde), while nucleophilic addition reactivity depends on the steric bulk and electronic character AT the carbonyl carbon specifically (where acetaldehyde's single small methyl group makes it MORE reactive than acetone's two methyl groups) — these are two distinct properties governed by related but not identical structural features, and they do not have to move in the same direction.
questions.hint: Separate the property that governs boiling point (whole-molecule intermolecular attraction) from the property that governs addition reactivity (local steric/electronic environment at one specific carbon).
distractor_logic: There is no general rule that boiling point trends must track addition-reactivity trends in the same direction; this specific pair (acetaldehyde vs. acetone) is a clear counter-example, since acetaldehyde is both lower-boiling AND more reactive.

This treats two genuinely distinct physical/chemical properties as if they were governed by the identical underlying factor; while both relate broadly to the carbonyl group, the specific structural features that determine each property are not the same.

Acetaldehyde and acetone are NOT equally reactive toward nucleophilic addition; the standard aldehyde-more-reactive-than-ketone trend applies here, with acetaldehyde being the more reactive of the two, even though it has the lower boiling point.
mixed_topics: Physical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones
Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)

questions.topic: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
questions.question: In a crossed aldol reaction between acetaldehyde (which has alpha-hydrogens) and benzaldehyde (which has no alpha-hydrogen), acetaldehyde's enolate attacks benzaldehyde's carbonyl carbon rather than the reverse. Relate this outcome to the general reactivity trend for nucleophilic addition to aldehydes vs ketones.
options: Acetaldehyde could equally well act as the electrophile in this reaction, making the direction of attack essentially arbitrary

Since benzaldehyde cannot form an enolate (no alpha-hydrogen), it can ONLY act as the electrophile here; separately, its being an aromatic aldehyde would in any case make it a somewhat LESS reactive electrophile than acetaldehyde, yet the reaction still proceeds because acetaldehyde's enolate is a strong enough nucleophile to attack it
Benzaldehyde is always more reactive as an electrophile than any aliphatic aldehyde, which is the only reason it is attacked here
This outcome contradicts the general aldehyde reactivity trend and must be considered an unexplained exception
questions.explanation: Benzaldehyde's structural inability to form an enolate (no alpha-hydrogen) FORCES it into the electrophile role in any aldol-type reaction with an enolisable partner, regardless of its intrinsic electrophilicity as a carbonyl compound (which, being aromatic, is actually somewhat lower than a comparable aliphatic aldehyde due to ring resonance donation); the reaction still proceeds efficiently because acetaldehyde's enolate remains a good enough nucleophile to attack it.
questions.hint: Separate the STRUCTURAL constraint (can this compound form an enolate at all?) from the ELECTRONIC reactivity trend (how electrophilic is its carbonyl carbon, all else being equal?).
distractor_logic: Acetaldehyde CAN act as the electrophile in principle (e.g. in its own self-aldol condensation), but in THIS specific crossed reaction, since benzaldehyde has no alternative (it cannot form an enolate at all), the reaction proceeds with acetaldehyde's enolate as nucleophile and benzaldehyde as the electrophile, not an arbitrary or interchangeable assignment.

Aromatic aldehydes are generally LESS reactive electrophiles than comparable aliphatic aldehydes (due to ring resonance donation reducing electrophilicity), not more; benzaldehyde's role here is determined by its inability to form an enolate, not by superior electrophilicity.

This specific outcome is fully explained and entirely consistent with standard aldol mechanism principles (only alpha-hydrogen-bearing compounds can form the required nucleophilic enolate); it is not an unexplained exception.
mixed_topics: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions

questions.topic: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
questions.question: Both HCN addition (giving a cyanohydrin) and 2,4-DNP condensation (giving a hydrazone) follow the general aldehyde-more-reactive-than-ketone trend. For a given aldehyde/ketone pair, which reaction is expected to show a LARGER relative rate difference between the aldehyde and the ketone, and why might that be?
options: HCN addition always shows a larger rate difference, since cyanide is a much weaker nucleophile than 2,4-DNP's amine nitrogen
Both reactions always show exactly the same relative rate difference between any given aldehyde/ketone pair, with no exceptions

The addition−elimination (2,4-DNP) pathway can show an even larger rate difference, since its overall rate depends on BOTH the initial nucleophilic addition step (sensitive to sterics/electronics, same as HCN addition) AND the subsequent elimination step, compounding the aldehyde/ketone reactivity gap across two successive steps rather than one
Neither reaction's rate depends at all on whether the substrate is an aldehyde or a ketone
questions.explanation: HCN addition is governed by a single nucleophilic addition step, whose rate reflects the standard steric/electronic aldehyde-vs-ketone difference. The 2,4-DNP condensation, by contrast, involves BOTH an addition step (with the same underlying sensitivity to aldehyde vs. ketone structure) AND a subsequent elimination step (loss of water) whose rate can ALSO be influenced by the same steric/electronic factors at the (former) carbonyl carbon — so the overall aldehyde/ketone rate gap can compound across the two sequential steps, potentially making it larger overall than for the single-step HCN addition.
questions.hint: Count the number of distinct mechanistic steps in each named reaction, and consider whether the aldehyde/ketone reactivity difference could apply at MORE than one of those steps.
distractor_logic: Cyanide's intrinsic nucleophilic strength relative to 2,4-DNP's nitrogen is a separate consideration from which reaction shows a LARGER aldehyde/ketone RATE GAP; the number of rate-limiting, sterically/electronically sensitive steps in each mechanism is the more relevant factor here.

The precise MAGNITUDE of the reactivity gap can differ meaningfully between different reaction types (a one-step vs. a two-step process), even though both broadly follow the same qualitative aldehyde-more-reactive trend; treating them as identical in magnitude ignores this mechanistic distinction.

Both reactions DO depend significantly on whether the substrate is an aldehyde or a ketone; this dependence is exactly the basis of the well-established aldehyde-more-reactive-than-ketone trend that applies to both reaction types.

questions.topic: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
questions.question: NaBH₄ reduces a mixture of an aldehyde and a ketone (present in equal amounts) in the same flask. Predict which carbonyl compound is reduced FASTER, and connect this to the same underlying reasoning used for nucleophilic addition reactivity generally.
options: Both are reduced at exactly the same rate, since NaBH₄ reduction is mechanistically unrelated to ordinary nucleophilic addition
The ketone is always reduced faster by NaBH₄, the opposite of the aldehyde/ketone trend seen with other nucleophiles

The aldehyde is reduced faster, since hydride reduction is itself a form of nucleophilic addition (H⁻ is the nucleophile), and the same steric/electronic factors that make aldehydes more reactive toward other nucleophiles (like CN⁻ or NH₂OH) apply equally here
NaBH₄ cannot reduce ketones at all, only aldehydes
questions.explanation: Hydride reduction with NaBH₄ IS a nucleophilic addition (the hydride ion, H⁻, attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, just as CN⁻ or an amine nitrogen would); the same steric hindrance and electronic (+I donation) factors that make ketones less reactive than aldehydes toward those other nucleophiles apply equally to hydride, so the aldehyde in the mixture is reduced measurably faster.
questions.hint: Recognise that a hydride ion is itself simply another type of nucleophile attacking the same electrophilic carbonyl carbon.
distractor_logic: NaBH₄ reduction is mechanistically a specific CASE of nucleophilic addition (with hydride as the nucleophile), not an unrelated process; the same reactivity principles that govern other nucleophiles' addition to carbonyls apply here too.
This reverses the well-established trend; aldehydes, not ketones, are reduced faster by NaBH₄, consistent with (not opposite to) the general nucleophilic addition reactivity pattern.
NaBH₄ does reduce ketones (just somewhat more slowly than aldehydes under comparable conditions); it is a general, though selectivity-tunable, reducing agent for both classes of carbonyl compound.

questions.topic: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
questions.question: A synthesis calls for reacting a Grignard reagent selectively with an ALDEHYDE group in a molecule that ALSO contains a ketone group elsewhere, without the Grignard reacting at the ketone. Is selective reaction achievable, and if so, on what basis?
options: The ketone will always react preferentially over the aldehyde, the reverse of the general reactivity trend
This scenario is impossible, since a molecule can never contain both an aldehyde and a ketone group simultaneously

Partial selectivity may be achievable in principle at low temperature or with a carefully controlled (limiting) amount of Grignard reagent, exploiting the fact that aldehydes are intrinsically more reactive toward nucleophilic addition than ketones, though achieving clean selectivity in practice can be challenging and may require a protecting-group strategy for full reliability
No selectivity is ever possible, since Grignard reagents react with all carbonyl groups at exactly the same rate regardless of type
questions.explanation: The same aldehyde-more-reactive-than-ketone trend that governs simple nucleophilic additions (like HCN addition) applies to Grignard addition as well; under carefully controlled conditions (low temperature, limiting reagent), the more reactive aldehyde group can often be made to react preferentially, though in synthetic practice a protecting group is frequently used on one of the two carbonyls to guarantee complete, reliable selectivity.
questions.hint: Apply the same general aldehyde-vs-ketone reactivity trend that governs other nucleophilic additions to this synthetic selectivity question.
distractor_logic: This reverses the well-established reactivity trend; aldehydes are more reactive than ketones toward Grignard addition, not the other way around.
Molecules with both an aldehyde and a ketone group in the same structure (keto-aldehydes) are chemically perfectly valid and do exist; this scenario is not structurally impossible.

Grignard reagents, like other nucleophiles, DO show a meaningful reactivity preference for aldehydes over ketones; this reactivity difference is exactly what can be exploited (at least partially) for selective addition.

questions.topic: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
questions.question: Contrast the reaction of a nucleophile (e.g. an amine) with a simple aldehyde versus with an acid chloride. Both reactions involve attack at an electrophilic carbonyl carbon, but the final outcome differs mechanistically. Explain the key difference.
options: Acid chlorides are entirely unreactive toward nucleophiles, unlike aldehydes
The aldehyde reaction is a substitution, while the acid chloride reaction is a simple addition, the reverse of the correct pairing

With an aldehyde, the nucleophile adds and the tetrahedral intermediate is simply protonated (true ADDITION, both original substituents retained); with an acid chloride, the tetrahedral intermediate instead EXPELS the chloride leaving group to re-form a C=O, giving overall SUBSTITUTION (the nucleophile replaces Cl, rather than simply adding across the double bond)
Both reactions give exactly the same type of product (simple addition across C=O) with no mechanistic distinction whatsoever
questions.explanation: An aldehyde has no good leaving group attached to its carbonyl carbon (only H and R), so after nucleophilic attack, the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate simply gets protonated, giving a true addition product. An acid chloride's carbonyl carbon DOES bear a good leaving group (Cl⁻); after the nucleophile attacks, the tetrahedral intermediate collapses by expelling chloride and re-forming the C=O, giving overall substitution (nucleophilic acyl substitution) rather than simple addition — a mechanistically distinct outcome despite both starting with the same initial nucleophilic attack step.
questions.hint: Ask whether each carbonyl compound's tetrahedral intermediate has a good LEAVING GROUP available to expel, re-forming a C=O.
distractor_logic: Acid chlorides are in fact HIGHLY reactive toward nucleophiles (often more so than simple aldehydes, due to chlorine's strong electron withdrawal), readily undergoing this substitution-type reaction; they are not unreactive.

This reverses the correct pairing; it is the ALDEHYDE reaction that is a simple addition (no leaving group to expel), while the ACID CHLORIDE reaction is a substitution (chloride is expelled), not the other way around.

The two reactions genuinely differ in their final outcome (addition vs. substitution) specifically because of whether a good leaving group is present on the carbonyl carbon; they are not mechanistically identical despite the shared initial nucleophilic attack step.

questions.topic: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
questions.question: Tollens' reagent oxidises aldehydes but not ketones. Relate this selectivity to the fundamental structural difference between an aldehyde's and a ketone's carbonyl carbon that also governs their differing nucleophilic addition reactivity.
options: Ketones are actually MORE electrophilic than aldehydes, which is why Tollens' reagent selectively avoids reacting with them
Tollens' reagent selectivity is completely unrelated to the structural difference between aldehydes and ketones; it is a coincidental, unexplained phenomenon

An aldehyde's carbonyl carbon retains a hydrogen atom directly attached to it, providing a specific C−H bond that can be oxidised (removed as part of the mechanism); a ketone's carbonyl carbon has no such hydrogen (it is flanked by two carbon-containing groups instead), so it simply cannot be oxidised by this mechanism at all
Both aldehydes and ketones react identically with Tollens' reagent, and any apparent difference is due to experimental error
questions.explanation: The oxidation of an aldehyde by Tollens' reagent proceeds via removal of the aldehyde's own characteristic C−H bond (the hydrogen directly on the carbonyl carbon), which is oxidised as the silver ion is reduced to metallic silver; a ketone's carbonyl carbon has no such hydrogen at all (both flanking positions are carbon-containing groups), so this particular oxidation pathway is simply unavailable to it — the same core structural difference (presence vs. absence of a carbonyl C−H) that also underlies the general aldehyde-vs-ketone nucleophilic addition reactivity trend.
questions.hint: Recall the one structural feature that fundamentally distinguishes an aldehyde's carbonyl carbon from a ketone's, and connect it directly to what Tollens' oxidation mechanistically requires.
distractor_logic: This is unrelated to the actual basis of Tollens' selectivity, and in any case aldehydes (not ketones) are generally the more electrophilic/more reactive class toward nucleophilic addition, the opposite ranking implied here.

Tollens' selectivity is directly and specifically explained by this same fundamental structural feature (presence or absence of a carbonyl C−H bond); it is not an unrelated or coincidental phenomenon.

Aldehydes and ketones give clearly and reliably DIFFERENT results with Tollens' reagent (positive for aldehydes, negative for ketones); this is a well-established, reproducible distinguishing test, not an experimental artifact.
mixed_topics: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions: Mechanism and Reactivity Trends (Aldehydes vs Ketones)
Distinguishing Tests for Aldehydes and Ketones (Tollens', Fehling's, Iodoform) and Uses

questions.topic: Reactions with Ammonia Derivatives and Other Addition–Elimination Reactions
questions.question: An unknown liquid gives a positive 2,4-DNP test (orange precipitate) but a NEGATIVE Tollens' test. What class of compound does this combination of results indicate?
options: An alcohol, since 2,4-DNP is specific to hydroxyl-containing compounds
A ketone, since 2,4-DNP reacts with BOTH aldehydes and ketones (confirming a carbonyl group is present), while Tollens' reagent is aldehyde-specific and gives a negative result for ketones
An aldehyde, since only aldehydes give a positive 2,4-DNP test
This combination of results cannot occur for any real compound
questions.explanation: 2,4-DNP is a general carbonyl-detecting reagent, reacting with BOTH aldehydes and ketones (positive result here confirms SOME kind of carbonyl group is present); Tollens' reagent, by contrast, is specific to aldehydes (oxidising the carbonyl C−H), giving a negative result for a ketone. The combination (positive 2,4-DNP, negative Tollens') is therefore most consistent with the unknown being a ketone.
questions.hint: Recall which of these two reagents is a general carbonyl test, and which is specific to just one sub-class of carbonyl compound.
distractor_logic: 2,4-DNP reacts with the C=O of a carbonyl group (aldehydes and ketones), not with the −OH of an alcohol; a simple alcohol would give a NEGATIVE 2,4-DNP test, inconsistent with the given positive result.
Aldehydes give a POSITIVE Tollens' test (that is exactly what the reagent is used to detect); the given negative Tollens' result rules OUT an aldehyde, not confirms one.
This combination of results is entirely consistent, expected, and commonly observed for a simple ketone; it is not an impossible or contradictory pairing of test results.

questions.topic: Reactions with Ammonia Derivatives and Other Addition–Elimination Reactions
questions.question: Both oxime formation (carbonyl + NH₂OH) and the DEHYDRATION step of aldol condensation (beta-hydroxy carbonyl → alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl + H₂O) share a common mechanistic theme. What is it?
options: Both are examples of simple nucleophilic substitution with no elimination step involved at all
Both reactions destroy the original carbonyl group's oxygen atom entirely, in both cases

Both involve the ELIMINATION of a small molecule (water, in each case) from an initially-formed addition intermediate, to generate a new pi bond (C=N in the oxime case, C=C in the aldol condensation case)
There is no meaningful mechanistic similarity between these two reactions
questions.explanation: Oxime formation proceeds via nucleophilic ADDITION of NH₂OH to the carbonyl, followed by ELIMINATION of a water molecule to form the C=N double bond. Aldol condensation's dehydration step similarly ELIMINATES a water molecule from the beta-hydroxy carbonyl addition product, forming a new C=C double bond conjugated with the remaining carbonyl. Both are examples of an addition−elimination (or, in this specific step, simply an elimination following a prior addition) sequence that removes water to generate a new pi bond.
questions.hint: In both cases, ask what small molecule is lost, and what NEW pi bond forms as a direct result of that loss.
distractor_logic: Both processes specifically DO involve a distinct elimination step (loss of water, forming a new pi bond); they are not simple, elimination-free substitutions.

In the oxime case, the original carbonyl oxygen IS lost (as part of the eliminated water); but in the aldol condensation's dehydration step, it is a DIFFERENT oxygen (from the newly-added beta-hydroxyl group) that is lost, while the original carbonyl's own oxygen is retained in the final alpha,beta-unsaturated product — so this claim about 'the original carbonyl group's oxygen' being destroyed in both cases is not quite accurate for the aldol case.
Both reactions share this genuine, specific mechanistic parallel (loss of water from an addition intermediate to form a new pi bond); the similarity is real and instructive, not absent.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: But-2-enal (crotonaldehyde, CH₃CH=CHCHO, the self-aldol condensation product of acetaldehyde) is subjected to excess catalytic H₂/Ni, which reduces BOTH the C=C and the C=O. What is the final saturated product?
options: Butan-1-ol
Butanal (only the alkene reduced, carbonyl untouched)
Butanoic acid
But-2-en-1-ol (only the carbonyl reduced, alkene untouched)
questions.explanation: Excess catalytic hydrogenation over Ni reduces BOTH multiple bonds present: the C=C is hydrogenated to a C−C single bond, and the C=O is reduced to a C−OH; starting from the 4-carbon enal, the fully saturated product is the 4-carbon primary alcohol, butan-1-ol.
questions.hint: The question specifies EXCESS H₂/Ni, sufficient to reduce every multiple bond present in the starting molecule, not just one of them.
distractor_logic: This describes the opposite partial reduction (alkene reduced, carbonyl left untouched); again, excess H₂/Ni as specified reduces both, not just the alkene.
H₂/Ni is a REDUCING system; it does not oxidise the aldehyde to a carboxylic acid. The carbonyl is reduced to an alcohol under these hydrogenation conditions, not oxidised further.
This describes only PARTIAL reduction (carbonyl reduced, alkene left untouched); with excess catalytic H₂/Ni as specified, both multiple bonds are reduced, not just one.

Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: In a crossed aldol condensation between acetone (which has alpha-hydrogens) and benzaldehyde (which has none), the major product is 4-phenylbut-3-en-2-one, formed via acetone's enolate attacking benzaldehyde's carbonyl. Given that ALDEHYDES are generally more electrophilic than ketones, why doesn't benzaldehyde's OWN alpha-position (if it had one) compete for enolate formation here?
options: Aldehydes can never act as electrophiles in any aldol-type reaction, which is the real reason here
Benzaldehyde does have ordinary alpha-hydrogens, but they simply react much more slowly than acetone's, which is why acetone's enolate is observed instead
This selectivity has nothing to do with alpha-hydrogen availability and is instead purely a matter of which reagent was added to the flask first

Benzaldehyde's carbonyl carbon is flanked only by the aromatic ring and a hydrogen; the ring carbon adjacent to the carbonyl is NOT a typical sp³ alpha-carbon capable of the usual enolate-forming deprotonation, so no competing enolate can form from benzaldehyde at all, regardless of its high electrophilicity as a carbonyl compound
questions.explanation: Benzaldehyde's carbonyl carbon is attached to the aromatic ring (not an ordinary aliphatic carbon bearing removable alpha-hydrogens in the usual enolisable sense) and to a single hydrogen (which is the aldehyde's own characteristic carbonyl C−H, not an alpha-hydrogen); there is therefore no accessible aliphatic alpha-carbon on benzaldehyde at all, so it structurally CANNOT form an enolate, leaving acetone as the only possible enolate source in this pairing, regardless of benzaldehyde's high intrinsic electrophilicity as an aldehyde.
questions.hint: Carefully distinguish benzaldehyde's own carbonyl C−H (part of the aldehyde group itself) from a true alpha-hydrogen (which would need to be on a SEPARATE carbon adjacent to the carbonyl).
distractor_logic: Aldehydes readily act as electrophiles in many reactions, including this very crossed aldol reaction (benzaldehyde IS the electrophile here); the premise that aldehydes can never play this role is incorrect.

Benzaldehyde structurally has NO alpha-hydrogen at all (its carbonyl carbon is flanked only by the ring and a single H, which is the aldehyde's own defining C−H, not a true alpha-hydrogen on an adjacent carbon); it is not simply a matter of slower reaction, but of complete structural unavailability.

The order of reagent addition to the flask is not the determining factor for which compound forms the enolate; the STRUCTURAL presence or absence of an alpha-hydrogen is what fundamentally determines which reactant(s) can act as the nucleophile.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: Two candidate methods are proposed for preparing an aldehyde suitable for undergoing the Cannizzaro reaction: (i) Gatterman−Koch formylation of benzene to give benzaldehyde; (ii) PCC oxidation of ethanol to give acetaldehyde. Which candidate aldehyde is ACTUALLY suitable for Cannizzaro reaction, and why does the other fail?
options: Benzaldehyde (from method i) is suitable, since it has no alpha-hydrogen; acetaldehyde (from method ii) is NOT suitable, since it DOES have alpha-hydrogens and would instead preferentially undergo aldol condensation under basic conditions
Both aldehydes are equally suitable for Cannizzaro reaction, regardless of alpha-hydrogen content
Neither aldehyde, however prepared, can ever undergo the Cannizzaro reaction
Acetaldehyde is suitable and benzaldehyde is not, the reverse of the correct pairing
questions.explanation: Cannizzaro reaction specifically requires an aldehyde with NO alpha-hydrogen (unable to form an enolate); benzaldehyde (its 'alpha' position being the aromatic ring, not a normal aliphatic alpha-carbon) fits this requirement and undergoes Cannizzaro under concentrated base. Acetaldehyde, by contrast, has ordinary alpha-hydrogens on its methyl group and would instead preferentially form an enolate and undergo aldol condensation under the same basic conditions, not Cannizzaro.
questions.hint: Apply the same alpha-hydrogen-presence test used throughout this topic to decide which of the two candidate aldehydes is structurally eligible for Cannizzaro reaction.
distractor_logic: The two aldehydes are NOT equally suitable; the presence or absence of an alpha-hydrogen is precisely the deciding structural factor for whether Cannizzaro (versus aldol condensation) occurs.

Benzaldehyde specifically CAN and does undergo the Cannizzaro reaction (it is in fact one of the classic textbook substrates for this reaction, alongside formaldehyde); the premise that neither aldehyde can ever undergo it is incorrect.

This reverses the correct pairing; benzaldehyde (no alpha-hydrogen) is the one suitable for Cannizzaro, while acetaldehyde (has alpha-hydrogens) is not, since it would follow the aldol pathway instead.
