questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: Both aldol condensation (base-catalysed) and Fischer esterification (acid-catalysed) begin with a nucleophile attacking an electrophilic carbonyl carbon, yet they form fundamentally different types of new bond. Contrast the two.
options: Both reactions form exactly the same type of new bond (carbon−oxygen) in both cases

Aldol condensation forms a new CARBON−CARBON bond (the nucleophile is a carbanion-like enolate attacking another carbon's carbonyl); Fischer esterification forms a new CARBON−OXYGEN bond (the nucleophile is an alcohol's oxygen attacking the acid's carbonyl carbon)
Neither reaction actually forms any new bond at all; both are purely rearrangement reactions
Aldol condensation forms a carbon−oxygen bond, while esterification forms a carbon−carbon bond, the reverse of the correct pairing
questions.explanation: In aldol condensation, the NUCLEOPHILE is a carbon-centred enolate (formed by removing an alpha-hydrogen), so the new bond formed when it attacks a second carbonyl carbon is a CARBON−CARBON bond. In Fischer esterification, the nucleophile is an alcohol's OXYGEN lone pair attacking the acid's electrophilic carbonyl carbon, forming a new CARBON−OXYGEN bond; the two reactions, despite both beginning with nucleophilic attack on a carbonyl, build fundamentally different types of new bond because their respective nucleophiles differ (carbon-centred vs. oxygen-centred).
questions.hint: Identify the specific ATOM of the nucleophile (a carbon of the enolate, or an oxygen of the alcohol) that directly forms the new bond in each reaction.
distractor_logic: The two reactions use nucleophiles centred on DIFFERENT atoms (carbon for the enolate, oxygen for the alcohol), so they form different TYPES of new bond, not the same type in both cases.

Both reactions genuinely form a brand NEW bond between two previously separate molecules (a new C−C bond joining two carbonyl-containing fragments in aldol condensation; a new C−O bond joining the acid and alcohol fragments in esterification); neither is simply an internal rearrangement with no new bond formed.

This reverses the correct pairing; aldol condensation (carbon-based enolate nucleophile) forms a C−C bond, while esterification (oxygen-based alcohol nucleophile) forms a C−O bond, not the other way around.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: The alpha-hydrogen of a simple ketone like acetone (pK₂ ≈ 20) is vastly LESS acidic than the O−H proton of a carboxylic acid like acetic acid (pK₂ ≈ 4.76), even though both protons are removed to form a resonance-stabilised conjugate base. Explain this large difference in acidity.
options: The carboxylate anion is stabilised by delocalisation of the negative charge over TWO electronegative oxygen atoms (a strong, symmetric resonance effect); the enolate anion (from removing an alpha-hydrogen) delocalises charge onto only ONE oxygen and partly onto a CARBON atom, a comparatively much weaker stabilisation, making the enolate a much less stable (and hence its parent alpha-C−H much less acidic) conjugate base by comparison
The enolate ion is actually MORE stable than the carboxylate ion, which should make the ketone's alpha-C−H the more acidic of the two, contradicting the given pK₂ values
Resonance stabilisation is irrelevant to both cases; acidity here is governed entirely by molecular mass
Both conjugate bases are stabilised to an identical extent, so the large pK₂ difference must come from some completely unrelated factor
questions.explanation: The carboxylate ion delocalises its negative charge over two chemically equivalent, highly electronegative oxygen atoms — an especially effective, symmetric stabilisation. The enolate ion (from a ketone's alpha-C−H) delocalises its charge between one oxygen and one carbon atom; carbon is far less electronegative and far less comfortable bearing significant negative charge than a second oxygen would be, so this delocalisation is considerably weaker — explaining why the enolate is a much less stabilised conjugate base, and correspondingly why the ketone's alpha-C−H (pK₂ ≈ 20) is vastly less acidic than the carboxylic acid's O−H (pK₂ ≈ 4.76).
questions.hint: Compare exactly WHERE the negative charge ends up being delocalised in each conjugate base — over two oxygens, or over one oxygen and one carbon.
distractor_logic: This has the stability comparison backwards; the carboxylate ion (two-oxygen delocalisation) is MORE stable than the enolate ion (oxygen-and-carbon delocalisation), which correctly corresponds to the carboxylic acid being the far more acidic of the two, consistent with the given pK₂ values.
Resonance stabilisation of the respective conjugate bases is in fact the PRIMARY factor explaining this large acidity difference; simple molecular mass has no direct bearing on it.

The two conjugate bases are NOT stabilised to an identical extent; the carboxylate's two-oxygen delocalisation is measurably more effective than the enolate's oxygen-and-carbon delocalisation, which is precisely the structural reason for the large observed pK₂ difference.

Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: But-2-enal (crotonaldehyde, the aldol condensation product of acetaldehyde) has a noticeably higher boiling point than butanal (a simple saturated aldehyde of the same carbon count). Suggest a structural reason for this difference.
options: But-2-enal and butanal are actually constitutional isomers with identical physical properties in every respect
Boiling point differences between these two compounds are due entirely to a difference in molecular formula (different total atom count)

The extended conjugation between the C=C and C=O in but-2-enal increases the molecule's overall polarity/polarisability, strengthening intermolecular dipole−dipole and dispersion interactions relative to the simple, unconjugated carbonyl of butanal
The presence of a C=C double bond always LOWERS boiling point relative to a saturated compound of the same size, regardless of any other structural feature
questions.explanation: Conjugation between the alkene and carbonyl in but-2-enal extends the pi system and increases the molecule's overall polarisability and dipole character compared to butanal's simple, isolated (non-conjugated) carbonyl group; this enhanced intermolecular attraction (on top of comparable molecular size) contributes to but-2-enal's higher boiling point.
questions.hint: Consider how having TWO conjugated pi systems (C=C and C=O working together) might affect a molecule's overall polarity/polarisability compared to just one isolated C=O.
distractor_logic: But-2-enal (C₄H₆O) and butanal (C₄H₈O) have different molecular formulas (but-2-enal has two fewer hydrogens, reflecting its additional degree of unsaturation from the C=C); they are not isomers of each other.

The two compounds do have slightly different atom counts, but the more significant, structurally meaningful explanation for the notable boiling-point difference is the extended conjugation in but-2-enal, not a simple atom-count argument alone.

Whether a C=C double bond raises or lowers boiling point relative to a comparable saturated compound depends on the specific structural context (e.g. whether it is conjugated with another polar group, as here); there is no absolute, universal rule that unsaturation always lowers boiling point.

Physical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Propanal (CH₃CH₂CHO), which is not significantly acidic, is oxidised by Tollens' reagent to propanoic acid (CH₃CH₂COOH), which IS a meaningfully acidic compound. Explain, in terms of structure, why this oxidation introduces significant acidity where there was none before.
options: Oxidation removes all oxygen atoms from the molecule entirely, which is what generates the new acidity
The aldehyde's own carbonyl oxygen is itself acidic in exactly the same way as the acid's −OH, so no real change in acidic character occurs upon oxidation

Oxidation replaces the aldehyde's C−H bond with a new O−H bond (installing an ionisable proton on oxygen), and the resulting carboxylate anion (upon loss of that proton) is strongly stabilised by resonance delocalisation over two equivalent oxygens — a stabilisation mechanism simply unavailable to the starting aldehyde, which has no such ionisable O−H group at all
Propanal is already just as acidic as propanoic acid, so this oxidation does not meaningfully change the molecule's acidity
questions.explanation: Propanal's carbonyl oxygen has no attached, ionisable hydrogen (there is no O−H bond in an aldehyde); oxidation to the carboxylic acid installs a genuine O−H group whose proton CAN be lost, generating a carboxylate anion that is strongly resonance-stabilised (charge spread over two equivalent oxygens) — this newly available, well-stabilised deprotonation pathway is precisely why the acid is significantly acidic while the parent aldehyde essentially is not.
questions.hint: Compare the oxygen-containing functional groups of the two compounds directly: does either one actually have an O−H bond that could lose its proton?
distractor_logic: Oxidation here ADDS oxygen-containing functionality (converting −CHO to −COOH); it does not strip oxygen atoms from the molecule.

A carbonyl oxygen with no attached hydrogen (as in the aldehyde) is fundamentally not the same as, and is not comparably acidic to, a hydroxyl oxygen WITH an attached, ionisable hydrogen (as in the carboxylic acid); the two are structurally and functionally different.
Propanal has no significant acidity in the same sense as a carboxylic acid (it lacks an ionisable O−H group entirely); the two compounds are not comparably acidic before and after this oxidation.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Given the set {ethanol, acetaldehyde, acetone, pentan-3-one}, use a COMBINATION of the iodoform test and the Tollens'/Fehling's tests to correctly identify which single compound gives a POSITIVE iodoform test but a NEGATIVE Tollens' test.
options: Pentan-3-one, since its symmetric structure guarantees a positive iodoform test
Acetaldehyde, since it gives a negative iodoform test despite being an aldehyde
Acetone, since it has a methyl group directly on its carbonyl carbon (positive iodoform) but is a ketone, not an aldehyde (negative Tollens')
Ethanol, since alcohols never give a positive iodoform test under any circumstances
questions.explanation: Acetone, CH₃COCH₃, has a methyl group directly bonded to its carbonyl carbon on BOTH sides, satisfying the iodoform test's structural requirement (positive result); being a ketone (no C−H on the carbonyl carbon itself), it gives a negative Tollens' test. Ethanol also gives a positive iodoform test (it is oxidised in situ to acetaldehyde, which fits the CH₃CHO/methyl-ketone-precursor pattern), but the question specifically asks for the compound satisfying BOTH conditions together, and acetone cleanly satisfies both as described.
questions.hint: Check each compound against BOTH criteria simultaneously: does it have the CH₃CO−/CH₃CH(OH)− motif (iodoform), and does it have a carbonyl C−H (Tollens')?
distractor_logic: Pentan-3-one's carbonyl carbon is flanked by two ETHYL groups, not methyl groups, so it lacks the required CH₃CO− motif and gives a NEGATIVE (not positive) iodoform test, despite its symmetry.
Acetaldehyde, CH₃CHO, DOES give a positive iodoform test (it has the required CH₃CO− motif directly); this option's premise that it gives a negative result is incorrect.

Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, actually DOES give a positive iodoform test (it is a well-known, specifically-cited exception among simple alcohols, since I₂/NaOH first oxidises it in situ to acetaldehyde, which fits the required pattern); the premise that alcohols never give this result is incorrect.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Explain why NaBH₄ reduces an aldehyde faster than the corresponding ketone, drawing an explicit parallel to the reasoning already used to explain why aldehydes undergo nucleophilic addition with other nucleophiles (like CN⁻) faster than ketones do.
options: The rate difference for NaBH₄ reduction depends only on molecular weight, unrelated to steric or electronic factors at the carbonyl carbon
Ketones are reduced faster than aldehydes by NaBH₄, contradicting the general aldehyde-more-reactive trend seen with other nucleophiles

Hydride (H⁻) is itself simply another nucleophile attacking the electrophilic carbonyl carbon; the aldehyde's single, smaller substituent (versus the ketone's two) means less steric hindrance to the incoming hydride and less electron donation (+I) reducing the carbonyl carbon's electrophilicity, exactly the same reasoning already used for CN⁻ or other nucleophiles
NaBH₄ reduction is a completely different type of mechanism from ordinary nucleophilic addition, so no such parallel reasoning applies
questions.explanation: NaBH₄ delivers a hydride nucleophile to the same electrophilic carbonyl carbon targeted by any other nucleophile; the identical structural reasoning (less steric bulk and less electron-donating character on an aldehyde's single flanking group, versus a ketone's two) that explains the general aldehyde-more-reactive trend for nucleophiles like CN⁻ applies directly and consistently to hydride reduction as well.
questions.hint: Treat hydride (H⁻) exactly like any other nucleophile attacking the carbonyl carbon, and reapply the same steric/electronic reasoning used elsewhere in this topic.
distractor_logic: While molecular weight can influence some physical properties, the RATE difference in this specific reaction is primarily governed by the same steric/electronic factors at the carbonyl carbon that govern nucleophilic addition generally, not simply by overall molecular weight.

This reverses the well-established, experimentally confirmed trend; aldehydes are reduced FASTER than ketones by NaBH₄, consistent with (not contradicting) the general nucleophilic addition reactivity pattern.

NaBH₄ reduction IS mechanistically a nucleophilic addition (with hydride as the nucleophile); it follows the same general mechanistic framework as CN⁻ or amine addition, not a fundamentally different type of reaction.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: NaBH₄ readily reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols, but does NOT reduce a carboxylic acid's −COOH group under the same mild conditions; LiAlH₄, a much stronger hydride source, IS able to reduce a carboxylic acid all the way to a primary alcohol. Explain this difference in reducing-agent requirement.
options: Carboxylic acids cannot be reduced by ANY hydride reagent under any conditions, contradicting the premise of the question

The carboxylic acid's carbonyl carbon is considerably LESS electrophilic than a simple aldehyde/ketone's, since the adjacent −OH oxygen's lone pair donates electron density into the carbonyl by resonance (partially neutralising its electrophilicity); this reduced electrophilicity requires a much stronger, more reactive hydride source (LiAlH₄) to overcome, unlike the milder NaBH₄ that suffices for ordinary aldehydes/ketones
NaBH₄ and LiAlH₄ are chemically identical reagents with no difference in reducing strength or selectivity
Carboxylic acids are actually MORE electrophilic than aldehydes or ketones, which is why they should in principle be even EASIER to reduce with NaBH₄, making the stated observation puzzling
questions.explanation: In a carboxylic acid, the −OH oxygen's lone pair can donate into the carbonyl group by resonance (much like in an ester or amide), partially offsetting the carbonyl carbon's electron deficiency and making it considerably LESS electrophilic than a simple aldehyde or ketone's carbonyl carbon; this reduced electrophilicity means the comparatively mild, less reactive NaBH₄ is generally not strong enough to reduce it efficiently, while the much stronger, more reactive LiAlH₄ can still accomplish the reduction (via a more forcing, multi-step hydride delivery, ultimately giving the primary alcohol).
questions.hint: Recall that a carboxylic acid's −OH lone pair, like an ester's alkoxy oxygen, can donate into the carbonyl group by resonance, similarly to how this affects reactivity elsewhere in this chapter's reasoning.
distractor_logic: Carboxylic acids CAN be reduced, just not by the milder NaBH₄ under standard conditions; the stronger LiAlH₄ is specifically able to accomplish this reduction, as stated directly in the question.

NaBH₄ and LiAlH₄ are genuinely different reagents with markedly different reducing strength and selectivity (LiAlH₄ being considerably more reactive/reducing a wider range of functional groups, including carboxylic acids, that NaBH₄ typically cannot touch under standard mild conditions).

This reverses the correct electronic comparison; the carboxylic acid's resonance-donating −OH oxygen makes its carbonyl carbon LESS electrophilic than a simple aldehyde/ketone's, not more, which is exactly why it needs a STRONGER reagent to reduce, not why NaBH₄ should work even better.

questions.topic: Distinguishing Tests for Aldehydes and Ketones (Tollens', Fehling's, Iodoform) and Uses
questions.question: An unknown liquid X turns blue litmus paper red and produces brisk effervescence (CO₂ gas) when added to aqueous NaHCO₃, but gives NEGATIVE results with both Tollens' and Fehling's reagents. What class of compound is X most consistent with?
options: An aldehyde, since aldehydes are always acidic enough to react with NaHCO₃
A ketone, since ketones typically turn litmus paper red
A carboxylic acid, since it is acidic enough to react with NaHCO₃ (releasing CO₂) and turn litmus red, but has no aldehyde C−H group to give a positive result with either oxidation test
This combination of results is inconsistent and cannot describe any real organic compound
questions.explanation: Reaction with NaHCO₃ to release CO₂ gas (effervescence) is a classic, specific test for a compound acidic enough to protonate bicarbonate — strongly indicative of a carboxylic acid (ordinary aldehydes/ketones/alcohols are not acidic enough to do this). Since X gives negative results with BOTH aldehyde-oxidation tests, it has no aldehyde C−H group, consistent with a simple carboxylic acid (which has no such C−H on its carbonyl carbon either) rather than an aldehyde.
questions.hint: The NaHCO₃ effervescence test specifically distinguishes carboxylic acids from most other organic compounds, which are generally not acidic enough to react this way.
distractor_logic: Ordinary aldehydes are NOT acidic enough to react with NaHCO₃ and release CO₂ gas; this specific reactivity is characteristic of carboxylic acids, not aldehydes in general.
Simple ketones are not significantly acidic and do not turn litmus paper red or react with NaHCO₃ to release gas; this behaviour is specific to a compound with a genuinely acidic (−COOH-type) proton.

This combination of results (acidic toward NaHCO₃/litmus, but negative for both aldehyde-oxidation tests) is entirely consistent with, and in fact a standard, expected identification profile for, a simple carboxylic acid.

questions.topic: Distinguishing Tests for Aldehydes and Ketones (Tollens', Fehling's, Iodoform) and Uses
questions.question: An unknown aldehyde gives a positive 2,4-DNP test but does NOT undergo aldol condensation when treated with dilute NaOH. What further conclusion can be drawn about this specific aldehyde's structure, and what reaction would it undergo instead under those basic conditions?
options: It must lack an alpha-hydrogen (like benzaldehyde or formaldehyde); rather than aldol condensation, it would instead undergo the Cannizzaro reaction under concentrated base
This combination of observations is impossible for any real compound, since all aldehydes undergo aldol condensation with base
It must be a ketone rather than an aldehyde, since only ketones fail to undergo aldol condensation
The compound must be completely unreactive toward any base under any conditions
questions.explanation: The 2,4-DNP test confirms a carbonyl group is present (aldehyde or ketone), consistent with the stated 'aldehyde'; the FAILURE to undergo aldol condensation with base specifically points to an aldehyde lacking an alpha-hydrogen (since aldol condensation requires one), which instead undergoes the alternative base-catalysed pathway available to such aldehydes, the Cannizzaro reaction.
questions.hint: Recall which structural feature is required for aldol condensation, and what the alternative base-catalysed pathway is for aldehydes lacking that feature.
distractor_logic: NOT all aldehydes undergo aldol condensation; specifically, those lacking an alpha-hydrogen (like formaldehyde and benzaldehyde) do not, and instead follow the Cannizzaro pathway under the same basic conditions — this is a well-established, non-universal exception, not an impossible combination of observations.

The question specifies the unknown is an ALDEHYDE (confirmed structurally, e.g. by other means, not merely by the 2,4-DNP test which does not by itself distinguish aldehydes from ketones); the deduction here is about which SUB-TYPE of aldehyde (alpha-hydrogen-bearing or not) it is, based on its base reactivity.

An aldehyde lacking an alpha-hydrogen is NOT completely unreactive toward base; it specifically undergoes the Cannizzaro disproportionation reaction under concentrated base conditions, which is a real, well-defined chemical transformation.

questions.topic: Distinguishing Tests for Aldehydes and Ketones (Tollens', Fehling's, Iodoform) and Uses
questions.question: The Tollens' silver-mirror test has a well-known practical application beyond the chemistry laboratory: it is historically related to the industrial process for manufacturing SILVERED GLASS MIRRORS. Explain the connection.
options: The connection is purely coincidental; the two processes share no actual underlying chemistry

The industrial silvering process uses essentially the same underlying chemistry as the laboratory Tollens' test: an aldehyde (often formaldehyde or glucose) reduces an ammoniacal silver salt solution, depositing a thin, even, reflective coating of metallic silver directly onto the glass surface
Silvered glass mirrors are manufactured using a completely different, unrelated metal (aluminium), with no connection to any aldehyde-based chemistry at all
Industrial mirror manufacturing uses Fehling's solution, not Tollens' reagent, to deposit the silver coating
questions.explanation: The classic silvering of glass mirrors historically exploits exactly the same redox chemistry as the laboratory Tollens' test: an aldehyde (industrially, often formaldehyde or a reducing sugar like glucose) reduces the silver ions in an ammoniacal silver salt solution, depositing a thin, smooth, highly reflective layer of metallic silver onto the glass surface — the same reaction that produces the 'silver mirror' appearance seen in the small-scale laboratory test tube.
questions.hint: Think literally about what the positive result of the Tollens' test actually looks like, and how that visual effect might be scaled up industrially.
distractor_logic: The connection is genuine and direct, not coincidental; both processes rely on the identical core redox reaction (an aldehyde reducing ammoniacal silver ions to metallic silver).

While aluminium-backed mirrors are also manufactured by other (vapour-deposition) methods today, the CLASSIC, historically significant silvering process is specifically silver-based and directly related to Tollens'-type aldehyde chemistry, not an unrelated aluminium process.

Fehling's solution uses a COPPER complex, not silver; it is specifically Tollens' reagent (an ammoniacal SILVER salt) that is chemically related to the silvering process, since silver metal (not copper) is what is being deposited.

questions.topic: Distinguishing Tests for Aldehydes and Ketones (Tollens', Fehling's, Iodoform) and Uses
questions.question: Both Tollens' reagent and Fehling's solution are oxidising agents that react with aldehydes but not ketones. Connect this shared selectivity to the fundamental structural feature that also governs the general nucleophilic addition reactivity difference between aldehydes and ketones.
options: In every case, the deciding structural feature is the presence (aldehyde) or absence (ketone) of a hydrogen directly bonded to the carbonyl carbon; this same feature both provides the specific C−H bond needed for oxidation by these two reagents AND (via its smaller size/weaker electron donation compared to a second alkyl group) makes the aldehyde's carbonyl carbon more accessible and electrophilic for ordinary nucleophilic addition
Tollens' and Fehling's reagents work by a completely different mechanism from ordinary nucleophilic addition, so no meaningful connection to that reactivity trend exists
Ketones are actually oxidised more readily than aldehydes by both reagents, contradicting the stated premise
The oxidation tests and the nucleophilic addition trend are governed by two entirely separate and unrelated structural features of the molecule
questions.explanation: The SAME single structural feature — whether the carbonyl carbon bears a hydrogen (aldehyde) or is instead flanked by two carbon-containing groups (ketone) — underlies both observations: that specific C−H bond is what gets oxidised by Tollens'/Fehling's reagents (unavailable in a ketone), and the SMALLER size/weaker electron-donating character of a hydrogen (versus a second alkyl/aryl group) is also exactly why an aldehyde's carbonyl carbon is more sterically accessible and more electrophilic toward ordinary nucleophiles in general nucleophilic addition reactions.
questions.hint: Identify the ONE specific structural difference between an aldehyde and a ketone's carbonyl carbon, and trace how it independently explains BOTH the oxidation-test selectivity and the general addition-reactivity trend.
distractor_logic: Tollens'/Fehling's oxidation is itself fundamentally a redox process initiated by the reagent interacting with the same electrophilic carbonyl carbon (and its available C−H) that governs ordinary nucleophilic addition chemistry; the two are mechanistically related through this shared structural feature, not entirely separate.

This reverses the well-established selectivity; aldehydes (not ketones) are the ones oxidised by Tollens' and Fehling's reagents, consistent with the question's own stated premise, not contradicting it.

Both observations trace back to the SAME underlying structural feature (presence/absence of a carbonyl C−H), not two separate, unrelated features; this is precisely the elegant, unifying connection the question is asking to identify.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Explain why acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO) does not turn blue litmus paper red, even though it shares the same C=O functional group present in acetic acid (CH₃COOH), which IS clearly acidic.
options: Both compounds are equally acidic; acetaldehyde simply reacts with litmus paper too slowly to observe any colour change
The C=O group itself is never associated with any acidity in any compound, in either case

Acetaldehyde has no O−H bond at all (its carbonyl oxygen has no attached hydrogen to lose as a proton); only acetic acid's separate hydroxyl group provides an ionisable proton whose loss generates a resonance-stabilised carboxylate anion
Acetaldehyde is actually MORE acidic than acetic acid, but this effect is masked by its high volatility
questions.explanation: Acidity in this context specifically requires an ionisable O−H (or similar) proton; acetaldehyde's carbonyl oxygen has NO attached hydrogen (it is simply C=O, with the carbon's other substituents being H and CH₃), so there is no acidic proton to lose at all. Acetic acid, by contrast, has a distinct −OH group attached to its carbonyl carbon (forming the full −COOH unit), whose proton CAN be lost to give the resonance-stabilised carboxylate anion, accounting for its genuine acidity.
questions.hint: Carefully compare the actual atoms directly bonded to each compound's carbonyl carbon: does either one have an O−H group specifically?
distractor_logic: The two compounds are NOT comparably acidic; acetaldehyde has no ionisable proton associated with its carbonyl group at all, unlike acetic acid's genuine −COOH group, so this is not merely a matter of reaction rate with litmus.

While a bare C=O group by itself provides no direct acidity, an ADJACENT O−H group (as in a carboxylic acid, forming the combined −COOH unit) does confer genuine acidity; the claim that C=O is never associated with acidity in ANY compound overgeneralises and ignores the specific −COOH case.

Acetaldehyde is not more acidic than acetic acid; it is essentially non-acidic in the sense measured by litmus paper, since it lacks any ionisable O−H proton, while acetic acid's genuine acidity is well documented and not an illusion masked by any physical property like volatility.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Vigorous oxidation (hot alkaline KMnO₄) of p-nitrotoluene gives p-nitrobenzoic acid. Predict whether this product is MORE or LESS acidic than plain benzoic acid, and connect this to the reasoning used for substituted carboxylic acid acidity generally.
options: The product cannot be a carboxylic acid at all, since −NO₂ groups are known to prevent alkylbenzene oxidation entirely
Less acidic, since −NO₂ is electron-donating and would destabilise the carboxylate anion

More acidic, since the strongly electron-withdrawing −NO₂ group (by both induction and resonance, even from the para position) further stabilises the carboxylate anion relative to plain benzoic acid's carboxylate
Exactly as acidic as plain benzoic acid, since ring substituents remote from the −COOH group have no measurable effect on its acidity
questions.explanation: −NO₂ is one of the strongest electron-withdrawing groups (by both induction and resonance, reaching the carboxylate anion even from the para position through the conjugated ring), further stabilising the negative charge of the carboxylate anion once deprotonated; this makes p-nitrobenzoic acid measurably MORE acidic than plain benzoic acid, consistent with the general principle that electron-withdrawing substituents increase carboxylic acid acidity.
questions.hint: Apply the same general electron-withdrawing-group-increases-acidity reasoning used elsewhere in this chapter, this time to an aromatic ring substituent reaching the −COOH group via conjugation.
distractor_logic: −NO₂ does not prevent the vigorous oxidation of an alkylbenzene side chain to −COOH; hot alkaline KMnO₄ oxidation of p-nitrotoluene to p-nitrobenzoic acid is a standard, well-precedented reaction.

−NO₂ is strongly electron-WITHDRAWING, not donating (it has no lone pair to donate into the ring in the relevant sense, and its structure inherently pulls electron density away); this option describes the opposite of −NO₂'s actual electronic character.

Even from the para position, a strongly conjugating substituent like −NO₂ DOES meaningfully affect the acidity of a remote −COOH group through the ring's conjugated pi system; ring substituents are not simply too far removed to matter.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Two routes are proposed to prepare 2-chlorobutanoic acid: (i) HVZ reaction (Br₂/red P... using Cl₂ instead) on butanoic acid; (ii) hydrolysis of 2-chlorobutanenitrile. Predict the relative ACIDITY of the product compared to plain butanoic acid, regardless of which route is used to make it.
options: The acidity of the final product depends on which of the two synthetic routes was used to make it, even though both give the same structure

2-Chlorobutanoic acid is more acidic than plain butanoic acid, since the electronegative chlorine on the alpha-carbon inductively stabilises the carboxylate anion, and this acidity increase is a property of the PRODUCT's structure, independent of which synthetic route was used to reach it
2-Chlorobutanoic acid is less acidic than plain butanoic acid, since chlorine donates electron density inductively
Chlorinated carboxylic acids cannot be prepared by either of these two named routes
questions.explanation: Whichever route is used to synthesise it, the FINAL PRODUCT (2-chlorobutanoic acid) has the same structure and therefore the same acidity, governed entirely by that structure (the electronegative alpha-chlorine's inductive electron withdrawal stabilising the carboxylate anion), not by the synthetic history of how it was made; both routes converge on the same, more-acidic-than-butanoic-acid product.
questions.hint: A compound's chemical/physical properties (like acidity) are determined by its final structure, not by which synthetic pathway was used to reach that structure.
distractor_logic: Acidity is an intrinsic property of a compound's STRUCTURE, not of its synthetic history; two different valid routes to the identical final structure necessarily give a product with identical acidity, not different acidities depending on the route.

Chlorine is electron-WITHDRAWING (inductively), not donating, due to its high electronegativity; this option describes the opposite of chlorine's actual inductive effect on the carboxylate anion's stability.

Both named routes are genuinely valid, standard methods for introducing an alpha-halogen onto a carboxylic acid skeleton (HVZ reaction directly on the acid, or via hydrolysis of a pre-halogenated nitrile); the premise that neither route can achieve this is incorrect.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Trichloroacetic acid, Cl₃C−COOH, is a dramatically STRONGER acid than plain acetic acid, CH₃COOH (pK₂ ≈ 0.7 vs. ≈ 4.76). Relate this large acidity difference to the SAME inductive-effect reasoning used earlier to explain why trichloroacetaldehyde is more reactive than acetaldehyde toward nucleophilic addition.
options: In both cases, the three highly electronegative chlorine atoms inductively withdraw electron density from the adjacent functional group's key reactive centre; for the aldehyde, this made the carbonyl carbon more electrophilic (increasing nucleophilic addition reactivity), and for the acid, this stabilises the resulting carboxylate anion far more strongly (increasing acidity) — the same inductive mechanism producing two related, but distinct, chemical consequences
This comparison is invalid, since trichloroacetaldehyde and trichloroacetic acid do not actually share a common substitution pattern
The two effects (increased carbonyl reactivity and increased acidity) are caused by completely unrelated aspects of the chlorine substituents in each case
Chlorine substituents increase reactivity in the aldehyde case but actually DECREASE acidity in the analogous acid case, the reverse of the correct parallel
questions.explanation: Both phenomena arise from the SAME underlying inductive electron-withdrawal by the three chlorine atoms: in trichloroacetaldehyde, this withdrawal increases the carbonyl carbon's electrophilicity (more reactive toward nucleophilic addition); in trichloroacetic acid, the same withdrawal instead acts on the OH-bearing carbon, further stabilising the resulting carboxylate anion upon deprotonation (dramatically increasing acidity) — a single shared inductive mechanism manifesting as two related but mechanistically distinct chemical consequences, depending on which functional group it is acting on.
questions.hint: Both molecules share the identical Cl₃C− substituent pattern; ask what the SAME inductive electron withdrawal does when attached next to a carbonyl carbon (as in the aldehyde) versus next to a carboxyl group (as in the acid).
distractor_logic: Both trichloroacetaldehyde (Cl₃C−CHO) and trichloroacetic acid (Cl₃C−COOH) share the identical Cl₃C− substituent directly attached to their respective functional groups, making this a valid and instructive structural comparison, not an invalid one.

Both effects trace back to the exact SAME inductive electron-withdrawing mechanism from the three chlorine atoms; they are not caused by unrelated aspects of the substituent, but by the same underlying electronic effect applied in two related contexts.

This reverses one part of the correct parallel; chlorine substituents INCREASE (not decrease) acidity in the carboxylic acid case, via the same electron-withdrawing inductive mechanism that increases reactivity in the aldehyde case — both effects point in the analogous, reinforcing direction, not opposite directions.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Starting from propan-1-ol, a chemist wants to make EITHER propanal OR propanoic acid, depending on which reagent is chosen. Match each target product to the single BEST reagent choice.
options: The same single reagent gives either product equally well, depending only on reaction time
Excess hot acidified KMnO₄ for propanal; PCC (anhydrous) for propanoic acid, the reverse pairing
PCC (anhydrous) for propanal; excess hot acidified KMnO₄ for propanoic acid
Neither target product can be obtained from propan-1-ol by oxidation under any conditions
questions.explanation: PCC, a mild, controlled, anhydrous oxidant, reliably stops the oxidation of a primary alcohol at the aldehyde stage, giving propanal. Excess hot acidified KMnO₄, a strong, vigorous oxidant, drives the oxidation all the way through to the carboxylic acid, giving propanoic acid — matching each named reagent to its characteristic stopping point.
questions.hint: Recall which of these two reagents is specifically valued for STOPPING at an intermediate oxidation stage, and which one is known for going 'all the way'.
distractor_logic: These two reagents differ fundamentally in oxidising strength and control, not merely in how long the reaction is run; simply extending PCC's reaction time does not typically push it past the aldehyde stage the way switching to a genuinely stronger oxidant does.
This swaps the two pairings; PCC (mild, controlled) gives the aldehyde, while strong excess KMnO₄ (vigorous, uncontrolled) gives the acid, not the reverse.

Both target products ARE readily obtainable from propan-1-ol by oxidation; PCC gives propanal and excess hot acidified KMnO₄ gives propanoic acid, matching each reagent to its characteristic stopping point.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: A synthesis converts bromoethane into propanoyl chloride via a two-step sequence: (1) Mg/dry ether, then CO₂, then dilute acid workup; (2) SOCl₂. Identify the intermediate isolated after step 1, and the final product after step 2.
options: Step 1 gives propanoic acid (CH₃CH₂COOH); step 2 converts it to propanoyl chloride (CH₃CH₂COCl)
Step 1 gives acetic acid; step 2 converts it to acetyl chloride, not propanoyl chloride
This sequence cannot give an acid chloride at all, since SOCl₂ only reacts with alcohols
Step 1 gives propan-1-ol; step 2 converts it directly to propanoyl chloride without any intervening acid
questions.explanation: Step 1 (Grignard formation, then reaction with CO₂, then acidic workup) adds one new carbon onto the ethyl group and gives propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH. Step 2 (SOCl₂) converts this carboxylic acid's −OH into −Cl, giving propanoyl chloride, CH₃CH₂COCl, the desired final product.
questions.hint: Work through each step's transformation in sequence, tracking exactly which functional group is present after each stage.
distractor_logic: The starting material, bromoethane, is a 2-carbon alkyl halide; reacting its Grignard with CO₂ adds one new carbon, giving a 3-carbon product (propanoic acid), not the 2-carbon acetic acid.

SOCl₂ reacts readily and specifically with carboxylic acids (converting −COOH to −COCl), which is exactly the transformation used in step 2 of this sequence; it is not restricted to reacting only with alcohols.
Grignard reaction with CO₂, followed by acidic workup, gives a carboxylic ACID directly (not an alcohol); no separate reduction step is involved in this specific sequence.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: A chemist wants to convert butanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CH₂CN, into EITHER butanal (using DIBAL-H at low temperature) OR butanoic acid (using aqueous acid hydrolysis), depending on the chosen conditions. Explain why the SAME starting material can give two different oxidation-level products depending on reagent choice.
options: Nitriles cannot be converted into either an aldehyde or a carboxylic acid by any known method
DIBAL-H always gives the carboxylic acid, while aqueous acid hydrolysis always gives the aldehyde, the reverse of the correct pairing
Both reagents perform an identical hydrolysis reaction, and any difference in observed products must be due to experimental error

DIBAL-H at low temperature delivers just ONE hydride, forming a stable intermediate that hydrolyses to the aldehyde (partial reduction, stopping at an intermediate oxidation level); aqueous acid hydrolysis instead directly converts the nitrile's C≡N group into a carboxyl group WITHOUT any reduction, via a completely different (hydrolytic, not reductive) mechanism, reaching the fully oxidised acid
questions.explanation: DIBAL-H (a REDUCING agent) at low temperature delivers a single controlled hydride to the nitrile carbon, forming a stable metal-imine intermediate that survives until hydrolysis releases the aldehyde — a partial REDUCTION. Aqueous acid hydrolysis, by contrast, is not a reduction at all; it adds water across the nitrile (via an amide intermediate) to directly install the fully oxidised carboxyl group, reaching the carboxylic acid oxidation level through a completely different (hydrolytic) mechanism — explaining why the same nitrile starting material can lead to two structurally different final oxidation-level products depending on which of these two mechanistically distinct methods is chosen.
questions.hint: Distinguish carefully between a REDUCTIVE mechanism (DIBAL-H, adding hydride) and a HYDROLYTIC mechanism (aqueous acid, adding water); these are fundamentally different types of reaction, not variations of the same one.
distractor_logic: Both transformations (nitrile to aldehyde via DIBAL-H, and nitrile to carboxylic acid via hydrolysis) are genuine, well-established, standard synthetic methods; nitriles CAN be converted into either product using the appropriately chosen method.

This reverses the correct pairing; DIBAL-H (a partial reduction) gives the aldehyde, while aqueous acid hydrolysis (a full hydrolysis, no reduction) gives the carboxylic acid, not the other way around.

DIBAL-H reduction and aqueous acid hydrolysis are mechanistically distinct processes (one reductive, delivering hydride; the other hydrolytic, adding water) that genuinely give different products; this is not an experimental error, but the deliberate, expected outcome of choosing different reagents.

questions.question: Vigorous oxidation of p-xylene (1,4-dimethylbenzene, with a methyl group on each para position) with excess hot alkaline KMnO₄ gives which product, and how does its expected acidity compare to plain benzoic acid?
options: The reaction leaves BOTH methyl groups completely untouched, since a para-disubstituted ring cannot undergo this oxidation at all
p-Toluic acid (4-methylbenzoic acid), since only one of the two methyl groups is oxidised, regardless of how much oxidant is used
p-Xylene cannot be oxidised by KMnO₄ under any conditions, since it has no benzylic hydrogens available

Terephthalic acid (benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid); it is expected to be MORE acidic than benzoic acid, since the second electron-withdrawing −COOH group (once one is deprotonated) further stabilises/is stabilised similarly to other electron-withdrawing ring substituents
questions.explanation: Hot alkaline KMnO₄, used in EXCESS, oxidises BOTH benzylic methyl groups of p-xylene (each having available benzylic hydrogens) down to −COOH groups, giving terephthalic acid, benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid; the presence of a second electron-withdrawing carboxyl-type group on the ring (once the first is deprotonated to carboxylate) contributes an additional electron-withdrawing influence, generally making such a diacid somewhat more acidic (for its first ionisation) than the mono-acid, benzoic acid.
questions.hint: With EXCESS oxidant specified, consider whether BOTH methyl groups (not just one) would be oxidised, given that both have available benzylic hydrogens.
distractor_logic: p-Xylene's methyl groups both have readily available benzylic hydrogens, and hot alkaline KMnO₄ is a strong, general oxidant for exactly this type of benzylic C−H bond; the premise that oxidation cannot occur at all here is incorrect.

With excess (not limited) oxidant specified, there is no reason for the reaction to stop after oxidising only ONE of the two equivalent, equally available benzylic methyl groups; both are oxidised under these vigorous, excess conditions.

p-Xylene's methyl groups DO have benzylic hydrogens (each methyl carbon is directly attached to the aromatic ring and bears three ordinary C−H bonds, which are activated toward this specific oxidation by their benzylic position); the premise that no benzylic hydrogens are present is incorrect.

questions.question: Explain why NaBH₄ is generally unsuitable for reducing a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol, while LiAlH₄ IS able to accomplish this reduction, connecting your answer to the resonance-based reduced electrophilicity of the carboxyl carbon.
options: The carboxyl carbon is actually MORE electrophilic than an ordinary aldehyde or ketone's carbonyl carbon, making this observation counterintuitive and unexplained
Carboxylic acids cannot be reduced to primary alcohols by any hydride reagent whatsoever, contradicting the premise given

The carboxyl carbon's electrophilicity is already reduced by resonance donation from the adjacent −OH oxygen (similar to how an ester's alkoxy oxygen reduces its own carbonyl's electrophilicity); NaBH₄'s comparatively mild hydride-donating power is generally insufficient to overcome this reduced electrophilicity efficiently, while LiAlH₄'s much stronger hydride-donating power can
NaBH₄ and LiAlH₄ have identical reducing power, so no such difference should exist in practice
questions.explanation: The carboxyl group's −OH oxygen lone pair donates into the carbonyl by resonance (partially neutralising the carbon's electron deficiency, much as in an ester), making the carboxyl carbon considerably less electrophilic than a simple aldehyde or ketone's; NaBH₄, being a comparatively mild hydride source, is generally not reactive enough to reduce this less-electrophilic carbon efficiently, whereas the considerably stronger LiAlH₄ can still deliver hydride effectively, ultimately reducing the acid all the way to the primary alcohol.
questions.hint: Recall the same resonance-based reduced-electrophilicity reasoning used to explain why NaBH₄ alone cannot reduce a carboxylic acid, but LiAlH₄ can.
distractor_logic: This reverses the correct electronic comparison; the carboxyl carbon is LESS electrophilic than a simple aldehyde/ketone's carbonyl carbon (due to resonance donation from the −OH oxygen), not more, which is exactly why it needs the stronger reagent, not a puzzling exception.

Carboxylic acids CAN be reduced to primary alcohols, specifically by strong hydride reagents like LiAlH₄, as explicitly stated in the question's own premise; this is a genuine, standard reaction, not a contradiction.

NaBH₄ and LiAlH₄ are meaningfully DIFFERENT in reducing strength (LiAlH₄ being considerably more powerful/reactive, reducing a broader range of functional groups); this difference is precisely why one succeeds where the other generally fails on a carboxylic acid.

questions.question: Both Fischer esterification (acid-catalysed, forming a C−O bond) and aldol condensation (base-catalysed, forming a C−C bond) are reversible, equilibrium-controlled reactions. Compare the strategy typically used to DRIVE each reaction toward its product side.
options: Esterification is driven forward by cooling the reaction mixture, while aldol condensation requires no forcing strategy at all
Both reactions are driven forward using exactly the same strategy: continuous removal of a hydrogen halide byproduct
Neither reaction is actually reversible in any meaningful sense, making the entire comparison moot

Esterification is commonly driven forward by removing water as it forms (or using excess alcohol), shifting the equilibrium toward ester; aldol condensation is commonly driven forward by heating to promote the essentially irreversible dehydration step, converting the reversible addition product into the more stable, conjugated alpha,beta-unsaturated condensation product
questions.explanation: Esterification's equilibrium is commonly shifted toward the ester product by removing the water byproduct (e.g. using a dehydrating agent, azeotropic distillation, or Dean−Stark apparatus) or by using a large excess of one reactant (typically the alcohol), per Le Chatelier's principle. Aldol condensation's initial addition step is itself reversible, but the SUBSEQUENT dehydration step (removing water to form the conjugated alpha,beta-unsaturated product) is typically promoted by heating and is effectively irreversible under the reaction conditions, pulling the overall process toward the stable condensation product.
questions.hint: In each reaction, identify what BYPRODUCT is formed, and consider how removing (or otherwise dealing with) that byproduct could shift an equilibrium toward the desired product.
distractor_logic: Esterification is typically driven forward by HEATING (often with continuous removal of water), not cooling; and aldol condensation's dehydration step specifically DOES require a forcing strategy (typically heat) to proceed to completion, contrary to the claim that no such strategy is needed.

No hydrogen halide byproduct is formed in EITHER reaction; esterification releases water (not HX), and aldol condensation's dehydration step also releases water, not a hydrogen halide, so this shared-byproduct claim is incorrect for both reactions.

Both reactions ARE genuinely reversible under appropriate conditions (esterification is a classic, textbook equilibrium reaction; the initial aldol addition step is also reversible), which is exactly why specific forcing strategies (as correctly described) are needed to drive them toward their respective products.

questions.question: Rank p-nitrobenzaldehyde, benzaldehyde, and p-methoxybenzaldehyde in DECREASING order of rate of oxime formation with hydroxylamine.
options: p-Methoxybenzaldehyde > benzaldehyde > p-nitrobenzaldehyde
p-Nitrobenzaldehyde > benzaldehyde > p-methoxybenzaldehyde
p-Methoxybenzaldehyde > p-nitrobenzaldehyde > benzaldehyde
All three react at exactly the same rate, since the ring substituent is too far from the carbonyl to matter
questions.explanation: The strongly electron-withdrawing −NO₂ group (inductive and resonance withdrawal, reaching the carbonyl carbon through the conjugated ring even from the para position) further increases the carbonyl carbon's electrophilicity beyond plain benzaldehyde, speeding up nucleophilic addition. The electron-donating −OCH₃ group instead donates electron density into the ring/carbonyl system by resonance, REDUCING electrophilicity and slowing the reaction relative to plain benzaldehyde.
questions.hint: Apply the same electron-withdrawing-increases-electrophilicity / electron-donating-decreases-electrophilicity reasoning used for carbonyl reactivity generally, now to a ring substituent reaching the carbonyl by conjugation.
distractor_logic: This is the exact reverse order; the electron-donating methoxy group slows the reaction (least reactive), while the electron-withdrawing nitro group speeds it up (most reactive), not the other way around.

This correctly identifies methoxy as slowing the reaction relative to benzaldehyde but incorrectly ranks it as the fastest overall; the electron-donating group should give the SLOWEST rate of the three, not the fastest.
A para ring substituent conjugated with the carbonyl DOES meaningfully affect its electrophilicity via the ring's pi system, even though it is geometrically distant; this is not too remote to matter.

questions.question: Trichloroacetaldehyde forms a stable, isolable crystalline HYDRATE (chloral hydrate, Cl₃C−CH(OH)₂), whereas plain acetaldehyde's hydrate exists only fleetingly and cannot be isolated. Explain this difference using the same electronic reasoning already established for trichloroacetaldehyde's enhanced reactivity.
options: The three electronegative chlorines inductively withdraw electron density, stabilising the electron-rich, negatively-polarised sp³ diol carbon of the hydrate far more than in acetaldehyde's hydrate, shifting the hydration equilibrium strongly toward the stable hydrate rather than reverting to the carbonyl form
Chlorine atoms make the hydrate LESS stable, which should favour reversion to the carbonyl, contradicting the given observation
This stability difference has nothing to do with the electron-withdrawing chlorines and is purely coincidental
Chloral hydrate is not actually a hydrate at all; it is simply solid trichloroacetaldehyde with no water incorporated
questions.explanation: The same inductive electron withdrawal by the three chlorines that increases trichloroacetaldehyde's carbonyl electrophilicity also stabilises the electron-rich sp³ diol carbon once hydration has occurred (the withdrawal helps accommodate the extra electron density around that carbon in the tetrahedral hydrate), shifting the hydration equilibrium strongly toward the stable, isolable hydrate; acetaldehyde's hydrate, lacking this extra stabilisation, readily reverts back to the carbonyl form and cannot be isolated.
questions.hint: Apply the same inductive-withdrawal reasoning already used to explain trichloroacetaldehyde's enhanced ELECTROPHILICITY, this time to the STABILITY of the resulting tetrahedral addition product.
distractor_logic: This is backwards; the electron-withdrawing chlorines STABILISE (not destabilise) the electron-rich hydrate carbon, which is exactly why the hydrate is favoured and isolable rather than reverting to the carbonyl.
This effect is a well-documented, classic consequence of the same inductive electron withdrawal already discussed for this substituent pattern; it is not coincidental or unrelated.

Chloral hydrate is a genuine, well-characterised, isolable crystalline compound in which water HAS added across the original C=O bond, giving the gem-diol structure Cl₃C−CH(OH)₂; it is not simply unreacted trichloroacetaldehyde.

questions.question: Rank the following carbonyl-containing electrophiles in DECREASING order of general reactivity toward nucleophilic attack at the carbonyl carbon: acid chloride, aldehyde, ketone, ester.
options: Acid chloride > aldehyde > ketone > ester
All four are equally reactive, since all contain the identical C=O core functional group
Ester > ketone > aldehyde > acid chloride
Ketone > acid chloride > ester > aldehyde
questions.explanation: The acid chloride's strongly electron-withdrawing, poorly-donating chlorine makes its carbonyl carbon the most electrophilic and offers the best leaving group, making it most reactive. Aldehydes (one small H substituent) outrank ketones (two alkyl/aryl substituents) by the usual steric/electronic reasoning. Esters, whose alkoxy oxygen donates electron density into the carbonyl by resonance (reducing electrophilicity, similar to but even more pronounced than a simple ketone's alkyl donation), are the least reactive of the four toward simple nucleophilic attack.
questions.hint: Consider both how strongly each substituent donates electron density into the carbonyl by resonance/induction, and (for the acid chloride specifically) whether a good leaving group is available.
distractor_logic: All four share the C=O core, but their surrounding substituents (Cl, H+alkyl, two alkyl groups, or alkoxy O) profoundly affect the carbonyl carbon's electrophilicity in different, well-documented ways; they are not equally reactive.

This is essentially the reverse order; the acid chloride (strongest electron withdrawal, best leaving group) is the MOST reactive, not the least, while the ester (resonance-donating alkoxy oxygen) is the LEAST reactive, not the most.

This misplaces the ketone as more reactive than the acid chloride and aldehyde; ketones are considerably less reactive than acid chlorides and aldehydes due to their two electron-donating alkyl substituents and lack of a leaving group advantage.

questions.question: Rank p-nitroacetophenone, acetophenone, and p-methoxyacetophenone in DECREASING order of rate of reduction by NaBH₄.
options: All three are reduced at identical rates, since NaBH₄ reduction is insensitive to ring substituents
p-Nitroacetophenone > acetophenone > p-methoxyacetophenone
p-Methoxyacetophenone > p-nitroacetophenone > acetophenone
p-Methoxyacetophenone > acetophenone > p-nitroacetophenone
questions.explanation: As with other nucleophiles, hydride's attack on the carbonyl carbon is accelerated by electron-withdrawing ring substituents (−NO₂, which increases electrophilicity) and slowed by electron-donating ones (−OCH₃, which decreases electrophilicity via resonance donation into the conjugated carbonyl system), giving the order p-nitroacetophenone > acetophenone > p-methoxyacetophenone.
questions.hint: Hydride reduction is a nucleophilic addition like any other; the same ring-substituent reasoning used for oxime/hydrazone formation rates applies here too.
distractor_logic: NaBH₄ reduction, being a nucleophilic addition to the same electrophilic carbonyl carbon, IS sensitive to ring substituents that change that carbon's electrophilicity, exactly as with other nucleophiles.
This correctly identifies methoxy as the slowest but misranks nitro below acetophenone; the electron-withdrawing nitro group should give the fastest rate of the three, not the middle rate.
This is the reverse order; the electron-withdrawing nitro group should give the FASTEST rate (most electrophilic carbonyl), and the electron-donating methoxy group the SLOWEST, not the opposite.

questions.question: In a crossed aldol reaction between propanal (CH₃CH₂CHO, alpha-carbon bears 2 H's) and 2-methylpropanal ((CH₃)₂CHCHO, alpha-carbon bears only 1 H, more hindered), both have alpha-hydrogens. If propanal's enolate is deliberately used to attack 2-methylpropanal's carbonyl carbon (rather than the reverse), what is the steric rationale?
options: Steric hindrance never affects which of two carbonyl compounds preferentially forms the enolate versus acts as the electrophile

2-Methylpropanal, being more sterically hindered at its own alpha-carbon, is a poorer source of a clean, high-yielding enolate, and its carbonyl carbon (though somewhat more hindered than propanal's) can still be attacked by the less-hindered propanal enolate, favouring this particular directionality for the crossed reaction
Both compounds are structurally identical, so no such directional preference could exist
2-Methylpropanal is always the better enolate source regardless of its steric hindrance, since it has more total alpha-hydrogens available across the whole molecule
questions.explanation: 2-Methylpropanal's single alpha-hydrogen sits on a more crowded, branched carbon, making clean, selective enolate formation there less favourable/more complicated than at propanal's less hindered, doubly-hydrogenated alpha-carbon; using propanal's more readily and cleanly formed enolate to attack 2-methylpropanal's carbonyl (itself somewhat more electrophilically accessible from certain steric approaches, though this is a secondary consideration) is therefore a sensible practical strategy for achieving a more controlled crossed aldol outcome.
questions.hint: Compare how crowded each alpha-carbon is, and consider that a LESS hindered alpha-carbon is generally easier to deprotonate cleanly to form a well-defined enolate.
distractor_logic: Steric hindrance is in fact a significant, well-recognised factor influencing which carbonyl compound in a crossed reaction preferentially forms the enolate (nucleophile) versus serves as the electrophile; it is not irrelevant to this choice.

Propanal and 2-methylpropanal are constitutional isomers with genuinely different branching patterns at their respective alpha-carbons (one unbranched, one branched); they are not structurally identical.

2-Methylpropanal has only ONE alpha-hydrogen (on its single, branched alpha-carbon), not more alpha-hydrogens overall than propanal (which has two, on its less hindered alpha-carbon); this option overstates 2-methylpropanal's enolate-forming advantage.

questions.question: An electron-withdrawing group (like −NO₂ or −Cl) attached near a functional group can simultaneously (i) increase a carbonyl carbon's electrophilicity toward nucleophilic addition, and (ii) increase a carboxylic acid's acidity. Explain why the SAME type of substituent produces both effects.
options: The two effects are completely independent phenomena caused by different, unrelated substituent properties
This unification is a coincidence with no shared underlying chemical explanation

In both cases, the substituent inductively withdraws electron density from the framework; for a carbonyl, this leaves the carbon MORE electron-deficient (more attractive to an incoming nucleophile), and for a carboxylic acid, this same withdrawal instead stabilises the NEGATIVE CHARGE of the conjugate base once deprotonated (increasing acidity) — two different consequences of the identical underlying electron-withdrawing mechanism, acting on two different aspects of reactivity
Electron-withdrawing groups always DECREASE both carbonyl electrophilicity and acid acidity, contradicting the premise given
questions.explanation: Both consequences trace back to the SAME core electronic effect (inductive electron withdrawal by the substituent): for a neutral carbonyl compound, withdrawing electron density from the carbonyl carbon leaves it MORE electron-poor and therefore more attractive to an incoming nucleophile (increasing electrophilicity/reactivity); for a carboxylic acid's conjugate base (the carboxylate anion), the same withdrawal helps stabilise the newly-formed NEGATIVE charge, making deprotonation more favourable (increasing acidity). The underlying mechanism (inductive electron withdrawal) is identical; only the specific chemical consequence it produces differs depending on which species (a neutral electrophile, or an anionic conjugate base) is being affected.
questions.hint: In both cases, ask what the electron-withdrawing substituent does to the LOCAL electron density, and then consider how that change in electron density benefits a DIFFERENT chemical process in each case (attracting a nucleophile, versus stabilising a negative charge).
distractor_logic: Both effects arise from the exact SAME underlying inductive electron-withdrawal mechanism, applied in two related but distinct contexts (a neutral electrophile's reactivity, versus a conjugate base's stability); they are not independent, unrelated phenomena.

This is a genuine, well-established, shared electronic principle (not a coincidence); recognising this common thread is exactly what connects the reactivity-trend reasoning and the acidity reasoning covered throughout this chapter.

This reverses BOTH established trends; electron-withdrawing groups INCREASE (not decrease) both carbonyl electrophilicity and carboxylic acid acidity, as extensively demonstrated elsewhere in this chapter's reasoning (e.g. trichloroacetaldehyde's reactivity, chloroacetic acid's acidity).

questions.question: A molecule contains both an aldehyde group and an ester group elsewhere in its structure. Predict which functional group a Grignard reagent (added in a controlled, limiting amount at low temperature) would react with FIRST, and why.
options: Both groups react at exactly the same rate with the Grignard reagent, so no selectivity is possible
The ester, since esters are always more electrophilic than aldehydes toward Grignard reagents
Grignard reagents cannot react with aldehydes when an ester is also present in the same molecule

The aldehyde, since its carbonyl carbon is considerably more electrophilic than the ester's (the ester's alkoxy oxygen donates electron density into its carbonyl by resonance, reducing its electrophilicity, much as it reduces a carboxylic acid's carbonyl electrophilicity), making the aldehyde the kinetically preferred site of initial attack
questions.explanation: The ester's alkoxy oxygen donates a lone pair into its carbonyl group by resonance (similar to, though somewhat less extensive than, a carboxylic acid's −OH donation), reducing the ester carbonyl carbon's electrophilicity relative to a simple aldehyde's (which has no such resonance-donating substituent); under carefully controlled, limiting, low-temperature conditions, the more electrophilic aldehyde group is therefore expected to react with the Grignard reagent first.
questions.hint: Apply the same resonance-donation reasoning already used to explain why a carboxylic acid's carbonyl is less electrophilic than a simple aldehyde/ketone's, now comparing an ester to an aldehyde.
distractor_logic: The two functional groups have measurably different electrophilicity at their respective carbonyl carbons (due to the ester's resonance donation), so they are not expected to react at identical rates with the same nucleophile.

This reverses the correct electronic comparison; the ester's resonance-donating alkoxy oxygen makes it LESS electrophilic than the aldehyde, not more, so the aldehyde (not the ester) is the more reactive, kinetically preferred site.

The presence of an ester elsewhere in the molecule does not prevent a Grignard reagent from reacting with a separate, more reactive aldehyde group; selective reaction at the more electrophilic site under controlled conditions is a real, useful synthetic strategy.

questions.question: Two unknown compounds, X (an aldehyde) and Y (a methyl ketone), both give a positive iodoform test. Predict which one is expected to react FASTER with 2,4-DNP, and explain using the general reactivity trend, independent of the iodoform result.
options: Both react at identical rates, since the iodoform test result determines 2,4-DNP reactivity directly

X (the aldehyde), since aldehydes are generally more reactive than ketones toward nucleophilic addition−elimination reactions like 2,4-DNP condensation, regardless of whether both happen to also give a positive iodoform test
Y (the ketone), since a positive iodoform test always indicates greater overall carbonyl reactivity than an aldehyde would show
Neither compound can react with 2,4-DNP, since they have already reacted with the iodoform reagent
questions.explanation: The iodoform test result (which depends specifically on the presence of a CH₃CO− or CH₃CH(OH)− structural motif) is a SEPARATE property from the general aldehyde-vs-ketone nucleophilic addition−elimination reactivity trend (governed by steric bulk and electron donation at the carbonyl carbon); X, being an aldehyde, is still expected to react faster with 2,4-DNP than Y, a ketone, independent of both giving a positive iodoform result.
questions.hint: Recognise that the iodoform test's structural requirement and the general aldehyde/ketone nucleophilic addition trend are governed by different structural features and do not have to correlate.
distractor_logic: The iodoform test result and 2,4-DNP reactivity are governed by different structural features (a specific alpha-methyl/hydroxyl pattern versus general steric/electronic character at the carbonyl carbon); one does not directly determine the other.

A positive iodoform test reflects a SPECIFIC structural motif (CH₃CO− or CH₃CH(OH)−), not a general measure of overall carbonyl reactivity toward nucleophilic addition; it does not override the separate, well-established aldehyde-more-reactive-than-ketone trend for reactions like 2,4-DNP condensation.

Reacting with one reagent (the iodoform test reagent) does not consume or prevent a SEPARATE sample of the same compound from reacting with a different reagent (2,4-DNP) in a separate test; both compounds remain fully capable of undergoing the 2,4-DNP condensation.

questions.question: In aqueous solution, formaldehyde exists almost entirely (>99%) as its hydrate, gem-diol HO−CH₂−OH, while acetone exists almost entirely (>99%) as the UNHYDRATED ketone. Explain this large difference in hydration equilibrium position, connecting it to the general aldehyde-vs-ketone reactivity trend.
options: Hydration equilibrium position is entirely random and has no connection to carbonyl structure at all
Acetone is actually MORE electrophilic than formaldehyde, which is why it resists hydration less effectively, contradicting the trend

Formaldehyde's carbonyl carbon, bearing no alkyl/aryl substituents at all, is maximally electrophilic and sterically unhindered, strongly favouring addition of water (the hydration equilibrium lies far toward the hydrate); acetone's two methyl groups sterically hinder and electronically deactivate its carbonyl carbon, strongly favouring the unhydrated ketone form instead
Both compounds exist in identical hydration equilibria, and any observed difference must be a measurement artifact
questions.explanation: This hydration equilibrium is governed by exactly the same steric/electronic factors already established for nucleophilic addition reactivity generally: formaldehyde's completely unhindered, maximally electrophilic carbonyl carbon favours extensive hydration (nearly complete conversion to the gem-diol), while acetone's two electron-donating, sterically bulky methyl groups strongly disfavour hydration, leaving the ketone essentially unhydrated in aqueous solution — directly reflecting the established aldehyde-more-reactive-than-ketone (and, within aldehydes, formaldehyde-most-reactive) trend.
questions.hint: Treat water as simply another nucleophile attacking the carbonyl carbon, and apply the same steric/electronic reasoning already used throughout this chapter for other nucleophiles.
distractor_logic: Hydration equilibrium position is directly and predictably connected to carbonyl structure (steric bulk and electron donation of the flanking substituents), following the same general reactivity principles established throughout this chapter, not a random phenomenon.

This reverses the well-established electrophilicity comparison; formaldehyde (no substituents at all) is MORE electrophilic than acetone (two methyl groups), which is exactly why it hydrates so much more extensively.

The two compounds show a dramatically DIFFERENT hydration equilibrium position (formaldehyde overwhelmingly hydrated, acetone essentially not), a real, well-documented, reproducible chemical fact, not a measurement artifact.

questions.question: A ketone bearing an ADJACENT electron-withdrawing group (e.g. 1,1,1-trifluoroacetone, CF₃COCH₃) is reduced by NaBH₄ considerably faster than plain acetone. Which reasoning correctly explains this rate enhancement?
options: Fluorine's small atomic size makes it sterically identical to hydrogen, so no rate difference should be observed at all
NaBH₄ only reduces ketones that contain fluorine substituents; plain acetone should not be reduced at all

The strongly electron-withdrawing −CF₃ group inductively increases the carbonyl carbon's electrophilicity (the same effect already established for trichloroacetaldehyde relative to acetaldehyde), making it more attractive to the incoming hydride nucleophile
The −CF₃ group is electron-donating, which should slow, not speed up, the reduction, contradicting the stated observation
questions.explanation: The −CF₃ group, like −CCl₃ in trichloroacetaldehyde, is strongly electron-withdrawing by induction (fluorine being even more electronegative than chlorine); this pulls electron density away from the adjacent carbonyl carbon, increasing its electrophilicity and making it more reactive toward the incoming hydride nucleophile from NaBH₄, consistent with the same reasoning already established for other strongly electron-withdrawing substituents near a carbonyl group.
questions.hint: Apply the exact same inductive-withdrawal-increases-electrophilicity reasoning already used for trichloroacetaldehyde, now to a trifluoromethyl-substituted ketone.
distractor_logic: While fluorine is indeed a relatively small atom, its dominant effect here is ELECTRONIC (strong inductive withdrawal), not steric; treating it as sterically/electronically equivalent to hydrogen ignores this significant electronic difference.
NaBH₄ readily reduces plain acetone as well (just somewhat more slowly than the fluorinated analogue); it is not restricted to reducing only fluorine-containing ketones.
Fluorine, like chlorine, is highly electronegative and electron-WITHDRAWING by induction, not donating; this option describes the opposite of −CF₃'s actual electronic character.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: Self-aldol condensation proceeds much more readily and completely for acetaldehyde than for acetone, even though both have accessible alpha-hydrogens. Explain this difference in terms of the equilibrium position of the ADDITION step.
options: Both reactions proceed with an identical equilibrium position, and any observed difference in practical yield is purely due to differences in reaction time used

Acetaldehyde's less hindered, more electrophilic carbonyl carbon favours a much more complete addition step (equilibrium lying well toward the beta-hydroxy addition product); acetone's bulkier, less electrophilic carbonyl carbon gives a much less favourable addition equilibrium (lying more toward the starting ketone), so acetone's self-aldol condensation often requires more forcing conditions or continuous product removal to proceed usefully
Acetone's carbonyl carbon is inherently more reactive than acetaldehyde's toward its own enolate, giving it the more favourable equilibrium, contradicting the stated observation
Alpha-hydrogen availability is the only relevant factor, and since both compounds have alpha-hydrogens, their aldol addition equilibria must be identical
questions.explanation: The addition step of aldol condensation is itself an ordinary nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl (here, the electrophile is a second molecule of the same starting material); acetaldehyde's more electrophilic, less hindered carbonyl carbon gives a considerably more favourable (more complete) addition equilibrium than acetone's bulkier, more electron-rich carbonyl carbon, which is why acetone's self-aldol condensation is comparatively less efficient and often needs special conditions (e.g. continuous extraction of product) to give useful yields.
questions.hint: Recognise that within the aldol mechanism, the SECOND carbonyl molecule (the electrophile being attacked by the enolate) is subject to the same aldehyde-vs-ketone electrophilicity trend used elsewhere.
distractor_logic: The two reactions do NOT have identical equilibrium positions; the underlying reactivity difference between an aldehyde and a ketone carbonyl carbon (as the electrophile being attacked) genuinely shifts the addition equilibrium differently for each, independent of how long the reaction is run.

This reverses the correct electrophilicity comparison; acetaldehyde's carbonyl carbon (as the electrophile in the addition step) is MORE reactive than acetone's, not less, which is exactly why its self-aldol addition equilibrium is more favourable.

While alpha-hydrogen availability is necessary for BOTH compounds to form an enolate at all, it does not by itself determine the FAVOURABILITY of the subsequent addition equilibrium, which depends separately on the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon being attacked.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: Mesityl oxide, 4-methylpent-3-en-2-one (CH₃)₂C=CH−CO−CH₃, the self-aldol condensation product of acetone, is subjected to the iodoform test (I₂/NaOH). Predict the result.
options: Positive, but only because the C=C double bond itself, not the methyl group, is what reacts with the iodoform reagent
Negative, since the conjugated C=C double bond destroys the required CH₃CO− structural motif entirely

Positive, since mesityl oxide retains a methyl group directly bonded to the carbonyl carbon (a CH₃CO− unit), exactly the structural requirement for the iodoform test, unaffected by the presence of the adjacent C=C double bond
Negative, since aldol condensation products never give a positive iodoform test
questions.explanation: Mesityl oxide's structure, (CH₃)₂C=CH−CO−CH₃, still has an intact CH₃CO− group (the terminal methyl directly bonded to the carbonyl carbon), which is exactly the structural feature the iodoform test requires; the conjugated C=C double bond elsewhere in the molecule does not interfere with or remove this specific alpha-methyl-ketone motif, so the test remains positive.
questions.hint: Carefully re-examine the full structure of the aldol condensation product and check specifically whether the CH₃CO− motif required for the iodoform test is still present, unaffected by the new C=C bond.
distractor_logic: The iodoform test's positive result specifically arises from the CH₃CO− group (methyl ketone), not from the C=C double bond, which plays no role in the haloform mechanism.

The C=C double bond is a separate structural feature from the CH₃CO− group; its presence does not chemically remove or interfere with the methyl-ketone motif still present elsewhere in the same molecule.

This is not a universal rule; whether an aldol condensation product gives a positive iodoform test depends entirely on whether it happens to retain the required CH₃CO− structural motif, which mesityl oxide specifically does.
