questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: The alpha-hydrogen of pentane-2,4-dione (a 1,3-diketone, with the alpha-carbon flanked by TWO carbonyl groups) is far more acidic (pK₂ ≈ 9) than the alpha-hydrogen of a simple monoketone like acetone (pK₂ ≈ 20), yet still LESS acidic than a simple carboxylic acid (pK₂ ≈ 4.76). Rank all three in DECREASING order of acidity and explain.
options: Carboxylic acid > 1,3-diketone > simple ketone; the carboxylate's two-equivalent-oxygen resonance is the strongest stabilisation, the 1,3-diketone's enolate is doubly stabilised by resonance delocalisation into BOTH flanking carbonyls (stronger than a simple ketone's single-carbonyl-stabilised enolate, but still weaker than the carboxylate's all-oxygen delocalisation), and the simple ketone's singly-stabilised enolate is the least acidic of the three
All three are equally acidic, since all contain at least one C=O group
1,3-Diketone > carboxylic acid > simple ketone, since having two carbonyls always outweighs having an O−H group
Simple ketone > 1,3-diketone > carboxylic acid, the complete reverse of the correct order
questions.explanation: The carboxylate ion's resonance delocalises charge over two chemically equivalent, highly electronegative oxygens (strongest stabilisation, most acidic parent compound). The 1,3-diketone's enolate anion (from removing the flanked alpha-hydrogen) is stabilised by delocalisation into BOTH adjacent carbonyl groups (two resonance pathways instead of one), making it considerably more stable — and the 1,3-diketone's alpha-C−H more acidic — than a simple ketone's enolate (only one adjacent carbonyl to delocalise into), but this double-carbonyl stabilisation is still not as strong as the carboxylate's fully oxygen-based delocalisation, giving the order carboxylic acid > 1,3-diketone > simple ketone.
questions.hint: Count how many resonance/delocalisation pathways are available to stabilise the negative charge in each case, and consider the electronegativity of the atoms bearing that charge in each resonance structure.
distractor_logic: The three compounds differ substantially and measurably in acidity (spanning roughly 15 pK₂ units from simple ketone to carboxylic acid), governed by how effectively each conjugate base delocalises its negative charge; they are not equally acidic despite all containing at least one C=O group.

Having two carbonyls (as in the 1,3-diketone) provides meaningful but not unlimited stabilisation; it does not outweigh the carboxylate's even more effective, symmetric, all-oxygen resonance delocalisation, so the carboxylic acid remains the most acidic of the three, not the diketone.

This is the reverse order; the simple ketone (only one resonance pathway for its enolate) is the LEAST acidic of the three, not the most, while the carboxylic acid (strongest, most symmetric stabilisation) is the most acidic.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: An aldol condensation product is identified as (E)-4-phenylbut-3-en-2-one (benzalacetone), C₆H₅−CH=CH−CO−CH₃. Deduce the two carbonyl starting materials that combined in the crossed aldol condensation that produced it.
options: Two molecules of acetophenone (C₆H₅COCH₃)
Cinnamaldehyde (C₆H₅CH=CHCHO) and formaldehyde (HCHO)
Benzaldehyde (C₆H₅CHO, the electrophile, since it has no alpha-hydrogen) and acetone (CH₃COCH₃, the enolate/nucleophile source, since it has accessible alpha-hydrogens)
Benzoic acid and acetone
questions.explanation: Splitting the product at the new C−C bond (between the ring-attached =CH− carbon and the −CO−CH₃ fragment) reveals a benzaldehyde-derived carbon (C₆H₅−CH=, which came from benzaldehyde's carbonyl carbon, now part of the new double bond after dehydration) and an acetone-derived fragment (=CH−CO−CH₃, whose alpha-carbon was acetone's own enolate carbon); since benzaldehyde has no alpha-hydrogen, it must have played the electrophile role, with acetone supplying the nucleophilic enolate.
questions.hint: Locate the new C=C bond (formed by dehydration after the aldol addition step) and work out which starting carbonyl compound each side of that double bond originally came from.
distractor_logic: Two molecules of acetophenone would give a symmetric product different from this one; acetophenone's own alpha-hydrogens are on its methyl group, not positioned to directly give this specific asymmetric, phenyl-vinyl-ketone structure from simple self-condensation.
Cinnamaldehyde and formaldehyde would combine via a different aldol pathway and carbon connectivity, not matching this product's specific benzaldehyde-plus-acetone-derived structure.

Benzoic acid is a carboxylic acid, not a carbonyl compound capable of forming an enolate or acting as a simple aldol electrophile in this type of base-catalysed C−C bond-forming reaction; it is not one of the two starting materials here.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: Acetaldehyde is treated simultaneously with BOTH dilute NaOH (which would promote self-aldol condensation) and one equivalent of semicarbazide (which would form a semicarbazone). Under normal, mild conditions, which product is typically favoured, and why?
options: The semicarbazone, since condensation with a good nitrogen nucleophile like semicarbazide is generally fast and essentially irreversible, competing favourably against the comparatively slower, reversible aldol addition step under these mild conditions
Both reactions are mutually exclusive; the presence of NaOH completely prevents semicarbazide from reacting at all
The aldol condensation product, since aldol condensation is always faster than any addition−elimination reaction with a nitrogen nucleophile
Neither product forms; acetaldehyde is unreactive toward either reagent under these mild conditions
questions.explanation: Semicarbazide (like other amine-type nucleophiles used to form solid carbonyl derivatives) reacts efficiently and essentially irreversibly with the carbonyl group under mild conditions; the base-catalysed self-aldol pathway, while certainly possible, generally proceeds more slowly and is more readily outcompeted when a good, efficient nitrogen nucleophile like semicarbazide is also present in comparable or excess amount, which is part of why semicarbazide (and similar reagents) are reliably used to trap and identify carbonyl compounds even in the presence of mild base.
questions.hint: Consider the relative efficiency and (practically) irreversibility of forming a solid nitrogen-based derivative compared to the slower, reversible early steps of aldol condensation under similarly mild conditions.
distractor_logic: NaOH being present does not chemically prevent semicarbazide (a good nucleophile) from also reacting with the carbonyl group; the two reagents can, in principle, compete for reaction with the same carbonyl compound, and semicarbazide's efficient reaction is not simply blocked.

There is no absolute universal rule that aldol condensation is always faster; under conditions favourable to forming a stable nitrogen-based derivative (as with semicarbazide), that reaction pathway is often the practically dominant one instead.

Acetaldehyde is in fact quite reactive toward both types of reagent (base-catalysed self-aldol condensation, and nitrogen-nucleophile condensation with semicarbazide); the premise that it is unreactive toward either is incorrect.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: Compare formaldehyde and benzaldehyde, both lacking alpha-hydrogens: which one is expected to undergo the Cannizzaro reaction FASTER with concentrated NaOH, and why?
options: Both react at exactly the same rate, since Cannizzaro reaction rate is entirely independent of the specific aldehyde's structure
Neither aldehyde can undergo Cannizzaro reaction at a measurable rate under any concentration of base

Formaldehyde, since its completely unhindered, maximally electrophilic carbonyl carbon (no substituents at all) is attacked more readily by the hydride-transfer step of the disproportionation mechanism than benzaldehyde's bulkier, resonance-stabilised (less electrophilic) aromatic carbonyl carbon
Benzaldehyde, since aromatic aldehydes are always more reactive than aliphatic ones in every reaction, without exception
questions.explanation: The Cannizzaro mechanism involves a hydride-transfer step between two aldehyde-derived species, and this step is subject to the same general carbonyl-electrophilicity reasoning used throughout this topic: formaldehyde's small, fully unhindered, maximally electrophilic carbonyl carbon reacts considerably faster in this hydride-transfer step than benzaldehyde's bulkier, ring-conjugated (less electrophilic) aromatic carbonyl carbon, making formaldehyde's Cannizzaro reaction generally faster.
questions.hint: Apply the same general carbonyl electrophilicity reasoning (formaldehyde most electrophilic of common aldehydes, aromatic aldehydes less electrophilic than aliphatic ones) to the hydride-transfer step of this specific reaction.
distractor_logic: The two aldehydes have measurably different carbonyl electrophilicity (formaldehyde being considerably more electrophilic due to having no flanking substituents at all), so their Cannizzaro reaction rates are not expected to be identical.

Both formaldehyde and benzaldehyde are classic, well-established, textbook substrates for the Cannizzaro reaction; both DO react at a measurable, useful rate with concentrated base, just at somewhat different relative rates.

This is a broad overgeneralisation; aromatic aldehydes are in fact generally LESS reactive than comparable aliphatic aldehydes toward nucleophilic-addition-type steps (including the hydride-transfer step of Cannizzaro reaction), due to ring resonance donation reducing electrophilicity, not more reactive in every case.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: But-2-enal (crotonaldehyde), the aldol condensation product of acetaldehyde, has a considerably HIGHER boiling point (104°C) than propanal (48°C), a simple saturated aldehyde with a similar (though not identical) carbon count. Beyond simple molecular size, what STRUCTURAL feature of but-2-enal contributes to this elevated boiling point?
options: This boiling point difference is entirely and solely due to but-2-enal simply having one extra carbon compared to propanal, with no other contributing structural feature
The presence of a C=C double bond always decreases boiling point relative to a saturated aldehyde of similar carbon count, with no exceptions
But-2-enal and propanal are actually structural isomers with identical connectivity, so no meaningful comparison is possible

The conjugation between the C=C and C=O groups extends but-2-enal's polarisable pi system, increasing its overall polarity and strengthening intermolecular dipole−dipole/dispersion attractions relative to a simple, non-conjugated aldehyde of comparable size
questions.explanation: Beyond the modest difference in carbon count, the CONJUGATION between but-2-enal's C=C and C=O groups extends and enhances the molecule's overall pi-electron polarisability and dipole character, providing additional intermolecular attraction (on top of ordinary dispersion/dipole−dipole forces) that a simple, unconjugated aldehyde like propanal lacks, contributing meaningfully to the elevated boiling point beyond what carbon count alone would predict.
questions.hint: Beyond simply counting carbons, consider what having TWO conjugated pi systems (rather than one isolated C=O) does to a molecule's overall polarity/polarisability.
distractor_logic: While the extra carbon does contribute somewhat to the elevated boiling point via increased dispersion forces, the CONJUGATION effect is an additional, structurally meaningful contributing factor beyond simple carbon-count-driven dispersion forces alone.

Whether a C=C bond raises or lowers boiling point relative to a comparable saturated compound depends on the specific structural context; when conjugated with another polar group (as here), it can meaningfully raise, not simply lower, boiling point via enhanced polarisability.
But-2-enal (C₄H₆O) and propanal (C₃H₆O) have different molecular formulas and different carbon counts (4 vs. 3); they are not structural isomers of each other.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: But-2-enal (the aldol condensation product of acetaldehyde) is subsequently oxidised (e.g. by Tollens' reagent, which selectively oxidises only the aldehyde C−H without touching the isolated C=C) to give but-2-enoic acid, CH₃CH=CHCOOH. Predict how this acid's acidity compares to plain butanoic acid (fully saturated), and explain.
options: But-2-enoic acid is less acidic than butanoic acid, since C=C double bonds are always electron-donating relative to a saturated chain
The two acids are exactly equally acidic, since the double bond is too far from the carboxyl group to matter at all

But-2-enoic acid is somewhat MORE acidic than butanoic acid, since the sp²-hybridised, more electronegative-behaving vinyl carbons of the C=C system provide additional inductive electron withdrawal toward the carboxyl group compared to the purely sp³ alkyl chain of butanoic acid
But-2-enoic acid cannot be formed from but-2-enal by oxidation, since Tollens' reagent always also reduces any C=C double bond present
questions.explanation: sp²-hybridised carbons (as in a C=C double bond) hold their bonding electrons somewhat closer to the nucleus (greater effective electronegativity) than sp³ carbons do, giving the vinyl portion of but-2-enoic acid's chain a modest additional inductive electron-withdrawing character (beyond a purely saturated chain like butanoic acid's), which slightly stabilises the resulting carboxylate anion and modestly increases acidity relative to the fully saturated parent acid.
questions.hint: Recall the hybridisation-and-electronegativity reasoning used elsewhere (comparing sp, sp², sp³ carbons) and apply it here to the inductive effect of a nearby C=C double bond on the acidity of a carboxyl group.
distractor_logic: A C=C double bond is not simply, generically electron-donating in this inductive sense; the greater s-character/effective electronegativity of its sp² carbons actually provides a modest electron-WITHDRAWING inductive contribution relative to a fully sp³ (saturated) chain.

The double bond, while somewhat further from the carboxyl group than an alpha-substituent would be, is still close enough (particularly given the through-bond inductive pathway) to have a small but genuine effect on acidity; it is not entirely negligible.

Tollens' reagent is specifically a MILD, SELECTIVE oxidant for the aldehyde's own C−H bond; it does not generally reduce or otherwise attack an isolated C=C double bond elsewhere in the molecule, so but-2-enoic acid can indeed form cleanly from but-2-enal via this selective oxidation.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: A synthesis plan uses aldol condensation of acetaldehyde (giving but-2-enal), followed by oxidation with hot acidified KMnO₄ (which oxidises BOTH the aldehyde AND cleaves/oxidises the C=C double bond under these vigorous conditions), to attempt to make but-2-enoic acid. Explain why this specific oxidant choice is likely to give a disappointing, impure result compared to using Tollens' reagent instead.
options: Tollens' reagent would actually destroy the C=C double bond just as readily as hot acidified KMnO₄ does, making the comparison meaningless
Both oxidants give an identical, equally pure but-2-enoic acid product, so the choice between them is inconsequential
Hot acidified KMnO₄ cannot oxidise aldehydes at all, making this proposed route entirely non-functional from the start

Hot acidified KMnO₄ is a vigorous, non-selective oxidant that would likely also cleave or dihydroxylate the C=C double bond (destroying the desired unsaturated product), unlike the mild, aldehyde-selective Tollens' reagent, which leaves the isolated C=C untouched
questions.explanation: Hot, acidified KMnO₄ is a strong, vigorous, relatively non-selective oxidant known to attack C=C double bonds directly (via dihydroxylation or oxidative cleavage) in addition to oxidising the aldehyde; using it on but-2-enal risks destroying or fragmenting the desired alpha,beta-unsaturated product, whereas Tollens' reagent's mild, aldehyde-C−H-specific mechanism selectively oxidises just the aldehyde group, leaving the C=C double bond intact and giving the desired but-2-enoic acid cleanly.
questions.hint: Compare the SELECTIVITY (not just the oxidising strength) of each named reagent toward the two different reactive sites present in but-2-enal (the aldehyde C−H, and the isolated C=C double bond).
distractor_logic: Tollens' reagent is specifically valued and used precisely because it does NOT attack an isolated C=C double bond under these conditions, unlike the vigorous KMnO₄; the comparison between the two reagents' selectivity is exactly the point of this question, not meaningless.

The two oxidants have very different selectivity profiles (KMnO₄ vigorous and non-selective toward C=C; Tollens' mild and specific to the aldehyde C−H), so they are expected to give meaningfully different, not identical, outcomes on this specific substrate.

Hot acidified KMnO₄ readily oxidises aldehydes (this part of the proposed route would work); the problem is specifically its lack of selectivity toward the ADDITIONAL C=C double bond present, which it is also likely to attack.

questions.topic: Aldol Condensation, Cannizzaro Reaction and Other Base-Catalysed Reactions
questions.question: In the aldol ADDITION step (before any dehydration), the enolate's nucleophilic alpha-carbon attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of a second molecule. If that second molecule is a KETONE rather than an aldehyde, how does this affect the rate/completeness of the addition step, and why?
options: The addition step is always faster when the electrophile is a ketone rather than an aldehyde, the reverse of the correct reasoning

The addition step is comparatively slower/less complete than if the second molecule were an aldehyde, since a ketone's carbonyl carbon (flanked by two alkyl/aryl groups) is both more sterically hindered and less electrophilic than an aldehyde's, making it a less favourable electrophilic target for the incoming enolate
The identity of the electrophilic partner (aldehyde vs. ketone) has absolutely no effect on the rate of the addition step
Ketones cannot ever serve as the electrophile in any aldol-type addition reaction, making this scenario impossible
questions.explanation: Regardless of which specific pair of carbonyl compounds is involved, the enolate's attack on the SECOND (electrophilic) carbonyl carbon is governed by the same general steric/electronic reactivity trend established throughout this chapter: a ketone's electrophile (two alkyl/aryl groups flanking the carbonyl) is more hindered and less electrophilic than an aldehyde's electrophile (one small substituent), making addition to a ketone electrophile comparatively slower and less complete than addition to an aldehyde electrophile, all else being equal.
questions.hint: Treat the SECOND carbonyl molecule (the one being attacked, i.e. the electrophile) exactly like any other electrophile subject to the standard aldehyde-vs-ketone reactivity comparison.
distractor_logic: This reverses the well-established trend; ketone electrophiles are LESS reactive (not more) than aldehyde electrophiles toward nucleophilic attack, including attack by an enolate in the aldol addition step.

The identity of the electrophilic carbonyl partner DOES significantly affect the addition step's rate and completeness, following exactly the same general aldehyde-vs-ketone reactivity principles established elsewhere in this chapter; it is not an irrelevant factor.

Ketones absolutely CAN and do serve as the electrophile in aldol-type addition reactions (e.g. in crossed aldol reactions involving a ketone and a more readily enolisable partner, or in self-aldol condensation of a ketone like acetone with itself); this scenario is a normal, well-precedented part of aldol chemistry, not an impossibility.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Rank {p-nitrobenzaldehyde, benzaldehyde, p-methoxybenzaldehyde} in DECREASING order of rate of oxidation by Tollens' reagent, applying the same reasoning already established for their relative electrophilicity toward nucleophilic addition.
options: Benzaldehyde > p-nitrobenzaldehyde > p-methoxybenzaldehyde
All three are oxidised at exactly the same rate by Tollens' reagent
p-Methoxybenzaldehyde > benzaldehyde > p-nitrobenzaldehyde
p-Nitrobenzaldehyde > benzaldehyde > p-methoxybenzaldehyde
questions.explanation: Tollens' oxidation proceeds via attack at the same electrophilic carbonyl carbon whose reactivity is governed by ring substituents exactly as established for other nucleophilic-addition-type reactions: the electron-withdrawing −NO₂ group increases electrophilicity (fastest oxidation), while the electron-donating −OCH₃ group decreases it (slowest oxidation), with plain benzaldehyde intermediate.
questions.hint: Apply the identical ring-substituent reasoning already used for oxime/hydrazone formation rate and NaBH₄ reduction rate, now to Tollens' oxidation.
distractor_logic: This correctly places methoxy as slower than benzaldehyde alone, but incorrectly ranks benzaldehyde above the more electrophilic nitro-substituted aldehyde, which should react fastest of the three.
The three aldehydes have measurably different electrophilicity at their carbonyl carbons due to their different ring substituents; they are not oxidised at identical rates.
This is the exact reverse order; the electron-withdrawing nitro group should give the fastest oxidation (most electrophilic carbonyl carbon), and methoxy the slowest, not vice versa.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Both acid chlorides and aldehydes can be reduced by hydride reagents, but acid chlorides require only a MILDER, specifically poisoned catalyst (Rosenmund conditions) to stop cleanly at the aldehyde stage, while aldehydes themselves need only a comparatively mild hydride (NaBH₄) to reach the alcohol. Relate this 'staged' reducibility to the relative electrophilicity of each species' carbonyl carbon.
options: Both species require identically strong reagents, and no meaningful reactivity staging exists between them
Rosenmund reduction and NaBH₄ reduction are the same reaction performed under two different names
Acid chlorides are actually LESS electrophilic than aldehydes, making the described 'staged' reactivity pattern impossible

Acid chlorides (very electrophilic, due to Cl's strong electron withdrawal and good leaving-group ability) react readily even with a deliberately weakened (poisoned) catalyst, stopping at the aldehyde; the resulting aldehyde (still meaningfully electrophilic, though less so than the acid chloride) is then reduced further by the comparatively milder NaBH₄, illustrating a general trend of decreasing electrophilicity (and correspondingly milder reagent requirement) as the oxidation level decreases from acid chloride to aldehyde
questions.explanation: This reflects a general, consistent trend across this chapter: more electrophilic carbonyl species (like acid chlorides, strongly activated by chlorine's electron withdrawal and good leaving-group character) react even with comparatively 'weaker' or specifically modified reagents (Rosenmund's poisoned catalyst), while a somewhat less electrophilic species (a simple aldehyde) still reacts readily with a correspondingly milder standard hydride reagent (NaBH₄) — the required reagent 'strength' tracks inversely with the substrate's own electrophilicity.
questions.hint: Think of this as a consistent pattern: the more inherently reactive/electrophilic the starting carbonyl species, the less forcing a reagent is needed to convert it, and vice versa.
distractor_logic: The two species do show a genuine reactivity difference (acid chloride more electrophilic than aldehyde), which is precisely why different reagent 'strengths' (a poisoned catalyst vs. a standard mild hydride) are appropriately matched to each step.

Rosenmund reduction (H₂/Pd−BaSO₄, specifically poisoned, converting an acid chloride to an aldehyde) and NaBH₄ reduction (a hydride reagent, converting an aldehyde to an alcohol) are mechanistically and practically distinct reactions, applied to different substrates at different oxidation levels, not the same reaction under two names.

This reverses the well-established electrophilicity comparison; acid chlorides are considerably MORE electrophilic than simple aldehydes (due to chlorine's strong electron withdrawal and its role as a good leaving group), not less, which is exactly why even a poisoned catalyst suffices for the first, more reactive step.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: An unknown aldehyde X gives NO reaction with dilute NaOH (no aldol condensation observed) but DOES react with concentrated NaOH to give an alcohol and a carboxylate salt. Separately, X gives a positive iodoform test. What specific aldehyde is most consistent with ALL of these observations together?
options: Trichloroacetaldehyde, since it satisfies all three observations simultaneously without contradiction
Acetaldehyde, since it satisfies all three observations simultaneously without contradiction

This combination is contradictory and cannot describe a single real compound: a genuine Cannizzaro substrate (no alpha-hydrogen) by definition cannot simultaneously give a positive iodoform test, which specifically requires an alpha-methyl (CH₃CO−) group adjacent to the carbonyl
Benzaldehyde, since it satisfies all three observations simultaneously without contradiction
questions.explanation: A compound undergoing Cannizzaro reaction (rather than aldol condensation) must lack an alpha-hydrogen entirely; but the iodoform test's CH₃CO− requirement specifically NEEDS an alpha-methyl group (which inherently provides alpha-hydrogens). These two structural requirements are mutually exclusive for a single carbonyl carbon's immediate environment, so no single simple aldehyde can genuinely satisfy both the 'no alpha-hydrogen' (Cannizzaro) and 'positive iodoform' (requires CH₃CO−, hence alpha-hydrogens) conditions simultaneously — the given combination of observations is self-contradictory.
questions.hint: Carefully check whether the STRUCTURAL requirement for a positive Cannizzaro reaction (no alpha-hydrogen) can coexist with the structural requirement for a positive iodoform test (an alpha-methyl group, which has hydrogens).
distractor_logic: Trichloroacetaldehyde also correctly lacks an alpha-hydrogen (satisfying the Cannizzaro-related observations), but its CCl₃ group means it also has no CH₃CO− motif, so it too would give a NEGATIVE, not positive, iodoform test, failing to satisfy all three observations simultaneously.

Acetaldehyde DOES have alpha-hydrogens (on its methyl group) and would therefore undergo aldol condensation with dilute NaOH, NOT Cannizzaro reaction with concentrated NaOH as described; it does not satisfy the 'no reaction with dilute NaOH / Cannizzaro with concentrated NaOH' observation.

Benzaldehyde correctly satisfies the Cannizzaro-related observations (no alpha-hydrogen, reacts via Cannizzaro with concentrated base), but it does NOT give a positive iodoform test (it has no CH₃CO− or CH₃CH(OH)− motif at all), so it fails to satisfy all three observations together.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Rank {2,2,2-trifluoroacetaldehyde, acetaldehyde} in terms of rate of oxidation by Tollens' reagent, and separately compare the ACIDITY of their respective oxidation products, trifluoroacetic acid vs. acetic acid. Do both comparisons point in the SAME direction (i.e. does the more reactive aldehyde also give the more acidic acid product)?
options: Both aldehydes are oxidised at the same rate, and both resulting acids are equally acidic, so neither comparison shows any real trend

Yes: 2,2,2-trifluoroacetaldehyde is oxidised faster (its carbonyl carbon is more electrophilic due to fluorine's inductive withdrawal), and its oxidation product, trifluoroacetic acid, is also considerably MORE acidic than acetic acid, for the SAME underlying inductive-withdrawal reason applied to the carboxylate anion's stability
Fluorine substitution has no effect on either the aldehyde's oxidation rate or the resulting acid's acidity
No: the more reactive aldehyde gives the LESS acidic acid product, an inverse relationship
questions.explanation: Both comparisons trace back to the SAME inductive electron-withdrawal effect of the electronegative fluorines: this withdrawal increases the aldehyde's carbonyl-carbon electrophilicity (faster Tollens' oxidation) AND, once oxidised, it also stabilises the resulting carboxylate anion's negative charge (higher acidity for trifluoroacetic acid) — so both the reactivity trend and the acidity trend point in the same direction, consistent with the single shared underlying inductive mechanism established elsewhere in this chapter.
questions.hint: Apply the same unified inductive-withdrawal reasoning already established (which showed that the same substituent type increases BOTH carbonyl reactivity AND acid acidity) to this specific fluorine-substituted example.
distractor_logic: Fluorine substitution DOES measurably affect both properties (it is a strongly electronegative, electron-withdrawing substituent); the claim that both comparisons show no real trend, or that fluorine has no effect at all, is incorrect on both counts.

This is factually incorrect on both points; fluorine's inductive withdrawal is a well-established, significant electronic effect that measurably increases both the aldehyde's reactivity and the resulting acid's acidity, not a negligible one.

This claims an inverse relationship, but both properties are driven by the exact same inductive electron-withdrawal mechanism and are expected to move in the SAME direction (both increased) for this class of substituent, not opposite directions.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: A synthesis needs to convert hexan-2-one into hexan-2-ol using NaBH₄, and SEPARATELY convert hexanoyl chloride into hexanal using Rosenmund reduction, in the SAME overall multi-step project. Rank the ease (general reagent 'strength' typically required) of these two specific individual reduction steps relative to each other, and relative to reducing a plain carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol (which requires LiAlH₄).
options: The acid-to-alcohol reduction is the EASIEST of the three, requiring only the mildest reagent, NaBH₄, contradicting the established need for LiAlH₄

Both the ketone-to-alcohol (NaBH₄) and acid-chloride-to-aldehyde (Rosenmund, a specifically controlled catalytic hydrogenation) steps are comparatively 'easier' (achievable with milder or specifically tuned reagents) than the acid-to-primary-alcohol reduction, which requires the considerably stronger LiAlH₄, reflecting the carboxylic acid's own reduced electrophilicity (from resonance donation by its −OH oxygen) relative to a simple ketone or an activated acid chloride
Rosenmund reduction and NaBH₄ reduction of a ketone are mechanistically identical processes performed on different substrates for no meaningful reason
All three reductions require exactly the same reagent strength, with no meaningful distinction between them
questions.explanation: This reflects the general electrophilicity-tracks-reagent-strength theme established throughout this chapter: a simple ketone (moderately electrophilic) is reduced by the comparatively mild NaBH₄; an acid chloride (highly electrophilic, good leaving group) can be selectively stopped at the aldehyde stage using a specifically controlled catalyst (Rosenmund); but a carboxylic acid's own carbonyl carbon (LESS electrophilic than a simple ketone or aldehyde, due to its −OH oxygen's resonance donation) requires the considerably stronger LiAlH₄ to achieve full reduction to the primary alcohol at all.
questions.hint: Recall that a carboxylic acid's carbonyl carbon is actually LESS electrophilic than a simple ketone's, due to resonance donation from its own −OH oxygen, and connect this to why it needs a stronger reagent despite being a 'more oxidised' functional group.
distractor_logic: This reverses the correct comparison; the carboxylic acid reduction is in fact the HARDEST (requiring the strongest reagent, LiAlH₄) of the three, not the easiest, precisely because its carbonyl carbon is comparatively electron-rich (resonance-stabilised) relative to a simple ketone.

Rosenmund reduction (a specifically poisoned catalytic hydrogenation of an acid chloride, stopping at the aldehyde) and NaBH₄ reduction of a ketone (a hydride delivery to a fully intact ketone, going to the alcohol) are mechanistically distinct processes on different substrates, each chosen for a specific reason related to the substrate's own reactivity and the desired stopping point.

The three reductions genuinely require reagents of different strength (NaBH₄, a specifically poisoned catalyst, and LiAlH₄ respectively), reflecting real, meaningful differences in the electrophilicity/reducibility of each starting carbonyl species; they are not interchangeable or equally 'easy'.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: An unknown ketone gives a POSITIVE iodoform test. Two structural possibilities are considered: pentan-2-one (CH₃CO−CH₂CH₂CH₃) and 3-methylbutan-2-one ((CH₃)₂CH−CO−CH₃). Could EITHER structure be consistent with this single test result, and if so, how would you further distinguish them?
options: No, only pentan-2-one gives a positive iodoform test; 3-methylbutan-2-one gives a negative result

Yes, both have a CH₃CO− group and would give a positive iodoform test; distinguishing them would require additional structural information (e.g. from NMR or a specific derivative's melting point), since the iodoform test alone cannot differentiate isomers that share this same key structural motif
No, only 3-methylbutan-2-one gives a positive iodoform test; pentan-2-one gives a negative result
Neither compound gives a positive iodoform test, since both have more than 4 carbons
questions.explanation: Both pentan-2-one and 3-methylbutan-2-one have a methyl group directly bonded to the carbonyl carbon (CH₃CO−), satisfying the iodoform test's structural requirement regardless of what the OTHER side of the carbonyl carbon looks like (a straight-chain propyl group in one case, a branched isopropyl group in the other); the iodoform test alone, being sensitive only to this one specific motif, cannot distinguish between these two structurally different but similarly-substituted methyl ketones.
questions.hint: Check whether BOTH candidate structures share the exact same key structural feature (a methyl group directly on the carbonyl carbon), regardless of what else differs between them.
distractor_logic: 3-Methylbutan-2-one also has a methyl group directly on its carbonyl carbon (on one side), so it too gives a positive iodoform test; the premise that only pentan-2-one does is incorrect.
Pentan-2-one also has a methyl group directly on its carbonyl carbon, so it too gives a positive iodoform test; the premise that only 3-methylbutan-2-one does is incorrect.

Carbon count beyond the immediate CH₃CO− motif (5 carbons in both these examples) is irrelevant to the iodoform test; what matters is specifically whether a methyl group sits directly on the carbonyl carbon, which both of these structures satisfy.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Both (i) Tollens' oxidation of an aldehyde and (ii) hot alkaline KMnO₄ oxidation of an alkylbenzene ultimately give a carboxylic acid, but via very different mechanisms and starting materials. Contrast the SELECTIVITY of these two oxidation methods.
options: Neither oxidant can actually produce a carboxylic acid product from any of these starting materials
Both oxidants are equally mild and equally selective, with no meaningful difference in scope or strength
Tollens' reagent is the more vigorous, less selective of the two, while hot alkaline KMnO₄ is the milder, more selective oxidant, the reverse of the correct comparison

Tollens' reagent is a MILD, highly selective oxidant that reacts specifically with the aldehyde's own C−H bond, leaving most other functional groups (including alkenes and alkylbenzene side chains) untouched; hot alkaline KMnO₄ is a VIGOROUS, much less selective oxidant capable of directly attacking a benzylic C−H bond (shortening an entire alkyl chain down to −COOH) as well as other oxidisable groups
questions.explanation: Tollens' reagent's mechanism is narrowly targeted at the specific, uniquely reactive aldehyde C−H bond, making it a mild and highly functional-group-selective oxidant. Hot alkaline KMnO₄, by contrast, is a vigorous, general-purpose oxidant capable of attacking benzylic C−H bonds directly (cutting an entire alkyl side chain down to a single −COOH, regardless of its original length) as well as other oxidisable functionality — a fundamentally less selective, more forcing oxidative process than the aldehyde-specific Tollens' reaction.
questions.hint: Compare what STRUCTURAL FEATURE each oxidant specifically targets (a single, uniquely reactive C−H bond, versus an entire benzylic side chain more generally) to gauge relative selectivity.
distractor_logic: Both oxidants DO successfully produce a carboxylic acid product from their respective, appropriate starting materials (Tollens' from an aldehyde; hot alkaline KMnO₄ from an alkylbenzene); this is a standard, well-established outcome for each, not an impossibility.

The two oxidants differ substantially in both strength and selectivity (Tollens' mild and narrowly aldehyde-specific; hot alkaline KMnO₄ vigorous and much more broadly reactive), not equally mild/selective.

This reverses the correct comparison; Tollens' reagent is the MILDER, more selective oxidant (specific to the aldehyde C−H), while hot alkaline KMnO₄ is the more VIGOROUS, less selective one (capable of shortening an entire benzylic side chain), not the other way around.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Cyclohexanone is reduced by NaBH₄ noticeably faster than 2,2,6,6-tetramethylcyclohexanone (a ketone with two bulky methyl groups flanking the carbonyl carbon on each side). Explain this rate difference using the same reasoning already established for hindered aliphatic ketones like di-tert-butyl ketone.
options: The methyl substituents make the tetramethyl derivative's carbonyl carbon MORE accessible to hydride, which should speed up (not slow down) its reduction, contradicting the stated observation

The four methyl groups immediately flanking the carbonyl carbon in the tetramethyl derivative create significant steric hindrance, blocking the approach of the hydride nucleophile far more than cyclohexanone's comparatively unhindered ring carbons do, slowing the reduction considerably
Steric hindrance has no bearing on hydride reduction rates for cyclic ketones, unlike the previously discussed acyclic examples
Both ketones are reduced at identical rates, since they share the same basic cyclohexanone ring skeleton
questions.explanation: The two methyl groups on each of the carbons directly flanking the carbonyl in 2,2,6,6-tetramethylcyclohexanone create substantial steric crowding immediately around the carbonyl carbon, hindering the approach of the incoming hydride nucleophile considerably more than in plain cyclohexanone (whose flanking ring carbons bear only ordinary hydrogens); this is directly analogous to the steric hindrance reasoning already established for acyclic hindered ketones like di-tert-butyl ketone, and slows the NaBH₄ reduction correspondingly.
questions.hint: Apply the exact same steric-hindrance-slows-nucleophilic-addition reasoning already established for di-tert-butyl ketone, now to this specific cyclic, tetramethyl-substituted example.
distractor_logic: Bulkier substituents directly flanking the carbonyl carbon BLOCK, rather than facilitate, the approach of an incoming nucleophile like hydride, slowing (not speeding up) the reduction; this option describes the opposite of the actual steric effect.

Steric hindrance is a general structural effect on nucleophilic addition that applies to BOTH cyclic and acyclic ketones alike; there is no reason for this well-established principle to suddenly become irrelevant simply because the substrate is a ring system.

While both ketones do share the same basic 6-membered ring skeleton, the presence of four extra bulky methyl substituents immediately flanking the carbonyl carbon in one of them creates a real, structurally significant difference in steric environment, giving genuinely different (not identical) reduction rates.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Rank Tollens' reagent, PCC, and hot, acidified KMnO₄ in INCREASING order of general oxidising strength, and identify which is the SAFEST choice for selectively oxidising an aldehyde group to a carboxylic acid in a molecule that also contains an isolated, non-conjugated C=C double bond elsewhere.
options: PCC < Tollens' reagent < hot acidified KMnO₄; Tollens' reagent is the safest choice, since it is mild and specific to the aldehyde C−H bond, leaving the isolated alkene untouched (note PCC itself stops at the aldehyde stage rather than reaching the acid, so it would not achieve the desired oxidation level here at all)
All three reagents are equally strong oxidants with identical selectivity toward alkenes, so any of the three would work equally well here
None of these three reagents can oxidise an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid under any circumstances
Hot acidified KMnO₄ < Tollens' reagent < PCC, the reverse ordering of oxidising strength
questions.explanation: PCC is a mild oxidant specifically used to stop AT the aldehyde stage (from an alcohol), so it is not even the right tool to reach the acid from an aldehyde. Tollens' reagent is mild and aldehyde-C−H-specific, oxidising the aldehyde to the acid while leaving an isolated alkene untouched. Hot acidified KMnO₄ is the most vigorous, least selective of the three, likely also attacking the alkene. For the stated goal (aldehyde to acid, alkene untouched), Tollens' reagent is the appropriate, selective choice.
questions.hint: Recall each reagent's typical role: which one stops at an intermediate oxidation stage, which one is mild and functional-group-specific, and which one is a vigorous, general oxidant.
distractor_logic: The three reagents have distinctly different strengths and selectivity profiles (as established throughout this topic); they are not interchangeable, and only Tollens' reagent reliably avoids attacking the isolated alkene here.

Tollens' reagent (and, under different, more vigorous conditions, hot acidified KMnO₄) DOES oxidise an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid; this is a standard, well-established transformation for at least two of these three reagents.

This reverses the strength ordering; hot acidified KMnO₄ is the most vigorous of the three (not the weakest), and PCC (used to make aldehydes from alcohols, mild but not for oxidising aldehydes further) is not stronger than Tollens' reagent for this specific transformation.

questions.topic: Oxidation, Reduction and the Haloform Reaction of Aldehydes and Ketones
questions.question: Both NaBH₄ reduction (forming an alcohol) and 2,4-DNP condensation (forming a hydrazone) begin with a nucleophile attacking the SAME electrophilic carbonyl carbon of a given aldehyde or ketone. Would you expect a strongly ELECTRON-WITHDRAWING ring substituent (like −NO₂) to speed up or slow down BOTH of these reactions similarly, for the same substrate?
options: Speed up NaBH₄ reduction but slow down 2,4-DNP condensation, an opposite effect on the two reactions
Slow down both reactions similarly, the reverse of the correct direction

Speed up both reactions similarly, since both reactions' initial (and often rate-determining) step is nucleophilic attack at the same electrophilic carbonyl carbon, whose electrophilicity is increased by the same electron-withdrawing substituent in both cases
Have no effect on either reaction's rate, since ring substituents only affect oxidation reactions, not reduction or condensation reactions
questions.explanation: Both reactions share the SAME initial mechanistic event (a nucleophile, whether hydride or the hydrazine-type nitrogen of 2,4-DNP, attacking the electrophilic carbonyl carbon); an electron-withdrawing substituent like −NO₂ increases that carbon's electrophilicity regardless of which specific nucleophile is subsequently attacking it, so both reactions are expected to speed up similarly for the same substituted substrate, consistent with the unifying reactivity-trend reasoning used throughout this topic.
questions.hint: Both named reactions begin with the identical mechanistic step (nucleophilic attack at the carbonyl carbon); ask whether the electron-withdrawing substituent's effect on that shared step should differ depending on which specific nucleophile follows.
distractor_logic: Both reactions share the same rate-sensitive initial step (nucleophilic attack at the same carbonyl carbon), so there is no clear mechanistic reason for the SAME electron-withdrawing substituent to affect them in opposite directions; both should be accelerated similarly.

This reverses the well-established direction of the effect; an electron-WITHDRAWING substituent increases (not decreases) carbonyl electrophilicity, and hence is expected to SPEED UP (not slow down) both of these nucleophile-attack-initiated reactions.

Ring substituents affect the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon quite generally, influencing ANY subsequent nucleophilic attack at that carbon (whether by hydride in a reduction, cyanide in cyanohydrin formation, or a nitrogen nucleophile in a condensation reaction), not only oxidation reactions specifically.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Rank the following four acids in DECREASING order of acid strength: 2,2-dichloropropanoic acid, 2-chloropropanoic acid, propanoic acid, and 2,2,2-trifluoropropanoic acid's simpler relative, 3-chloropropanoic acid (i.e. rank: 2,2-dichloropropanoic acid, 2-chloropropanoic acid, 3-chloropropanoic acid, propanoic acid).
options: All four are equally acidic, since they share the same basic carbon skeleton and the same −COOH group
Propanoic acid > 3-chloropropanoic acid > 2-chloropropanoic acid > 2,2-dichloropropanoic acid
3-Chloropropanoic acid > 2,2-dichloropropanoic acid > 2-chloropropanoic acid > propanoic acid
2,2-Dichloropropanoic acid > 2-chloropropanoic acid > 3-chloropropanoic acid > propanoic acid
questions.explanation: TWO chlorines on the alpha-carbon (2,2-dichloro) withdraw more electron density inductively than a single alpha-chlorine (2-chloro), giving the strongest acidifying effect and highest acidity. A single alpha-chlorine (2-chloro, closer to −COOH) has a stronger effect than a single beta-chlorine (3-chloro, one carbon further away, per the standard distance-dependent inductive falloff). Plain propanoic acid, with no electron-withdrawing substituent, is the least acidic of the four.
questions.hint: Combine two separate distance/count principles: MORE electron-withdrawing atoms at the same position increase the effect further, and the SAME atom has a weaker effect the further it sits from −COOH.
distractor_logic: The four compounds differ measurably in both the NUMBER and POSITION of electron-withdrawing chlorine substituents, both of which measurably affect acidity through the inductive effect; they are not equally acidic despite sharing the same basic skeleton.

This is the exact reverse order; propanoic acid (no substituent) is the LEAST acidic, not the most, and the doubly-substituted 2,2-dichloro acid (strongest combined inductive effect) is the MOST acidic, not the least.

This misorders the singly-substituted acids relative to the doubly-substituted one; 3-chloropropanoic acid (a single, more distant substituent) should NOT outrank 2,2-dichloropropanoic acid (two substituents, closer to −COOH), which combines both a stronger position AND a doubled effect.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Comparing formic acid (HCOOH) with acetic acid (CH₃COOH), formic acid is MORE acidic. Using the SAME reasoning already established for why formaldehyde is more reactive toward nucleophilic addition than acetaldehyde, explain formic acid's greater acidity.
options: Formic acid's methyl-free structure makes its carboxylate anion LESS stable than acetic acid's, contradicting the stated greater acidity

This comparison is unrelated to the earlier formaldehyde/acetaldehyde reactivity comparison, since acidity and nucleophilic addition reactivity are governed by completely different, unconnected factors
Formic acid is not actually more acidic than acetic acid; the premise of the question is factually incorrect

Formic acid's carboxyl carbon has no alkyl group attached at all (just H), so there is no weak +I (electron-donating) alkyl contribution destabilising the carboxylate anion, unlike acetic acid, whose methyl group's mild electron donation slightly destabilises its own carboxylate anion, making acetic acid comparatively less acidic
questions.explanation: Just as formaldehyde's complete lack of any alkyl substituent makes its carbonyl carbon maximally electrophilic (most reactive toward nucleophiles, since there is no alkyl +I donation to offset the electron deficiency), formic acid's similarly complete lack of an alkyl substituent on its carboxyl carbon means there is no weakly electron-donating alkyl group to destabilise its carboxylate anion upon deprotonation; acetic acid's methyl group, by mild +I donation, slightly destabilises ITS OWN carboxylate anion in comparison, making acetic acid somewhat less acidic than formic acid.
questions.hint: Recall that alkyl groups are weakly electron-DONATING (+I); ask how the presence or absence of such a group would affect the stability of the negatively-charged carboxylate anion specifically.
distractor_logic: This reverses the correct stability comparison; formic acid's carboxylate (no destabilising alkyl +I donation) is MORE stable, not less, than acetic acid's (which does have a mildly destabilising methyl group), consistent with formic acid being the more acidic of the two.

This comparison is in fact directly, structurally analogous to the formaldehyde/acetaldehyde reactivity comparison (both cases hinge on the presence or absence of an alkyl group's weak electron-donating +I effect at the key reactive centre); the two phenomena share a genuine, instructive underlying connection, not an unrelated one.
Formic acid IS in fact measurably more acidic than acetic acid (pK₂ ≈ 3.75 vs. ≈ 4.76); the premise stated in the question is factually correct, not incorrect.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Two routes are used to prepare substituted benzoic acids: (i) oxidation of p-chlorotoluene (hot alkaline KMnO₄) to give p-chlorobenzoic acid; (ii) oxidation of p-methyltoluene (i.e. p-xylene, giving after mono-oxidation p-toluic acid). Predict which product is MORE acidic than plain benzoic acid, and which is LESS acidic, and why.
options: p-Chlorobenzoic acid is MORE acidic than benzoic acid (electron-withdrawing Cl, even para, stabilises the carboxylate somewhat via induction); p-toluic acid (4-methylbenzoic acid) is LESS acidic than benzoic acid (electron-donating methyl group destabilises the carboxylate slightly)
Neither p-chlorotoluene nor p-methyltoluene (p-xylene) can be oxidised to a carboxylic acid by hot alkaline KMnO₄ under any conditions
p-Chlorobenzoic acid is LESS acidic and p-toluic acid is MORE acidic than benzoic acid, the reverse of the correct pairing
Both products are exactly as acidic as plain benzoic acid, since neither substituent is close enough to the −COOH group to matter
questions.explanation: Chlorine, though it can donate weakly by resonance, is net electron-withdrawing overall (its strong inductive pull dominates), so p-chlorobenzoic acid is somewhat MORE acidic than plain benzoic acid. A methyl group is net electron-donating (weak +I/hyperconjugation, no competing strong inductive withdrawal), so p-toluic acid is somewhat LESS acidic than plain benzoic acid — matching the same general electron-withdrawing-increases-acidity / electron-donating-decreases-acidity principle used throughout this topic, now applied via aromatic ring conjugation from the para position.
questions.hint: Apply the same substituent-electronic-character-determines-acidity-direction reasoning already used for chlorine-substituted aliphatic acids, now to these two aromatic (para-substituted benzoic acid) examples.
distractor_logic: Both alkylbenzene precursors (p-chlorotoluene and p-xylene/p-methyltoluene) have benzylic hydrogens available and are readily oxidised by hot alkaline KMnO₄ to their corresponding substituted benzoic acids, as described; this is a standard, well-precedented reaction, not an impossibility.

This reverses both pairings; the electron-withdrawing chlorine substituent should INCREASE acidity (not decrease it), and the electron-donating methyl substituent should DECREASE acidity (not increase it), relative to plain benzoic acid.

Even from the para position, both substituents' electronic character (net withdrawing for Cl, net donating for methyl) DOES reach and measurably affect the −COOH group's acidity through the ring's conjugated system; they are not too remote to matter.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: The alpha-halo acid product of the HVZ reaction on acetic acid (giving chloroacetic acid, ClCH₂COOH) is subjected to a SECOND round of HVZ halogenation, giving dichloroacetic acid, Cl₂CHCOOH. Predict how each successive halogenation affects acid strength, and give the overall trend across acetic acid, chloroacetic acid, and dichloroacetic acid.
options: All three acids are equally acidic, since the number of alpha-chlorines does not affect the overall inductive effect on the distant carboxyl group
Acetic acid > chloroacetic acid > dichloroacetic acid, the reverse of the correct trend

Acetic acid < chloroacetic acid < dichloroacetic acid, since each additional electron-withdrawing chlorine on the alpha-carbon further stabilises the carboxylate anion, compounding the acidifying inductive effect
Only the FIRST chlorine substitution increases acidity; a second chlorine substitution at the same position has no further measurable effect at all
questions.explanation: Each additional electron-withdrawing chlorine at the alpha-carbon provides an ADDITIONAL increment of inductive electron withdrawal, further stabilising the resulting carboxylate anion's negative charge; acidity therefore increases progressively (though with somewhat diminishing marginal effect per additional chlorine) as more chlorines are added at the same position, giving the trend acetic acid < chloroacetic acid < dichloroacetic acid (and, following the same logic, trichloroacetic acid would be even more acidic still).
questions.hint: Each additional electronegative substituent at the same position adds MORE inductive withdrawal on top of what is already there, compounding (not cancelling) the acidifying effect.
distractor_logic: The NUMBER of electron-withdrawing chlorines at the alpha-position directly and measurably affects the total inductive withdrawal reaching the carboxyl group; more chlorines produce a stronger combined effect, so the three acids are not equally acidic.
This is the reverse trend; MORE electron-withdrawing chlorine substituents should INCREASE (not decrease) acidity, so dichloroacetic acid should be the most acidic of the three, not the least.

While the MARGINAL acidifying effect of each successive chlorine does tend to diminish somewhat, a second chlorine at the same position still provides a genuine, measurable ADDITIONAL increase in acidity, not zero further effect.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Cannizzaro reaction of benzaldehyde gives sodium benzoate (the salt of benzoic acid) as one product. Predict whether acidifying this sodium benzoate solution to liberate free benzoic acid changes the fundamental resonance-based ACIDITY explanation used elsewhere for why carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenols.
options: No: regardless of how a given sample of benzoic acid was originally generated (via Cannizzaro reaction, or via any other synthetic route), its acidity is an intrinsic property of its final STRUCTURE (the −COOH group and its resonance-stabilised carboxylate conjugate base), not of its synthetic history
Yes: benzoic acid produced via the Cannizzaro reaction is fundamentally MORE acidic than benzoic acid produced by any other method, due to some residual effect from the disproportionation mechanism
Benzoic acid produced via Cannizzaro reaction has no resonance-stabilised conjugate base at all, unlike benzoic acid made by other routes
Acidifying the sodium benzoate solution actually converts it back into benzaldehyde, not benzoic acid, reversing the entire Cannizzaro reaction
questions.explanation: Once formed, benzoic acid (or its sodium salt) is simply benzoic acid (or sodium benzoate); its acidity is governed entirely by its own structure — specifically, the same carboxylate resonance stabilisation (charge delocalised symmetrically over two equivalent oxygens) discussed throughout this topic — and is completely independent of whichever specific reaction (Cannizzaro disproportionation, oxidation of toluene, or any other method) was used to originally synthesise that particular sample.
questions.hint: A compound's intrinsic chemical properties, like acidity, depend only on its final structure, not on the specific reaction pathway used to make it.
distractor_logic: Acidity is an intrinsic structural property; it does not vary between otherwise-identical samples of the same compound based on which synthetic route was used to prepare them, so there is no meaningful 'Cannizzaro-derived' acidity boost.

Benzoic acid, however it was synthesised, has the same −COOH group and therefore the identical capacity for carboxylate resonance stabilisation upon deprotonation; there is no chemical mechanism by which its origin would remove this inherent structural feature.

Acidifying a carboxylate SALT (protonating the carboxylate anion, RCOO⁻ + H⁺ → RCOOH) regenerates the free carboxylic ACID, not the original aldehyde; this is simple acid−base protonation, not a reversal of the earlier oxidation/reduction (Cannizzaro) chemistry.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Both benzaldehyde's reduced electrophilicity (relative to an aliphatic aldehyde) toward nucleophilic addition, and benzoic acid's INCREASED acidity (relative to a simple aliphatic acid), might seem to be in tension, since both involve conjugation with an aromatic ring. Resolve this apparent tension.
options: There is no real tension: the ring's resonance DONATION reduces the neutral aldehyde's carbonyl electrophilicity (a donation-based effect suppressing a positive/electrophilic character), while for the acid, it is primarily the SAME ring's ability to further stabilise the NEGATIVELY charged carboxylate (via resonance/induction, working on an anion rather than a neutral electrophile) that governs acidity — two different effects (donation to a neutral species vs. stabilisation of an anion) that are not actually contradictory

Benzaldehyde is actually MORE electrophilic than an aliphatic aldehyde, and benzoic acid is actually LESS acidic than a simple aliphatic acid, both contrary to established fact, resolving the tension by simply reversing both premises
Aromatic rings have no measurable electronic effect on either reactivity or acidity in any case, making the entire comparison moot
This is a genuine, unresolved contradiction in the general theory of resonance effects on reactivity and acidity
questions.explanation: These are simply two different phenomena, each governed by how the aromatic ring's conjugation interacts with a DIFFERENT kind of adjacent group: for a neutral aldehyde, ring resonance DONATION into the electron-poor carbonyl carbon reduces its electrophilicity; for an ACID's already-formed carboxylate ANION, the ring's conjugated system (along with simple aromatic ring induction) can help further delocalise/stabilise that negative charge, contributing to increased acidity — there is no genuine contradiction, since the ring is interacting differently with a neutral electrophilic carbon versus an anionic, already-charge-bearing carboxylate group.
questions.hint: Consider that the aromatic ring is interacting with two DIFFERENT kinds of species in these two examples: a neutral, electron-poor carbonyl carbon in one case, and an already-negatively-charged carboxylate anion in the other.
distractor_logic: Both established facts (benzaldehyde's reduced electrophilicity, benzoic acid's context-dependent acidity behaviour relative to aliphatic acids) are well-documented and should not simply be reversed to force an artificial resolution; the actual resolution lies in recognising the two different mechanisms at play, not in denying the premises.

Aromatic rings DO have well-documented, measurable electronic effects on both reactivity (as with benzaldehyde's reduced electrophilicity) and acidity (as with various substituted benzoic acids' acidity trends); the claim that they have no effect at all is incorrect.

This apparent tension is fully resolvable once the two different underlying mechanisms (donation into a neutral electrophile, versus stabilisation of an existing anion) are properly distinguished; it is not a genuine, unresolved contradiction in resonance theory.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Predict and rank the acidity of pentanoic acid, 4-chloropentanoic acid, 3-chloropentanoic acid, and 2-chloropentanoic acid, all in one series, from MOST to LEAST acidic.
options: 2-Chloropentanoic acid > 3-chloropentanoic acid > 4-chloropentanoic acid > pentanoic acid
All four compounds are equally acidic regardless of chlorine position, since all ultimately belong to the same pentanoic acid family
4-Chloropentanoic acid > 2-chloropentanoic acid > 3-chloropentanoic acid > pentanoic acid
Pentanoic acid > 2-chloropentanoic acid > 3-chloropentanoic acid > 4-chloropentanoic acid
questions.explanation: The inductive electron-withdrawing effect of chlorine weakens progressively with distance from the −COOH group through the sigma-bond framework: closest (2-chloro, alpha-carbon) gives the strongest acidifying effect, followed by 3-chloro (beta), then 4-chloro (gamma, weakest of the three substituted positions but still more acidic than no substituent at all), with plain pentanoic acid (no substituent) the least acidic of the four.
questions.hint: Apply the same distance-dependent inductive falloff principle used consistently throughout this topic: the closer the electron-withdrawing group sits to −COOH, the stronger its acidifying effect.
distractor_logic: The four compounds are NOT equally acidic; both the presence and specifically the POSITION of the chlorine substituent measurably change the acidity through the distance-dependent inductive effect, even though all four share the same parent pentanoic acid skeleton and functional group.

This misorders the substituted acids, placing the most distant substituent (4-chloro) as the most acidic; the inductive effect weakens with distance, so 4-chloro should give the WEAKEST acidifying effect among the three substituted acids, not the strongest.

This is the exact reverse order; plain pentanoic acid (no electron-withdrawing substituent at all) is the LEAST acidic, not the most, and the substituent closest to −COOH (2-chloro) gives the STRONGEST acidifying effect and highest acidity, not the weakest.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: An unknown compound X gives a strongly positive result with aqueous NaHCO₃ (brisk effervescence) AND a positive iodoform test. Propose a single structure for X consistent with BOTH observations, and justify it.
options: Acetone alone is fully consistent with both observations, since ketones are always acidic enough to react with NaHCO₃
This combination of results is impossible, since a single molecule can never contain both an acidic −COOH group and a methyl-ketone-type CH₃CO− group simultaneously

Pyruvic acid, CH₃CO−COOH: the free −COOH group accounts for the NaHCO₃ effervescence, while the adjacent CH₃CO− (methyl ketone) portion of the SAME molecule independently accounts for the positive iodoform test
Acetic acid alone is fully consistent with both observations, since carboxylic acids always give a positive iodoform test as well
questions.explanation: Pyruvic acid (2-oxopropanoic acid), CH₃CO−COOH, contains BOTH a genuine −COOH group (acidic enough to release CO₂ from NaHCO₃) AND a separate CH₃CO− methyl-ketone unit (satisfying the iodoform test's structural requirement) within the same molecule, making it fully consistent with both observations simultaneously.
questions.hint: Consider a molecule that combines TWO different functional groups, each independently satisfying one of the two given test results.
distractor_logic: Plain acetone (CH₃COCH₃) does give a positive iodoform test, but being a simple ketone (not an acid), it is NOT significantly acidic and would NOT react with NaHCO₃ to release CO₂ gas; ketones are not generally acidic enough for this specific test.

Molecules containing both an acidic −COOH group and, elsewhere in the same structure, a separate CH₃CO− motif are chemically perfectly valid (pyruvic acid being a real, common example); this combination is not structurally impossible.

Plain acetic acid (CH₃COOH) is acidic (satisfying the NaHCO₃ test), but it has no CH₃CO−-adjacent methyl-ketone-type structural motif of the kind the iodoform test requires (its methyl is attached to the carboxyl carbon itself, not to a separate ketone carbonyl), and it in fact gives a NEGATIVE iodoform test; carboxylic acids do not automatically give a positive iodoform result.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Both a carboxylic acid's LOW carbonyl electrophilicity (toward simple nucleophilic addition) and its HIGH acidity (toward simple deprotonation) are explained by the SAME structural feature: the −OH oxygen's lone-pair resonance donation into the carbonyl group. Explain how one structural feature produces these two seemingly opposite-sounding consequences.
options: The −OH oxygen's resonance donation only affects acidity and has absolutely no bearing on the neutral acid's carbonyl electrophilicity at all
This is a genuine contradiction with no valid chemical resolution; a single structural feature cannot logically explain both effects
Both consequences are caused by completely different, entirely unrelated oxygen atoms within the −COOH group, not the same oxygen at all

The −OH oxygen's resonance donation makes the NEUTRAL carboxylic acid's carbonyl carbon electron-RICHER (less electrophilic, resisting simple nucleophilic addition); but ONCE deprotonated, that SAME donating oxygen (now as part of a fully formed, symmetric carboxylate anion, delocalising charge over both oxygens equally) provides exactly the resonance stabilisation that makes losing the proton in the first place so favourable (high acidity) — the donation matters differently for the intact acid's reactivity than for its already-deprotonated anion's stability
questions.explanation: The KEY is recognising that resonance donation from the −OH oxygen plays two DIFFERENT roles depending on the molecule's protonation state: in the NEUTRAL acid, this donation reduces the carbonyl carbon's electron deficiency (lowering electrophilicity, resisting ordinary nucleophilic addition); but the SAME donating capacity is what allows the TWO oxygens to become fully equivalent and share the negative charge symmetrically once the acid is deprotonated to the carboxylate anion (providing strong resonance stabilisation, and hence favouring that deprotonation, i.e. high acidity) — one structural feature, two related but genuinely distinct consequences depending on which species (the neutral acid, or its anion) is being considered.
questions.hint: Carefully distinguish what the resonance donation does to the NEUTRAL, intact carboxylic acid (before losing a proton) from what it does to the CARBOXYLATE ANION (after losing a proton) — these are two different molecular species.
distractor_logic: The same −OH oxygen's resonance-donating capacity IS directly relevant to the neutral acid's reduced carbonyl electrophilicity as well as to the anion's stability; it is not limited to affecting acidity alone.

This tension is fully and coherently resolvable (as described in the correct explanation) once the neutral-acid case is properly distinguished from the deprotonated-anion case; it is not a genuine, unresolvable logical contradiction.

Both consequences trace back to the SAME hydroxyl oxygen's lone pair and its ability to conjugate with the adjacent carbonyl system; they are not caused by two separate, unrelated oxygen atoms within the −COOH group.

questions.topic: Nomenclature, Structure and Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Rank benzoic acid, p-nitrobenzoic acid, p-chlorobenzoic acid, and p-toluic acid (4-methylbenzoic acid) together in ONE combined series, from MOST to LEAST acidic.
options: p-Toluic acid > benzoic acid > p-chlorobenzoic acid > p-nitrobenzoic acid
All four are equally acidic, since all are simply substituted benzoic acids sharing the identical −COOH group
p-Chlorobenzoic acid > p-nitrobenzoic acid > p-toluic acid > benzoic acid
p-Nitrobenzoic acid > p-chlorobenzoic acid > benzoic acid > p-toluic acid
questions.explanation: Ranking by the net electron-withdrawing/donating character of each para substituent: −NO₂ (strongest electron-withdrawer, by both induction and resonance) gives the highest acidity; −Cl (net electron-withdrawing, inductive effect dominating its weaker resonance donation) gives the next highest; plain benzoic acid (no substituent) is intermediate; −CH₃ (net electron-donating) gives the lowest acidity of the four.
questions.hint: Rank each substituent independently by its net electronic character (strongly withdrawing, mildly withdrawing, none, or donating), then order the four acids accordingly.
distractor_logic: This is the exact reverse order; the electron-donating methyl group (weakest acid) is placed first and the strongly electron-withdrawing nitro group (strongest acid) is placed last, the opposite of the correct ranking.

The four para substituents have measurably different net electronic effects (strongly withdrawing, mildly withdrawing, none, and donating respectively); they do not all leave benzoic acid's acidity unchanged.

This misorders chlorine and nitro; −NO₂ is a considerably stronger electron-withdrawer (by both induction and resonance) than −Cl (inductive withdrawal only, partly offset by weak resonance donation), so p-nitrobenzoic acid should outrank p-chlorobenzoic acid, not the reverse; this option also misplaces benzoic acid relative to p-toluic acid.
